days.title: Somebody Else Went First

body.p: Most of us begin a year by resolving. We decide what we will start, what we will stop, and how long we think we can hold it. By the second week the resolving is what has worn us out, not the thing we resolved.
The Bible opens on a beginning that is not ours. Before there is a person to make a resolution, there is God, already working, already moving over water that has no shape yet.
That order matters more than it looks. It means beginning is not something you originate out of nothing. It is something you join.
The earth in verse two is described as without form and void — not evil, not opposing, simply unformed. God does not condemn it. He moves over it and starts speaking.
Whatever your life looks like this morning, unformed is not a disqualification. It is the raw material the first chapter of the Bible is about.

line.a: You are not starting from nothing.
line.b: You are joining something already begun.

after: A year of holy habits does not begin with your willpower. It begins with the fact that God was working long before you woke up and will be working long after today's effort runs out.
Join it. That is a lighter thing to carry than starting it.
days.prayer: Father, before I resolve anything, let me remember that You began. Move over what is still unformed in me and speak. I would rather join Your work than manufacture my own.
days.question: What are you trying to originate on your own?

days.title: The Hour Nobody Saw

body.p: The night before, the whole city had gathered at the door. Mark says it plainly — all the city. Jesus healed until it was late and by any measure the day had gone well.
A great while before day. In the dark. Out to a solitary place. After the most successful evening of the chapter.

What strikes me is that nobody was there to see it. The crowd saw the healings. The disciples find him later and their first words are that everyone is looking for him. The prayer had no audience at all.
That is the shape of a habit as opposed to a performance. A performance needs a room. A habit happens whether or not anyone knows it happened.
And it is placed here on purpose: immediately after the success, not after a failure. The pressure to skip it came from things going well.

after: If your devotion only happens when someone would notice, it is not yet a habit. It is a performance with a religious subject.
He went out while it was still dark, and came back with a direction the crowd could not have given him.
days.prayer: Lord, build something in me that happens when no one is watching. Give me one hour that belongs to You and to nobody else, and keep me faithful to it on the mornings that went well.
days.question: Does your devotion need an audience?

days.title: He Had Always Opened That Window

body.p: The decree is signed. For thirty days, anyone who prays to any god or man except the king goes into the den of lions. Daniel holds one of the highest offices in the empire and has the most to lose.
As he did aforetime. Four words, and they are the whole story.
Daniel did not decide, in the crisis, to become a man who prays three times a day at an open window. He already was one. The decree changed the cost of the habit; it did not change the habit.

Which means the courage everybody remembers him for was not summoned that afternoon. It had been accumulating quietly, three times a day, for years, in an ordinary upstairs room, on days when nothing was at stake.
He did not have to find strength. He only had to keep doing what he was already doing.

line.b: It did not change the habit.

after: We tend to think the test reveals whether we have courage. More often it reveals what we have practised.
Build the habit now, while it costs you nothing. That is the only time it can be built cheaply.
days.prayer: God, let my faithfulness be settled before it is tested. Build in me the kind of ordinary consistency that will still be standing when it becomes expensive.
days.question: What would still be standing if it became costly?

days.title: Deciding Once So You Stop Deciding Daily

body.p: Joshua is old and near the end. He gathers the tribes and puts a choice in front of them, and the way he phrases it is worth noticing.
Choose you this day. Not choose every day. One decision, made once, on a particular afternoon, at a particular place, in front of witnesses.
There is a kind of exhaustion that comes from re-deciding the same thing every morning. Whether to pray. Whether this is worth it. Whether today counts. The deciding costs more than the doing.
Joshua's answer to that is to settle it. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord — stated in the present tense about the future, which is what a commitment is.
After that, the mornings are not decisions. They are simply what a person who decided does.

line.b: so you stop choosing every day.

after: Some of what you are calling weak discipline is actually an unmade decision being remade every twenty-four hours.
Make it once. Then the mornings get much quieter.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been renegotiating with You every morning and calling the tiredness weakness. Today I settle it. As for me and my house, we will serve You.
days.question: What are you re-deciding every morning?

days.title: Daily Was The Word He Chose

body.p: This verse is usually read as the hard one — deny yourself, take up your cross. It is hard. But the hardest word in it is the smallest.
Daily. Luke is the only gospel that includes it, and it changes the scale of the whole sentence.
A cross taken up once is a moment of drama. A cross taken up daily is a routine, and routines are made of ordinary Tuesdays, not of moments.
It also means the thing is repeatable. If it were once, missing it would be final. Daily implies tomorrow, which implies that today's failure is not the end of the arrangement.
There is mercy hidden in that word as well as weight. He is describing something you will have to do again, which is also something you get to do again.

after: Nobody follows Christ heroically for thirty years. They follow him on a Tuesday, and then on a Wednesday.
If you missed yesterday, the word daily has already made room for that.
days.prayer: Jesus, give me grace for today only. Not for the whole year, not for the version of me I wish I were — for this one day, and then teach me to come back tomorrow.
days.question: Are you trying to be faithful for a year or for a day?

days.title: And Will Look Up

body.p: David is describing a morning, and he describes it in three movements, each of which is deliberate.
My voice shalt thou hear. I will direct my prayer unto thee. And will look up.
The middle phrase is the one that gets lost in modern English. To direct is a word used for laying wood in order on an altar, or for setting out an argument. It is arrangement, not outpouring.
So the morning is not only saying things to God. It is putting them in order before Him — this first, then this, then this. Naming what the day holds rather than feeling generally anxious about it.
And then, having laid it out, he looks up. He watches for the answer. The prayer is not filed and forgotten by breakfast.

after: An unshaped dread handed to God at speed is better than nothing. But there is something steadying about setting the day out in front of Him piece by piece.
Then expect an answer. That is what looking up means.
days.prayer: Father, this morning I will not just spill my worry at You. I will set it out in order, name it plainly, and then watch for what You do about it.
days.question: Do you pray in the morning, or only react all day?

days.title: The Light That Keeps Getting Brighter

body.p: A week into a new habit is where the honest disappointment usually arrives. You expected to feel different by now, and you feel roughly the same.
The path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
That is a description of dawn, and dawn is the least dramatic light there is. Nobody can point at the moment it happened. You look up at some stage and notice the room is bright.
The proverb does not promise a flash. It promises a gradient — more and more — and it sets the destination a long way off, at the perfect day.
Which means a week in, feeling roughly the same, is exactly what the verse predicts. You are on the part of the curve that does not look like anything yet.

line.b: They notice the room is bright.

after: Growth you can feel day to day is usually emotion. Growth you can only see across years is usually formation.
Keep walking. The gradient is doing what it says.
days.prayer: Lord, I want to feel further along than I am. Give me patience with a light that grows slowly, and keep me walking on the mornings when nothing seems to be changing.
days.question: What are you giving up on because it is slow rather than because it is wrong?

days.title: Who Despises Small Days

body.p: The exiles have come home and started rebuilding the temple. The foundation is laid, and it is visibly smaller than the one the old men remember. Ezra records that some of them wept when they saw it.
For who hath despised the day of small things? The question is asked because somebody had.
It is easy to despise a small beginning, and the people most likely to do it are the ones who remember something bigger — a season when you prayed better, read more, felt more.
But the verse pairs that question with an image: the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel. A plumb line. The tool you use when you are actually building, not when you are reminiscing.
God is not comparing this foundation to the old one. He is checking whether it is straight.

line.a: They wept that it was small.
line.b: God was checking that it was straight.

after: Ten minutes prayed honestly today is a foundation. Comparing it to a season you remember is how people talk themselves out of laying one.
Small and straight beats large and remembered.
days.prayer: Father, I have been despising what I am able to give You today because I remember giving more. Let me build what I can build now, and let it be straight.
days.question: What are you refusing to begin because it would be small?

days.title: Every Morning, And It Melted

body.p: The manna arrives daily and comes with two rules that seem designed to frustrate a sensible person. Gather what you need for today. Do not keep any of it overnight.
Some of them tried anyway. It bred worms and stank.
And when the sun waxed hot, it melted. There was a window, and outside the window there was nothing to gather.
For forty years, this is how an entire nation was fed. Not with a storehouse. With a morning.
You cannot stockpile this. Sunday's sermon does not cover Wednesday. What you received in a good season is genuinely good and it is genuinely spent.
That is not stinginess on God's part. It is the mechanism by which a people learn, every single day for four decades, that they are being fed by someone.

after: The daily-ness that feels like inefficiency is the whole design. A God who filled your barn once would be a God you visited annually.
Go out this morning and gather. It is there.
days.prayer: Lord, I keep trying to store enough of You to last the week. Teach me to come out every morning and gather what You have put there for today.
days.question: What are you living on that you received months ago?

days.title: Rose Up Early

body.p: God asks Abraham for Isaac. It is the hardest sentence in Genesis and the text gives no record of the night that followed it.
Abraham rose up early in the morning. He saddled the donkey. He cut the wood. He took two young men and his son, and he went.
There is no speech. No wrestling recorded, no bargaining like the one he made over Sodom a few chapters earlier. Just a list of ordinary preparations done in order, early.
I have come to think the plainness is the point. When obedience is enormous, it still arrives as a series of small physical acts: get up, load the animal, cut wood, walk.
He could not do the whole thing that morning. Mount Moriah was three days away. He could only saddle a donkey.

line.a: He could not do the whole thing.

after: Whatever God has asked of you, today's portion of it is probably small and physical and unremarkable.
Rise early. Cut the wood. The three days will take care of themselves.
days.prayer: Father, I am overwhelmed by the size of what You have asked. Show me only this morning's part of it, and give me grace to get up and do that much.
days.question: What small first act have you been postponing?

days.title: They Kept Turning Up

body.p: Three thousand people are added in a day. It is the most dramatic growth in the New Testament, and what Luke describes next is remarkably undramatic.
They continued stedfastly. The word carries the sense of persisting, of attending to something with strength, of refusing to drift away from it.
And what they continued in is a short and ordinary list: teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers. No strategy. Four practices, repeated.

It is worth sitting with how unimpressive that list would look if you wrote it on a page today. Listen to teaching. Eat with people. Share a table. Pray. Nothing there requires talent, funding or a platform, and every item can be done by anyone on an ordinary weekday.
The verses that follow describe wonders, shared possessions, daily growth. But those are the fruit. Verse forty-two is the root, and the root is attendance.
They kept turning up to four ordinary things, together, for long enough that a city noticed.

after: The church that turned the empire over did not have a plan you could put on a slide. It had a habit list of four items and people who kept showing up to them.
Steadfastly is not a feeling. It is a diary.
days.prayer: Lord, make me steadfast in small ordinary things — the Word, Your people, the table, prayer. Let me keep turning up long after the feeling has gone.
days.question: Which of the four have you quietly dropped?

days.title: The Thing You Did At First

body.p: The letter to Ephesus opens with genuine praise. He commends their works, their labour, their patience, the fact that they cannot bear evil and have tested false apostles and have not fainted. By any external measure this is a strong church.
Thou hast left thy first love. Not lost — left. It is the word for departing from a place you were standing in.
And the remedy he gives is stranger than the diagnosis. Remember from where you have fallen, repent, and do the first works.
Do the things you did at the beginning. Not feel what you felt at the beginning — do what you did. The prescription for a cooled heart is an action, and specifically an old action.
That is unexpectedly practical. He does not tell them to work up the affection. He tells them to go back and repeat the early practices, and lets the affection follow the practice.

after: A first love is not recovered by staring at how cold you have become. It is recovered by doing the small early things again, deliberately, before you feel like it.
The feeling was never the engine. It was the exhaust.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I have not stopped working. I have left something, and I know it. Bring me back to the first works — the simple things I did when I loved You most — and let my heart follow my feet.
days.question: What did you do at the beginning that you have quietly stopped doing?

days.title: Shut Thy Door

body.p: Jesus has just described people who pray standing in the synagogue and on street corners, and he says something blunt about them: they have their reward. Not that they get nothing. That they get exactly what they were praying for, which was to be seen.

Enter into thy closet. The word is a storeroom — the small windowless room at the back where a household kept its supplies. It was chosen because it was the one room in a first-century house with a door and nothing interesting in it.
And shut thy door. That instruction is not about secrecy so much as about removing the audience, including the imagined one.
Most of us do not pray on street corners. We do something subtler: we pray while half-composing how we would describe the prayer. The door is for that.
What he promises the person behind it is not a better prayer. It is a Father who is there in secret, which is to say a relationship that does not require a witness to be real.

line.a: The door is not for secrecy.
line.b: It is for removing the audience.

after: A storeroom was the least spiritual room in the house. That is probably why he picked it.
Find your version of it, and shut the door on the version of yourself that is watching.
days.prayer: Father, I have prayed with one eye on how it sounded. Take me into the room with the door and meet me there, where there is nothing to perform and no one to impress.
days.question: Who are you still performing for when you pray alone?

days.title: By Taking Heed

body.p: The question in this verse is asked by someone young enough to have a lot of life in front of him and honest enough to know he cannot navigate it on instinct.
Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? The answer given is unglamorous: by taking heed thereto according to thy word.
Taking heed is a watchman word. It means paying attention on purpose, keeping your eye on something that would drift if you stopped looking.
Notice what the answer is not. It is not a single decisive experience, or a feeling, or a resolve made in a hard moment. It is sustained attention to a text.
Two verses later he adds the practice that makes it possible: thy word have I hid in mine heart. Hidden, in advance, before it was needed. You cannot take heed to something you have not stored.

after: A life does not usually go wrong at a crossroads. It drifts, in small increments, in the direction nobody was watching.
Taking heed is simply the decision to keep looking.
days.prayer: Lord, keep my eyes on Your Word rather than on my own instincts. Hide it in me now, before the day I need it, and teach me to pay attention on purpose.
days.question: Where has your life drifted because nobody was watching that part?

days.title: Both Men Heard It

body.p: The Sermon on the Mount ends with two builders, and the detail everybody remembers is the rock and the sand. The detail worth noticing is that both men heard the same sermon.
Whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them. The difference between the two houses is not information. It is not sincerity either. It is one verb.

And the houses look identical until the weather comes. Jesus is careful about this: the rain, the floods and the winds beat on both. The foundation is invisible in fair conditions and decisive in bad ones.
Which means you cannot tell, on a calm Tuesday, which kind of hearer you are. The two look the same from the outside and feel the same from the inside.
The only way to know is to check whether hearing has turned into doing anywhere in particular, this week, in something you could name.

after: Agreeing with a truth produces a warm feeling that is very easy to mistake for obedience.
Name one thing you heard recently and have not done. That is where the foundation is being poured or not poured.
days.prayer: Lord, I have heard a great deal and done less. Show me one thing I already know and have not obeyed, and give me the will to do it this week.
days.question: What have you agreed with but never acted on?

days.title: When Thou Sittest In Thine House

body.p: Moses is giving Israel the words they are to build a national life on, and having stated them, he immediately becomes practical about where they are to be said.
When thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
That is a list of four ordinary domestic moments, and between them they cover most of a day. Sitting, travelling, going to bed, getting up.
There is no religious hour in the list. No festival, no assembly, no priest. The instruction locates the words of God in the parts of life that have no ceremony attached to them at all.
And the verse before it puts them first in the heart of the person speaking. You cannot talk about them by the way if they are not already in you when you set out.

after: Faith that only exists in the religious hour is not being transmitted to anyone, least of all to the people who live with you.
Pick one of the four. Start there.
days.prayer: Father, let Your words be in my heart first, and then in the ordinary hours — the kitchen, the commute, the last thing at night. Make my faith audible where there is no ceremony.
days.question: Which four hours of your day never hear anything about God?

days.title: He Did Not Know Who Was Calling

body.p: The chapter opens with a line that explains everything after it: the word of the Lord was precious in those days, and there was no open vision. Precious meaning rare.
So when God calls Samuel by name, the boy assumes it is Eli. Three times. He is not being slow; he has never heard this before and has no category for it.
What changes is not Samuel's hearing. It is that an old man tells him what to say if it happens again, and gives him one sentence: Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth.
Two things are worth taking from that. The first is that recognising God's voice is learned, usually from somebody further along who has heard it before.

The second is that the sentence Eli teaches him is a posture, not a technique. It puts God in the position of speaking and Samuel in the position of listening, and it commits to the listening before the content arrives.

line.b: He had no category for it.

after: If you have never been sure whether God has spoken to you, that is not evidence against you. Samuel had the same problem in the same room as the ark.
Learn the sentence. Say it before you know what the answer will be.
days.prayer: Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening. I commit to the listening before I know what You will say, and I ask You to teach me Your voice.
days.question: Have you committed to obey before you know the content?

days.title: And I Knew It Not

body.p: Jacob is running. He has deceived his father, defrauded his brother, and left home with nothing. He stops at nightfall in an unremarkable place, uses a stone for a pillow, and sleeps.
Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.
He had already slept there. The ladder, the angels and the promise arrive at a location he had chosen for no reason except that the sun had gone down.
And the thing he says on waking is not about the vision. It is about his own not-knowing. God had been present in a place Jacob had assessed as nowhere.
He marks it with the stone he had been sleeping on. Same stone. He does not import anything; he sets upright the thing that was already there.

line.a: The Lord was in this place.

after: The places we file as nowhere — the commute, the ward, the year that went wrong — are not vacated by God because we have written them off.
Set up the stone you already have.
days.prayer: Lord, I have decided that certain parts of my life are nowhere. Open my eyes where I have already stopped looking, and let me find that You were there before I noticed.
days.question: Which part of your life have you assumed God has no interest in?

days.title: Sitteth Down First

body.p: Jesus is talking to a large crowd that is following him enthusiastically, and instead of consolidating the enthusiasm he tries to slow it down.
Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost.
Sitteth down first. Before the enthusiasm becomes a foundation, there is a chair and a calculation.

There is also a quiet mercy in being told to sit down. The crowd was moving and he stopped them. Nobody in that moment was told they were unwelcome; they were told to work out what following would cost before the enthusiasm made the decision for them.

And the failure he describes is not collapse. It is an unfinished tower with people walking past it — everyone that beholdeth it begins to mock him, saying, this man began to build and was not able to finish.
That is a particular kind of loss. Not a project that failed, a project abandoned at a visible height. It is what a January resolution looks like in March.

line.b: there is a chair and a calculation.

after: Deciding what you can actually sustain is not a lack of faith. It is the thing he told the crowd to do before following him.
Build a shorter tower and finish it.
days.prayer: Lord, save me from beginning what I have not counted. Show me what I can carry all year rather than what I can carry all week, and let me finish what I start.
days.question: What have you begun this month that you cannot sustain?

days.title: Let Us Rise Up And Build

body.p: Nehemiah arrives in Jerusalem and does nothing for three days. Then he goes out at night, alone, on one animal, and inspects the broken wall without telling anybody what he is doing.
Only after he has seen the whole ruin himself does he speak to the people.
And they said, Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work.

The order is worth keeping. Silence, then a night ride round the actual damage, then a plain account of it, then the call — and the response comes immediately because the people can tell he has seen it.
Vision that has not looked at the rubble does not move anyone. Nehemiah knew the size of the job before he asked anyone to join him in it.

line.a: He rode round the ruin first.
line.b: Then he said, let us build.

after: Before you rebuild anything — a marriage, a habit, a faith — go and look at the actual state of it in the dark, on your own, without softening it.
Then rise up and build. In that order.
days.prayer: Father, give me the courage to look honestly at what is broken before I announce that I am fixing it. Then strengthen my hands for the work.
days.question: What are you rebuilding without having looked at the damage?

days.title: Day And Night

body.p: The first psalm describes a blessed person by two things: where he does not stand, and what he does with his attention.
In his law doth he meditate day and night. The Hebrew word for meditate is used elsewhere of a lion growling over prey and of a dove murmuring. It is a low continuous sound, not silent contemplation.
So the picture is of someone muttering a text to himself through the day, turning it over, saying it under his breath.

And the tree that follows is planted by rivers — not near water, planted by it, deliberately positioned. Its fruit comes in season and its leaf does not wither, which is a description of consistency rather than intensity.
Nothing here is dramatic. A man with a phrase in his mouth all day becomes a tree that does not dry out.

line.b: A phrase in your mouth all day.

after: You are already meditating on something. Most of us run a low continuous commentary of worry or grievance without ever calling it that.
Change the text. The mechanism is already installed.
days.prayer: Lord, my mind is already turning something over all day. Let it be Your Word. Plant me where the water is and keep my leaf from withering.
days.question: What are you already meditating on without meaning to?

days.title: Heartily, As To The Lord

body.p: Paul is writing to slaves, which makes this one of the most uncomfortable passages in the letter and also one of the most radical.
Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
Whatsoever is doing a lot of work. He is not describing religious activity. He is describing tasks that were, by any measure, unchosen and unrewarded.

He also names the payer. Ye serve the Lord Christ, he writes in the next verse, to people who served somebody else all day and were paid by nobody. The wage is not withheld; it is simply issued by a different house.
And he relocates the audience. The work is unchanged; the person it is done for changes. That is the only variable Paul adjusts, and he treats it as sufficient.
Heartily is literally from the soul. It is the opposite of doing something at the minimum acceptable standard because nobody who matters is looking.

line.b: The person it is done for does.

after: Most of a life is unglamorous and unwitnessed. This verse says that is not a lower category of existence.
Do today's ordinary thing as though it were handed in to God, because it is.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been doing my work at the standard the watching person requires. Let me do it from the soul, as to You, in the hours nobody is assessing.
days.question: Which task are you doing at the minimum because nobody checks?

days.title: If We Faint Not

body.p: Three weeks into a new pattern is where the arithmetic starts to feel wrong. You have put in more than you have got back, and the ledger is visible.
Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
There are two conditions in that sentence and they are easy to blur. Due season is the first — the harvest has a date and the date is not ours to set.

Paul is writing to people who had begun well and were being pulled elsewhere, which is why the verse is set among instructions about sowing. Sowing is the least rewarding stage of farming. Nothing about the act itself tells you whether it worked.
If we faint not is the second. The word means to lose heart, to slacken, to give out. Paul is not warning about failure. He is warning about quietly easing off.
Which tells you what the danger actually is at this point in a habit. Not collapse. Attrition.

after: Sowing and reaping are separated by a season, and the gap is not evidence that the sowing failed. It is what a season is.
Do not decide the harvest is not coming while you are standing in the field in February.
days.prayer: Father, I am tired of putting in more than I can see coming back. Keep me from quietly easing off. I will sow again today and leave the season to You.
days.question: Where are you easing off rather than stopping?

days.title: Two Minds

body.p: James is describing someone asking God for wisdom, which is a good thing to ask for, and he attaches an unexpected warning to it.
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways. The word is literally two-souled, and it appears to have been coined for this letter.
The image before it is a wave driven with the wind and tossed — not a wave that is sinking, a wave that is going wherever the last gust sent it.

What makes this bracing is the phrase in all his ways. Two-mindedness about one thing does not stay in its lane. It leaks into everything, because a person who has not settled the central question cannot settle the smaller ones either.
The remedy in the passage is not more effort. It is asking in faith — settling whose you are, and then asking from that position.

line.a: Not a wave that is sinking.
line.b: A wave going wherever the wind sent it.

after: Instability is usually downstream of an unsettled question rather than of weak character.
Settle the central thing. The smaller decisions get much easier once it is settled.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been two-minded and calling it open-mindedness. Settle me. Let me ask You in faith rather than drifting with whatever moved me most recently.
days.question: What central question have you left open?

days.title: Teach Us To Number Them

body.p: This is the oldest psalm in the collection, attributed to Moses, and it is unsparing about how short a life is. Our years are spent as a tale that is told.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Numbering is an odd request. He does not ask for more days, or for the days to be easier. He asks to be taught to count what he has.
And the reason given is entirely practical: that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. Counting is not for melancholy. It is so that the heart gets applied to something worth applying it to.
A person who thinks time is unlimited postpones. A person who has counted spends differently, and the psalm treats that as a skill to be taught rather than a mood to be caught.

line.a: He does not ask for more days.
line.b: He asks to be taught to count them.

after: You will not drift into a well-spent year. Nobody has.
Count the weeks that are actually left in this season, and let the number decide something.
days.prayer: Teach me to number my days, Lord. Not to frighten me, but so that I stop postponing what I already know matters, and apply my heart to what is worth it.
days.question: What would you change if you counted the weeks?

days.title: Lay Aside The Weight

body.p: The chapter before this is the long list of people who lived by faith and mostly did not receive what was promised. Chapter twelve begins by putting the reader inside the same race.
Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience.
Two things are laid aside and they are not the same thing. There is sin, and there is weight — and weight is not described as sinful. It is described as heavy.
A runner strips off what is merely extra. Not wicked, not shameful. Extra. Commitments, possessions, arguments, subscriptions to other people's opinions of you.
And then, having stripped, run with patience — a phrase that sounds contradictory until you notice the race is described as the one set before us, not the one we would have chosen.

line.b: Weight is not sinful. It is heavy.

after: Some of what is slowing you down this year is not wrong. It is simply extra, and it is still slowing you down.
Name one weight. Put it down. It does not have to be a sin to be laid aside.
days.prayer: Lord, show me the difference between what is sinful and what is merely extra, and give me the freedom to put down things that are not wrong but are not mine to carry.
days.question: What is not wrong, but is slowing you down?

days.title: Shall Ye Not Know It

body.p: Isaiah is speaking to people in exile, to whom the past was better and the present is a desert, and the promise he brings has a question buried in the middle of it.
Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?

That question is not decorative. He is asking whether they will recognise it, and the answer is genuinely in doubt — because the verse before says forget the former things, and people looking backwards do not see forwards.
The new thing is described as springing forth, which is what a seed does. Small, low, easy to walk past.
And the location is the wilderness. He does not promise to take them somewhere better and then act. He promises a road in the place they are already standing.

after: A new thing that arrives small in a hard place is very easy to miss if you are still comparing everything to the old thing.
Look down. Springing forth starts at ground level.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been looking backwards and calling it faithfulness. Open my eyes to the small new thing already springing up in the dry place I am standing in.
days.question: What are you missing because you are comparing it to before?

days.title: Forgetting Those Things Which Are Behind

body.p: Paul has just listed his credentials and then written them off. What follows is the only sentence in his letters where he says explicitly that he has not arrived.
This one thing I do: forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.
Forgetting here cannot mean amnesia. He remembers his past well enough to have catalogued it three verses earlier. It means refusing to let it set the terms of what comes next.
And what is behind includes the good parts. Paul is not only laying down his failures; he is laying down a résumé that would have impressed anyone in the room.
This one thing I do. After a life of that size, the summary is a single sentence with one verb in it.

line.a: He is not only laying down failure.
line.b: He is laying down his résumé.

after: The past that most often stops people is not shame. It is a season that went well, held up as the standard everything since has failed to match.
One thing. Reaching forward. That is the whole instruction.
days.prayer: Father, I keep measuring today against a version of my life that is finished. Help me lay down what is behind — the failures and the successes — and reach forward.
days.question: Which past season are you still measuring yourself against?

days.title: A Time To Every Purpose

body.p: The list that follows this verse is famous and is usually read as poetry about life's variety. Read in context it is doing something harder than that.
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.

The pairs that follow are not all pleasant. A time to kill, a time to break down, a time to lose, a time to cast away. The Preacher is not describing a balanced life; he is describing one you do not control.
Which lands strangely in the middle of a month about building habits. A habit is an attempt to impose regularity on time. Ecclesiastes says the seasons are already appointed and not by you.
Both are true, and holding them together is the discipline. Build the practice. Hold the timetable loosely. The season you are actually in may not be the one you planned for.

after: A rigid plan meeting an unexpected season usually breaks the person rather than the plan.
Ask what season you are actually in, and let the practice fit it rather than fighting it.
days.prayer: Lord, You appoint the seasons and I do not. Let me keep building faithfully while holding my plans loosely, and give me the honesty to see which season I am actually in.
days.question: Are you building for the season you are in or the one you wanted?

days.title: He Withdrew Himself

body.p: A leper has been cleansed, the news has spread, and Luke says great multitudes came together to hear and be healed. The demand is at its highest point so far in the gospel.
And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.
The tense in Greek is continuous — he was withdrawing, repeatedly, as a practice. Luke is not reporting one afternoon. He is describing what Jesus habitually did when the crowds grew.

Luke has already shown us what the pressure looked like. Men were tearing a roof apart to get to him; a whole city had gathered at a door the chapter before. Against that, withdrawing looks almost irresponsible, and he did it anyway.
Which is the opposite of the instinct. Growing demand normally produces more availability, not less.
There is no note that anyone was turned away permanently or that the ministry suffered. The withdrawing is presented as ordinary, unexplained and repeated, in the same breath as the multitudes.

after: If you only get alone with God when nothing is happening, the busiest seasons of your life will be the least accompanied.
He did it when it was least convenient, and did it often enough that Luke used a continuous tense.
days.prayer: Jesus, teach me to withdraw when the demand is highest rather than when it finally slackens. Make it a habit rather than a rescue.
days.question: Do you get alone with God only when life goes quiet?

days.title: He That Began It Will Finish It

body.p: A month of beginnings ends here, and by the last day of January most people have already broken something they meant to keep. That is the ordinary arithmetic of resolutions and it is worth naming.
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
Note who the subject is. Paul is not confident in the Philippians. He is confident in the one who began the work, which takes the weight of the sentence off them entirely.
The month opened in Genesis with a beginning that was not ours. It closes with a completion that is not ours either. Between those two facts sits everything we have tried to build this month.
Which does not make the habits pointless. It makes them a response rather than a foundation. You are not holding this together. You are keeping step with someone who is.

line.a: He is not confident in them.
line.b: He is confident in the one who began.

after: If January went well, it was not your discipline that started it. If January went badly, your discipline is not what will finish it.
The good work has an author and a completion date, and neither of them is you.
days.prayer: Father, You began this work and You will finish it. Where I have kept my word this month, thank You. Where I have broken it, hold me anyway, and lead me into February.
days.question: Are you holding this together, or keeping step with someone who is?

days.title: Somebody Loved First

body.p: A month about love usually starts by asking people to produce some. Be kinder. Forgive faster. Try harder with the person you find difficult. Most of us have been given that instruction often enough to know it does not generate anything.
We love him, because he first loved us. The sentence has a direction, and the direction is the whole doctrine.
John does not command love here. He explains where it comes from, which is somewhere other than the person being asked to show it.

That matters practically. If love originates in you, then running out of it is a character failure and the only remedy is effort. If it originates elsewhere, running out is a supply problem, and the remedy is to go back to the source.
Most people trying to love a difficult person are attempting to manufacture something they were meant to pass on.

after: This month will ask hard things of you about people. None of it starts with your reserves.
Receive first. Everything after that is overflow rather than output.
days.prayer: Father, I have been trying to produce love out of an empty tank and calling the exhaustion failure. Let me receive from You first, and love people out of what You have given rather than what I can generate.
days.question: Are you manufacturing love or passing it on?

days.title: Fearfully, And Wonderfully

body.p: There is a kind of self-dislike that has learned to sound like humility. It says small things about itself and calls it not being proud, and it is very hard to argue with because it looks like a virtue.
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Notice who is being praised. The verse is not a compliment to David. It is worship, and the thing being worshipped is God's workmanship.
Which is why the self-dislike does not survive contact with it. To say I am nothing much is not modesty about yourself; it is a review of somebody else's work.
The psalm goes further than most of us are comfortable with. Covered in my mother's womb. Written in thy book. In continuance fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
You were not assembled at speed out of leftover parts. Whatever you have concluded about your worth, it was reached without consulting the person who made you.

line.b: A review of someone else's work.

after: Self-worth in this psalm is not achieved and it is not earned. It is inherited from the fact of being made deliberately.
Praise Him for it. That is the only posture the verse offers.
days.prayer: Lord, I have said small things about myself and called it humility. Teach me to see Your workmanship where I have only seen my faults, and to praise You for how I was made.
days.question: What have you concluded about your worth without consulting God?

days.title: Suffereth Long

body.p: This chapter is read at weddings, which has quietly softened it. Paul wrote it to a church that was suing each other, splitting into factions and competing over spiritual gifts.
Charity suffereth long, and is kind. The first word describes waiting under something without retaliating. The second describes being actively good to the person you are waiting under.
Read the list that follows and notice how much of it is negative. Envieth not. Vaunteth not. Is not puffed up. Doth not behave itself unseemly. Seeketh not her own. Is not easily provoked.
More than half of the definition is things love does not do. That is a strange way to describe an emotion, and a very useful way to describe a practice.
You cannot make yourself feel patient. You can decline to retaliate today, which is what suffering long actually consists of.

line.b: is things love does not do.

after: If love were a feeling, this chapter would be describing something you cannot be commanded to produce.
Most of it is restraint, and restraint is available to you this afternoon.
days.prayer: Lord, I cannot feel my way into patience with this person. Help me instead not to retaliate, not to keep score, not to say the accurate wounding thing — and let that be love until the feeling follows.
days.question: Which item on Paul's list are you failing today?

days.title: A Great Way Off

body.p: The son has rehearsed a speech. He has it word for word — I am no more worthy to be called thy son, make me as one of thy hired servants — and it is a good speech, honest and appropriately ashamed.
But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him.
Saw him first. Which means the father had been looking down that road, habitually, for long enough to recognise a silhouette at distance.
And then the father runs. In that culture an older man gathering his robes and running was undignified, and Jesus puts it in on purpose.

The son gets through about half his speech. The father interrupts him with instructions about a robe and a ring and shoes — not one of which the son asked for, all of which restore him as a son rather than hire him as a servant.
The speech was not wrong. It was simply answering a question the father had never been asking.

after: Some of us have been rehearsing an apology for years and have never come up the road to deliver it.
He is already looking. He will interrupt you.
days.prayer: Father, I have been rehearsing what I would say to You instead of coming home. I am coming. Interrupt me with mercy before I finish explaining myself.
days.question: What speech have you been preparing instead of coming home?

days.title: As I Have Loved You

body.p: He calls it a new commandment, which is odd. Loving one another was already in the law — Leviticus had said love thy neighbour as thyself centuries earlier.
What is new is the standard. Not as thyself. As I have loved you.
And he says it in a room where he has just washed their feet, including the feet of the man who is about to sell him, an hour or so before he is arrested.
So the measure is not an abstraction. They had watched it that evening, in a basin, on the floor.

It is a harder commandment than the old one, and also a clearer one. Loving your neighbour as yourself requires you to work out what you would want. Loving as he loved requires you to remember what he did.

after: The new standard is higher, but it is also more concrete. You are not guessing at a level.
Ask what he did in the room that night, and do the equivalent for one person this week.
days.prayer: Jesus, You set the measure by kneeling in front of men who would fail You that night. Give me the humility to love at that level with somebody I would rather not serve.
days.question: What would loving them as he loved you look like this week?

days.title: Go Yet, Love Her

body.p: Hosea is the most uncomfortable book in the prophets because the prophet is not given a sermon to preach. He is given a marriage to live, and it is a marriage that keeps failing publicly.
Go yet. Two words carrying an entire second act. He has already done this once, and he is being sent again.
And the instruction is not go and rebuke her, or go and be reconciled if she has changed. It is love her, stated as an action he is to perform toward someone who is currently in another man's house.
The next verse is stranger still. He buys her back — fifteen pieces of silver and a quantity of barley, which is roughly the price of a slave, scraped together in cash and grain.
God says the whole arrangement is a picture: according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods.

after: This is not a passage about staying in danger, and it has been misused that way. It is about what God's love costs Him.
He went yet. He is still going yet, in your direction, having done it before.
days.prayer: Lord, I do not deserve a second sending and You have sent Yourself again. Thank You for a love that goes yet, and let me be honest about how much it has cost You.
days.question: Where has God come after you more than once?

days.title: They Seemed But A Few Days

body.p: Jacob agrees to work seven years for Rachel. Seven years is a long time to be paid nothing, in a foreign country, for an uncle who will later cheat him.
And they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
That is not a statement about how time works. Seven years took seven years. It is a statement about what love does to the experience of cost.
Most of what we call sacrifice in relationships is really accounting — a private tally of what has been given and what has come back. The tally is usually accurate and it is always corrosive.
Jacob is not keeping one. The years are real, the labour is real, and he is not adding them up.
The verse is placed just before the deception that costs him seven more. He works those too.

after: The question is not whether you are giving more than you receive. In most seasons of most relationships, somebody is.
The question is whether you are keeping the ledger.
days.prayer: Father, I have been keeping an accurate and quietly bitter account of what I have given. Take the ledger. Let me serve without counting the years.
days.question: Who are you keeping a private tally against?

days.title: Whither Thou Goest

body.p: Naomi has lost her husband and both sons, and she does the decent thing: she releases her daughters-in-law. Go back to your mothers, find husbands, do not tie your life to mine.
Orpah goes, and the text does not blame her. She is doing exactly what she was told.
Ruth is a Moabite. She is committing to a bitter widow, an unfamiliar country, a foreign God and no visible future, and the language she uses is covenant language.
Where thou lodgest. Thy people. Thy God. Where thou diest, will I die. It escalates from address to identity to death, in one breath.
Naomi's response is recorded plainly: when she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her. She stopped arguing. There are commitments that end a conversation.

after: Loyalty that only holds while it is convenient is not loyalty; it is agreement. Ruth shows up when the sensible advice is to leave.
Somebody near you has been released by everyone. Go back.
days.prayer: Lord, make me the kind of person who stays when leaving would be understandable. Show me who has been quietly released by everyone else, and send me to them.
days.question: Who has everyone else reasonably walked away from?

days.title: Knit With The Soul

body.p: David has just killed Goliath, and the person with the most to lose from it is Jonathan. He is the king's son and the natural heir, and the crowd is already singing that David has killed more than his father.
The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David. Knit is a weaving word — two things bound so that pulling one moves the other.
And then he does something with his clothes. He strips off his robe, his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle, and gives them to David.
Those are not gifts. That is the wardrobe of a crown prince, and handing it to the man the country is singing about is an abdication performed in public.
Jonathan loved the person who cost him the throne, and the text records no bitterness about it anywhere in the chapters that follow.

line.a: He had the most to lose.

after: Rivalry is the ordinary response to somebody who is gaining what you wanted. Jonathan is in scripture partly to show it is not the only one.
There is somebody whose rise has cost you something. Bless them out loud.
days.prayer: Father, deal with the rivalry in me toward the person who is getting what I wanted. Let me love them honestly rather than tolerating them politely.
days.question: Whose success has quietly cost you something?

days.title: Tenderhearted

body.p: Paul has spent the previous verses listing what to put away: bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, evil speaking, malice. It is a precise list and most of it describes how people talk.
Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Tenderhearted is the word that stands out. It is a physical term — well-disposed in the gut — and it names something that bitterness slowly removes.
You can be technically forgiving and completely hard. Most long-running family arrangements run on exactly that: no active hostility, and no tenderness left either.
And the standard at the end is not proportional. Not forgive as much as they deserve. As God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you, which is a debt nobody in the sentence can calculate.

after: Hardness is the settlement most families reach when forgiveness has been declared but never felt.
Ask for tenderness back. It is a slower repair than forgiveness and a more thorough one.
days.prayer: Lord, I have forgiven this person and I am still hard toward them. Give me back a soft heart, not because they have earned it but because You have not withheld one from me.
days.question: Who have you forgiven without softening?

days.title: While We Were Yet

body.p: Paul is building an argument about assurance, and he does it by fixing the timing of the cross rather than its meaning.
While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
The word yet is doing everything. Not after we repented. Not once we had shown promise. While — during, in the middle of, at the time when nothing had improved.
Which settles a question most people carry quietly: whether God's affection is a response to progress.

Paul frames it as a demonstration — God commendeth his love toward us. It is exhibited, put on display, at the least deserving moment available, so that the moment can never be used as evidence against you.
If He loved you then, the case for Him loving you now does not rest on how this week has gone.

after: Most self-condemnation is an argument that God's love is conditional on a trajectory.
The cross happened at the low point on purpose. It was dated deliberately.
days.prayer: Father, I keep trying to earn back something that was given while I was at my worst. Settle it in me: You loved me then, and this week has not changed the arrangement.
days.question: Do you believe God's love is responding to your progress?

days.title: Many Waters

body.p: The Song is a love poem and it is unembarrassed about being one. Near the end it stops describing and makes a claim.
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
The verse before compares it to a seal, to death, to the grave, to coals of fire — a most vehement flame. This is not sentimental language. It is language about things that do not let go.
And then the strangest line: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned. Offering to buy it is not merely refused. It is despised.
Which means love in this poem cannot be purchased and cannot be extinguished, and those two facts belong together. Whatever cannot be bought cannot be drowned either.

after: Marriages and friendships go through water. The poem does not deny the flood; it denies the flood's power to finish the thing.
Whatever you are in the middle of, waters and quenching are different verbs.
days.prayer: Lord, the water has been high for a long time in this relationship. Let me believe that many waters cannot quench what You have joined, and hold on through the flood.
days.question: What are you assuming the flood has already finished?

days.title: The Third Time

body.p: Peter denied him three times beside a fire of coals. In this chapter there is another fire of coals on a beach, and John mentions it deliberately.
Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me?
Three questions for three denials. Jesus does not raise the denials once. He does not require an account of that night, or an explanation, or a promise it will not happen again.
He asks one question about affection, three times, and after each answer gives Peter work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep, feed my sheep.

That is the restoration. Not a lecture, not a probation, not a reduced role. The same commission, issued in the place where the failure happened, over a fire that would have smelled exactly like the one in the courtyard.
Being grieved was part of it. Jesus let him feel it and then handed him sheep anyway.

after: Restoration in this passage is not the removal of the memory. Peter never stops knowing what he did.
It is being given the work back, by the person you failed, in the place you failed.
days.prayer: Jesus, You know all things. You know that I love You, and You know exactly how I have failed. Restore me the way You restored him — not with a lecture, but with work to do.
days.question: Do you believe you can be trusted with the work again?

days.title: She Loved Much

body.p: A woman with a bad reputation comes into a Pharisee's dinner uninvited and begins washing Jesus' feet with her tears. The host says nothing out loud, but Jesus answers what he is thinking.
He points out what the host did not do. No water for the feet. No kiss. No oil for the head. The basic courtesies were all withheld, politely.
Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.
Read carefully, the logic runs the other way from how it sounds. She is not forgiven because she loved. She loves because she has grasped the size of what she was forgiven.
And the warning is aimed at the respectable man at the table. Little forgiven, little love — not because his debt was smaller, but because he had never counted it.

line.a: She did not love her way in.

after: Cold affection toward God is very often a symptom of an uncounted debt rather than of a hard heart.
The dinner host was not hostile. He was simply unmoved, and Jesus treated that as the more dangerous condition.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been polite with You and unmoved. Show me the actual size of what You have forgiven me, and let the love follow the counting.
days.question: Has your debt to God ever been counted, or only assumed to be small?

days.title: As Thyself

body.p: A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest, expecting a debate. Jesus gives him two, and the second one contains an assumption that is easy to walk past.
Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
The standard for how you treat other people is how you treat yourself, and it is stated without comment, as though the second half were obviously fine.
For a lot of people it is not fine. If the internal voice is contemptuous and unforgiving, that measure will export accurately — impatience with your own failure becomes impatience with theirs.
This is not a licence for self-absorption; the commandment is aimed outward. But it does mean that how you speak to yourself at two in the morning is not a private matter.
It sets the exchange rate for everyone you meet.

after: People who cannot forgive themselves are usually generous in theory and severe in practice, and they cannot work out why.
The measure is the same instrument. Fix the instrument.
days.prayer: Father, the voice I use on myself is not one I would use on anyone I loved. Change it — not so I can think more of myself, but so there is something worth exporting.
days.question: Would you speak to a friend the way you speak to yourself?

days.title: He Will Joy Over Thee With Singing

body.p: Zephaniah is a short and largely furious book. Two and a half chapters of judgement, and then this, without much warning.
He will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
Most people can believe God tolerates them. Some can believe He forgives them. Very few carry around a picture of God enjoying them.

The phrase in the middle is the one that undoes the argument. He will rest in his love — the word suggests being quiet, ceasing from something. God is described as settled about you, not still deliberating.
And then singing. Not speaking, not pronouncing. The prophet reaches for the least official verb available and puts it in God's mouth.
That is written to a people who had earned two and a half chapters of judgement, which is the only reason it is worth anything.

after: If your picture of God's face when He thinks of you is neutral at best, this verse is a correction and not a decoration.
He is settled about you. That is what resting in his love means.
days.prayer: Father, I have believed You put up with me. Teach me that You rest in Your love and rejoice over me, and let that change how I come to You today.
days.question: What do you imagine God's face does when He thinks of you?

days.title: Graven Upon The Palms

body.p: Zion has just made an accusation, and Isaiah records it without softening: the Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me.
God's answer begins with the strongest human bond available. Can a woman forget her sucking child? And then concedes the point — yea, they may forget.
Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.
Graven is not written. It is cut, incised, carved into a surface that will not release it. You do not erase an engraving; you would have to remove the hand.
And the placement is deliberate. Palms are what you see when you open your hands to work, which means the memory is not stored somewhere and retrieved. It is in front of Him constantly.
Christian readers have never quite been able to read that verse without thinking about what was eventually driven through those palms.

after: The complaint that opens this passage is allowed to stand. God does not tell Zion she is wrong to feel forgotten; He tells her what is on His hands.
Being forgotten is a feeling. Being engraved is a fact.
days.prayer: Lord, I have felt forgotten and I have said so. Thank You that You did not rebuke the complaint but answered it. Let me live from what is carved into Your hands.
days.question: Where have you concluded that God has forgotten you?

days.title: What Manner Of Love

body.p: John writes this as an old man, decades after the events he witnessed, and the sentence still has an exclamation in it.
Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God.
What manner of is an old phrase for what country is this from — the sense is of something foreign, unlike anything produced locally.
And the result is a name rather than a feeling. Called the sons of God. Adoption in the Roman world was a legal act that transferred inheritance and could not be reversed by the child's behaviour.
John then adds a clause most of us skip: therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not. Being loved like this makes you slightly illegible to people who have not encountered it.
He is warning them that the family resemblance will not read as impressive from outside.

line.b: And a name you cannot lose.

after: Adoption language is chosen over friendship language on purpose. Friends can drift. Sons inherit.
Behold it. John's first instruction here is simply to look at it for a while.
days.prayer: Father, help me stop and look at this rather than agreeing with it in passing. I am called Your child. Let that be the thing I am most certain of today.
days.question: Do you live as an employee of God or a child of God?

days.title: Greater Love Hath No Man

body.p: This verse is on war memorials, which is right but incomplete. In its own setting it is said at a dinner table, hours before the speaker demonstrates it.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.

The next sentence is the surprising one. Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you — and then, two verses later, he stops calling them servants and calls them friends because he has told them everything.
A servant knows the task. A friend knows the reason. That is the distinction he draws, and he moves them across it deliberately on the last night.
Laying down a life is the headline. But the friendship it is offered inside is defined by disclosure — by being told what the master is doing and why.

after: Most of us relate to God as servants: keeping the instructions and never asking what they are for.
He has already moved you. The category changed on the last night.
days.prayer: Jesus, You called Your disciples friends and told them everything. Let me stop relating to You as a servant with a task list and come as someone You have taken into Your confidence.
days.question: Are you God's servant or God's friend in practice?

days.title: At All Times

body.p: Proverbs is mostly practical and occasionally devastating in a single line. This is one of the short ones and it makes two claims.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
At all times is the test. Not at convenient times, not during the interesting part of your trouble, not for the fortnight when everyone is rallying.
Most support is intense and brief. The proverb is describing the person still there in month nine, when the crisis has become a condition and nobody is asking about it any more.
The second half turns it around. A brother is born for adversity — the relationship exists for the hard part, not despite it.
Which raises an uncomfortable question, since the verse can be read as a description or as a job specification.

after: Think of somebody whose crisis stopped being news. That is where this proverb is asking you to be.
Adversity is what the relationship was born for. It is not the interruption to it.
days.prayer: Lord, make me a friend who is still there in the ninth month, when the crisis has gone quiet and everyone else has moved on. Bring one name to mind and let me act on it today.
days.question: Whose long trouble have you stopped asking about?

days.title: Esau Ran To Meet Him

body.p: Jacob has stolen the blessing and fled. Twenty years later he is coming home and hears that Esau is riding to meet him with four hundred men, which is not a welcome party.
He spends the night in dread. He divides his family into groups so that if one is attacked the other might escape. He sends waves of gifts ahead. He bows to the ground seven times as he approaches.
And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.
Every part of the reunion Jacob had rehearsed turned out to be unnecessary. The gifts, the strategy, the choreographed bowing — none of it was what Esau had come for.
Twenty years of imagined confrontation, and the actual meeting takes one verse and four verbs, all of them physical, none of them planned.

after: Reconciliation is often less dramatic than the version we have been carrying, and it is nearly always delayed by the version we have been carrying.
You do not know what the other person has done with those years.
days.prayer: Father, I have rehearsed a confrontation for years and it has kept me away. Give me the courage to approach, and surprise me with what You have been doing in them.
days.question: What reunion have you delayed by imagining it?

days.title: Forbearing One Another

body.p: Paul is describing what the church is to put on, and he uses clothing language throughout — bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering.
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any.
Two separate instructions sit side by side and they are often confused. Forgiving deals with what has been done. Forbearing deals with what a person is simply like.
Some of what wears you down about someone is not sin and never will be. It is temperament, pace, volume, the way they tell a story. There is nothing to forgive because nothing wrong has happened.
Forbearance is the word for carrying that without commentary. It assumes ongoing friction as the normal condition of people living close together, rather than a problem to be solved.
And the clause at the end fixes the measure again: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.

line.a: Forgiving deals with what was done.
line.b: Forbearing deals with what they are like.

after: Trying to forgive a personality is a category error, and it exhausts people who are genuinely trying to do the right thing.
Some things are not to be resolved. They are to be carried.
days.prayer: Lord, teach me the difference between what I must forgive and what I must simply carry. Give me grace for the friction that is not sin and will not change.
days.question: What are you trying to forgive that is really just a difference?

days.title: Charity Shall Cover

body.p: Peter is writing to scattered churches under pressure, and his instruction for that situation is not strategy. It is what they are to have among themselves, above all things.
And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.
Fervent is an athletic word — stretched out, strained, at full extension. It is not a warm feeling; it is effort held at the limit.
And cover is not the same as excuse. It is closer to what you do with something that would shame a person if it were left in the open.
There is a version of honesty that is really exposure — accurate, defensible, and destructive to somebody who is already sorry.
Peter says a church survives pressure by covering rather than displaying, and puts it above all things, ahead of every other instruction in the paragraph.

after: The thing you know about them is probably true. That is not the question.
The question is whether telling it serves anyone but you.
days.prayer: Lord, I have called exposure honesty. Give me love that covers rather than displays, and keep me from saying the accurate thing that would only wound.
days.question: What true thing are you about to repeat about someone?

days.title: When My Father And Mother Forsake Me

body.p: This psalm is confident for nine verses — the Lord is my light, whom shall I fear, though an host encamp against me. Then it names the one thing the confidence had been built over.
When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up.
The verse assumes it as a possibility rather than a hypothetical. David does not say if. He builds the sentence on when.
That is unusual honesty in a hymn. The relationships that are supposed to be unconditional are the ones people are most ashamed to admit have failed.
Take me up is a word used for gathering something in — the way you would collect a person who had been left somewhere.
Nothing here says the forsaking did not matter, or that God is a replacement for what was owed to you. It says only that the gathering happens after it, and by someone else.

after: Not everyone reading this had parents who stayed. The psalm does not ask anyone to pretend otherwise.
The word is gathered. Somebody comes and collects what was left.
days.prayer: Lord, You know who was meant to hold me and did not. I bring the whole of it to You. Gather me up, and heal what that absence taught me about myself.
days.question: What did their leaving teach you about your worth?

days.title: In Honour Preferring One Another

body.p: Paul writes a run of short instructions here with almost no connecting argument, which makes each one land on its own.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another.
The second phrase is the striking one. Preferring is a word about going first — leading the way in showing honour, getting there before the other person does.

It is worth noticing where Paul places this. The verse before is about love without dissimulation, and the one after is about not being slothful in business. He treats honouring people as ordinary work, sitting between sincerity and diligence rather than among the spiritual gifts.
So it describes a race in which the aim is to be first to esteem somebody else. That is a competitive instinct pointed in an unusual direction.
Most groups run the opposite race. Recognition is scarce, so people wait to be acknowledged before acknowledging, and everyone ends up waiting.
Paul's instruction breaks the deadlock by telling you to lose that race on purpose, repeatedly, first.

after: Waiting to be appreciated before appreciating is the most common and least discussed cause of coldness between people who like each other.
Go first. It costs nothing except the satisfaction of being right about who owed whom.
days.prayer: Father, I have been waiting to be seen before I would see anyone else. Let me go first this week — with honour I do not owe, to someone who has not earned it.
days.question: Who are you waiting to be acknowledged by?

days.title: Love Your Enemies

body.p: This is the hardest sentence Jesus ever spoke to ordinary people, and it is worth noticing how practical he makes it.
Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
Four verbs, and not one of them is a feeling. Love, bless, do good, pray. Every item is something you can perform this week without any change in how you feel about the person.
The reason he gives is family resemblance: that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven, who sends rain on the just and the unjust.
God's kindness is not distributed on merit and never has been. The weather is the evidence.

Praying for someone is the item most people skip, and it is the one that changes the person praying. It is very difficult to keep a settled contempt for somebody you are genuinely asking God to bless.

line.b: Not one of them is a feeling.

after: He does not ask you to feel warmly toward them. He asks you to act, and to pray, and lets the rest follow or not.
Start with the prayer. It is the one that works on you.
days.prayer: Father, You send rain on people who curse You. I am naming the person I resent, and I am asking You to bless them — not because I feel it, but because You told me to.
days.question: Could you pray honestly for their good today?

days.title: Perfect Love Casteth Out Fear

body.p: John has been writing about confidence in the day of judgement, and he makes a claim about the relationship between two things most people carry at once.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment.
Casteth out is a forceful phrase — the same kind of word used of driving something from a house. The two do not negotiate; one displaces the other.
And the clause at the end names the mechanism. Fear hath torment, and the word means punishment. The fear John is describing is specifically the fear of being punished.
Which is why love drives it out rather than courage doing so. You cannot brave your way past the suspicion that God is holding something against you. You can only be convinced otherwise.
He that feareth is not made perfect in love — not a rebuke, a diagnosis. Where fear remains, love has not finished its work.

after: Anxiety before God is not usually a failure of nerve. It is an unfinished conviction about how He feels toward you.
The remedy is not to try harder to be unafraid.
days.prayer: Father, my fear of You is really a fear of punishment. Finish Your work in me. Let Your love drive out what my willpower has never managed to argue away.
days.question: Are you afraid of God, or afraid of being punished?

days.title: With An Everlasting Love

body.p: Jeremiah is the prophet of the exile, and most of his book is loss. This chapter is the exception, and the verse is placed among people who have every reason to think the relationship is over.
Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
Everlasting runs in both directions. It has no start date, which means there was no point at which God began — no moment when you qualified, and therefore no moment when you could stop qualifying.
Therefore is the hinge. Because the love is everlasting, the drawing happens. The pull you feel toward God is downstream of a decision made before you existed.
And lovingkindness is the covenant word, the one used of loyal love that keeps its commitments when the other party has not.
Two verses later He is talking about vineyards being planted again. The love comes first; the rebuilding follows it.

after: If God's love began at some point because of something, it could end at some point because of something.
Everlasting removes both ends of that sentence.
days.prayer: Lord, You loved me before there was any of me to love, and You have drawn me with kindness rather than force. Settle that in me where I still suspect I am on probation.
days.question: When do you think God started loving you?

days.title: Nor Anything Else

body.p: Paul ends the chapter with a list, and the list is not rhetorical. Tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword — he had experienced most of them personally by the time he wrote it.
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

He goes through the categories methodically. Death and life. Angels and principalities. Things present and things to come. Height and depth. Then, having run out, he adds a catch-all: nor any other creature.
That last phrase exists because Paul knew his list could not be complete. Somebody would eventually face a thing he had not named, and he closes the gap in advance.
Note also what is absent. He never says these things will not happen. Verse thirty-six quotes a psalm about being killed all the day long.
The promise is not protection from the list. It is that nothing on the list, named or unnamed, can get between you and the love.

line.a: He does not promise the list will not come.
line.b: He promises it cannot separate you.

after: A month about love ends here on purpose. Everything else in February can be lost — relationships, reputation, the way you feel about yourself.
The one thing on this page that cannot be taken is the last verse of Romans 8.
days.prayer: Father, I have feared that something would eventually separate me from You. Paul could not name it and neither can I. Hold me in the love that nothing on any list can reach.
days.question: What are you afraid would finally separate you from God?

days.title: The Weight Was Never The Problem

body.p: There is a way of carrying something heavy badly, and anyone who has ever moved a wardrobe knows it. The weight is not what breaks your back. The angle is.
The invitation is to people who labour and are heavy laden, which is a specific description. Not people in crisis. People carrying something ordinary for a long time.
And what he offers is not the removal of the load. He offers a yoke, which is a piece of farm equipment for pulling. He is proposing that you keep working.

But a yoke is built for two animals, and the whole craft of making one is distributing weight so the beam sits where the shoulders can take it. A badly made yoke will destroy an ox carrying a light load. A well made one lets it pull all day.
He says his is easy, and the word means well fitted. Not light. Fitted.

line.a: He did not offer to take the load.
line.b: He offered to take the other side.

after: Most of what exhausts us is not the size of the thing. It is carrying it at an angle we were never built for, alone, at a pace nobody set for us.
The offer is a better harness and company in it.
