Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God.
Not laying again the foundation. He names the basics — repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, eternal judgement — and declines to rebuild them.
A foundation relaid every year is not a deeper foundation. It is a building site.
And that is the danger for anyone who has spent a month on renewal. It is possible to keep starting, sincerely, and never to go on.
Let us go on unto perfection. The word is maturity, completeness — arriving at what something was made to be rather than achieving flawlessness.
April ends by refusing to begin again. Everything laid this month was laid so that something could be built on it.

after: Repeated fresh starts can be a way of avoiding the harder work of going on from where you already are.
Do not lay it again. Build.
days.prayer: Lord, I am good at starting and I have laid this foundation more than once. Let me go on from here instead of beginning again, and build something that lasts.
days.question: Are you starting again to avoid going on?

days.title: Purpose Before You Feel Ready

body.p: Jesus does not say try to be salt. He does not say that one day, once you have grown up a little, you may become light. He says Ye are the light of the world.

Look at who was listening. Fishermen, a tax collector or two, sick people who had followed him up the hill, and a crowd that had not yet seen the cross or the empty tomb. None of them were ready. He named them anyway.

Purpose here is not a reward handed out after training. It is a description of what you already are because of whose you are. Salt is salt before it touches the meat. The lamp is lit before anyone sets it on the stand.
The only question the passage leaves open is where the lamp sits. Nobody lights a candle to put it under a bushel. Readiness is not really the issue here. Placement is.
So the nurse starting her first night shift, nervous and checking every chart twice, is already light in that ward. She does not have to feel it to be it.

line.a: You keep waiting to become light.
line.b: He has already said you are.

after: Feeling ready usually arrives after obedience, not before it.
Wherever you are standing this morning is a candlestick, not a bushel.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, you called me light before I had done anything to earn the name. I confess I keep waiting to feel ready. Help me believe what you have said about me, and stop hiding the little light I have under my excuses. Put me where I can give light to someone in the house today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you waiting to feel before you will let your light be seen?

days.title: Purpose In the Next Step

body.p: There is an odd turn in the middle of verse sixteen. People are meant to see your good works, and yet they are meant to praise someone else for them.

That is the strange shape of the purpose Jesus describes. You do the work in plain sight, and the credit travels straight past you to your Father which is in heaven. A lamp is only noticed because of what it lets you see.
Notice too how small the room is. The candle on its stand lights all that are in the house. Not the city, not the nation. The house. Purpose usually begins within arm's reach.

Then Jesus adds, I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. He was not starting something unrelated to what God had already been doing. He was finishing it. Your next step is rarely a clean break from everything before it. It is usually the next faithful piece of the same story.
Perhaps it is fixing your neighbour's broken gate, or helping a younger colleague with a report and not mentioning it in the meeting. Small, visible, and not about you.

after: Do the good thing in front of you, and let the thanks go upward.
The house you are in today is a large enough place to shine.
days.prayer: Father, I want my good works to point to you and not to me. Keep me from needing the credit. Show me the next small step in the house where you have placed me, and let whoever sees it think of you. Thank you that Jesus came to fulfil and not to destroy, and that he finishes what he starts. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who is in your house today that needs the light you could give?

days.title: Purpose When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: Paul has just said Not of works, and in the very next breath he says we were created unto good works. The order matters. Works do not make us his. Being his produces the works.
The word workmanship means something made with care, like a carved chair or a length of woven cloth. You are not a rough draft that God is still unsure about.

And the works themselves were prepared ahead of time. God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Walk is a quiet verb. Nobody walks dramatically. You put one foot down, then the other, on ground somebody else levelled first.

Verse eleven tells the Ephesians to remember where they came from. They were outsiders, called names by people who thought themselves closer to God. The quiet road was laid for people like that, not for people who had earned it.
So when the week feels flat, when you are queueing at the bank or sitting in traffic on the way to a job nobody praises, you are not off the path. You may be standing exactly where it was laid.

line.a: You did not build the road.
line.b: You only have to walk it.

after: Quiet days are still days on a prepared path.
Being his workmanship means you do not have to prove you were worth making.
days.prayer: Father, thank you that I am your workmanship and not my own project. On quiet days when nothing seems to happen, help me trust that you prepared good works for me to walk in. Keep me walking, one ordinary step after another, and keep me from boasting when the path goes well. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What prepared good work might be sitting on your ordinary path this week?

days.title: Purpose Without an Audience

body.p: These words were first read aloud to slaves. That is worth sitting with before anything else. Paul is speaking to people whose work belonged to someone else and was rarely thanked.
He names a temptation they knew well, eyeservice. Working hard while the master is looking, easing off the moment he leaves the room. It is a very human way to survive, and Paul does not mock it.
Instead he changes the audience, telling them to do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. The person checking your work may not be fair. The One watching it always is.

He also promises them something no earthly master could give, the reward of the inheritance. Slaves could not inherit anything. Paul says these ones would. Their unseen labour was being recorded in a place no one could take from them.

Think of the cleaner who mops the hospital corridor at three in the morning, when no supervisor walks through. If she does it heartily, it is done as to the Lord. That corridor has an audience after all.

line.a: Eyes on you change how you work.

after: The work nobody checks is still work done for someone.
You serve the Lord Christ in the boring hours as much as in the visible ones.
days.prayer: Lord Christ, I confess I work harder when people are watching. Free me from eyeservice. Let me do today's tasks heartily, the ones no one will notice and the ones no one will thank me for, because you see them. Comfort everyone whose labour is unseen and unfairly treated today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which part of your work do you only do well when someone is looking?

days.title: Purpose For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: Before the famous promise comes a quieter warning. All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes. Every plan looks good to the person who made it.

That is why verse three matters. Commit thy works unto the LORD. The Hebrew word behind commit carries the picture of rolling something heavy off your own back onto someone else's. It is not a signature on a form. It is a transfer of weight.
And notice what gets steadied. Not your works first, but your thoughts. You hand him the doing and, somehow, the thinking becomes less frantic. thy thoughts shall be established.

None of this needs a special day. Tuesday is full of works. Emails, school runs, a meeting about a budget, a pot on the stove. Each one can be rolled onto him before it is begun, a short sentence breathed while the kettle boils.
And because the Lord weigheth the spirits, he is not fooled by the plan that only looks clean. That is a mercy, not a threat. He can show you what you could never see in your own reflection.

line.a: Your plans look clean to you.
line.b: Roll them onto someone who can weigh them.

after: Commit the next task before you start it, not after it goes wrong.
Steady thoughts are often the fruit of handed over work.
days.prayer: Lord, my ways always look clean to me, and you know how often I am wrong. I roll today's work onto you, each small task as it comes. Weigh my motives honestly and steady my anxious thoughts. Let this ordinary day be lived in your hands and not only in mine. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What task on today's list have you not actually handed to God yet?

days.title: Purpose When Plans Change

body.p: Proverbs never tells you to stop planning. A man's heart deviseth his way is simply a description, and there is no rebuke in it. Planning is part of being made by a God who plans.
But look at the two different sizes in the verse. The man devises a way. The LORD directs steps. We think in roads and destinations. God works in footfalls.

That is why plans change and purpose does not. The road you drew may bend. The job may fall through, the visa may be refused, the wedding date may move. Yet each step on the bent road is still directed.

Verse eight sits just before it like a guard at the gate. Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. When plans collapse, the temptation is to grab the shortcut. The proverb says a smaller life lived honestly is the better one.

Maybe you are on a bus home from an interview that did not go your way, already rewriting the plan in your head. Rewrite it. Just hold the pencil loosely, and expect the next step to be given rather than forced.

after: A changed plan is not a lost purpose.
Choose the honest little over the dishonest much.
days.prayer: Lord, I made plans and some of them have fallen apart. I am disappointed and I will not pretend otherwise. Direct my steps on this changed road. Keep me from shortcuts that cost my integrity, and teach me to plan with an open hand. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which changed plan are you still trying to force back into its old shape?

days.title: Purpose In the Work at Hand

body.p: God speaks of before. Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee. Jeremiah answers with now. I cannot speak: for I am a child.
That is the whole conversation in miniature. We judge our purpose by what we can see in ourselves today. God speaks from a place that existed before we had a body to judge.

Jeremiah's protest is not wicked. It is honest. He was young, the nations were large, and the message would be hard to carry. God does not scold him for feeling small. Read a verse further and you find God simply keeps talking, and reaches out to touch his mouth.
Being known first changes the work at hand. You do not need to prove your worth in the task, because your worth was settled before the task existed. You only need to do the task.

A young teacher facing a class of forty, a first time supervisor on a building site in Abuja, a mother with a newborn at two in the morning. Each can say what Jeremiah said, that they are too young for this. And each is already known.

line.a: You say you are too young.
line.b: He says he knew you before you were born.

after: Your adequacy was never the foundation of your calling.
Do the work at hand as someone already known.
days.prayer: Lord God, like Jeremiah I look at myself and say I cannot. You look further back and say you knew me. Help me hear your before louder than my now. Give me courage for the task in front of me today, and give me words when mine run out. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you letting your present weakness outvote the God who knew you first?

days.title: Purpose When You Need Clarity

body.p: The order in this chapter is easy to miss. First the coal touches Isaiah's lips and his sin is purged. Only then does he hear the voice asking Whom shall I send.
God does not issue a command. He asks a question into the room, as if he is waiting to see who will answer. Isaiah, freshly forgiven, answers before he knows the assignment. Here am I; send me.
Then comes verse nine, and the assignment is hard. Go and speak to people who will hear and not understand. Isaiah's clarity was never about outcomes. It was about who had sent him.

When we ask God for clarity we usually mean a map with the ending marked in red. What Isaiah received was simpler than a map. He knew he was forgiven, and he knew who was speaking. That was enough to go.

If you are lying awake asking which way to turn, start where Isaiah started. Let yourself be forgiven first. The question of sending sounds very different to someone whose lips have just been touched.

line.a: You want to know how it ends.
line.b: He tells you who is sending.

after: Forgiveness tends to come before assignment, not after it.
You can say Here am I without knowing every detail of where.
days.prayer: Holy God, I keep asking for a clear map. Touch my life first with your forgiveness, and let me hear your voice more clearly than my fears. If you are asking who will go, give me the courage to answer even before I understand what it will cost. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you asking God for clarity about the outcome, or about who is sending you?

days.title: Purpose One Choice at a Time

body.p: Peter starts with the least glamorous gift of all. Use hospitality one to another. Before prophets and preachers, he mentions the person who opens the door and puts the rice on.
And he adds two words that anyone who has hosted will recognise, without grudging. Hospitality offered with a sigh is still hospitality, but Peter wants something better for us than that.

Then he says every man hath received the gift. Every one. Nobody in the church gets to say they have nothing to give. The grace of God is manifold, a word with the sense of many coloured, so the gifts do not all look alike.

A steward does not own what he handles. He chooses, day by day, how to use what belongs to someone else. That is how purpose works here, one choice at a time. Serve, if you serve, with the ability which God giveth, not the ability you wish you had.
It might be one choice in the next hour. A neighbour knocks just as you sit down to eat. The steward's choice is small, and it is real.

line.a: The gift was never yours to keep.
line.b: It is yours to hand on.

after: Every choice to serve is a small act of stewardship.
Give with the strength God gives today, not the strength you had last year.
days.prayer: Gracious God, thank you for the gifts you have placed in my hands, even the ones I think are small. Make me a faithful steward today. Help me open my home and my time without grudging, and serve with the strength you give, so that you are glorified and not me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What gift have you been treating as your own rather than as something entrusted to you?

days.title: Purpose Under Pressure

body.p: Paul does not say we are members of the church. He says we are members one of another. That is a far more personal sentence. Your hand belongs to my body, and mine to yours.
Under pressure that truth gets lost. We start to believe that if anything is going to get done, we will have to do all of it ourselves. Preach, teach, comfort, organise, and pay for the fuel.

Paul answers with a phrase that sounds almost restful. let us wait on our ministering. Stay with your piece. If you teach, teach. If you serve, serve. Gifts are differing according to the grace that is given to us, which means you were never meant to carry every one.
There is real relief in that. Burnout often comes from carrying a gift that was never handed to you. The body has other members for a reason.

Perhaps you are the one in your family everyone calls when there is a crisis, and your phone has not stopped ringing all week. Ask what is truly yours to carry, and let another member of the body carry the rest.

line.b: The body says do your part.

after: You are a member, not the whole body.
Waiting on your own ministry is not laziness, it is faithfulness.
days.prayer: Lord, I feel the weight of trying to do everything. Remind me that I belong to others and they belong to me. Show me what my part is, and give me grace to wait on that ministry and leave the rest to the members you have given gifts I do not have. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you carrying this week that belongs to another member of the body?

days.title: Purpose After the Excitement Fades

body.p: Of all the examples Paul could have chosen, he picks the two things everybody does several times a day. Whether therefore ye eat, or drink.

The setting was an argument about food. Some believers in Corinth worried about meat sold after idol sacrifices. Paul himself was being criticised for meals he had given thanks over, evil spoken of because of an ordinary dinner.
His answer lifts the whole quarrel to a higher place. Eat or do not eat, but do all to the glory of God, and do not trip anyone else up while you do it.

That is good news for the season after the excitement fades. The conference is over, the first glow has dimmed, and the days are back to breakfast, lunch and supper. Paul says those meals are not gaps between spiritual moments. They are the moments.

So the plate of beans at your desk, the tea you share with the security guard at the gate, the meal you eat alone in a quiet flat, can each be received with thanks and offered back. It is not glamorous. It was never meant to be.

line.b: Breakfast remains, and so does the glory.

after: Give thanks for the next meal as if it mattered, because it does.
Ordinary days are where most of God's glory is quietly given.
days.prayer: Father, the excitement I once felt has faded and I miss it. Teach me to glorify you in eating and drinking, in the routine and the repeated. Let me give thanks honestly for small things, and keep me from causing anyone else to stumble. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What everyday routine could you start offering to God with thanks?

days.title: Purpose In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: Paul thinks like a farmer here. What you sow, you reap, and the field has no opinion of its own. he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.

A difficult conversation is a sowing moment. The words you choose in the tense ten minutes with your brother, your landlord or your manager are seeds. Some will be sown to the flesh, to winning and to pride. Some can be sown to the Spirit.
Then comes the encouragement. let us not be weary in well doing. Paul knows that doing good in a hard conversation is tiring. You hold your tongue, you answer gently, and nothing seems to change.
The harvest comes in due season, and the season is God's, not ours. You may see no fruit by the end of the call. Paul only asks that you do not faint before it comes.

Verse ten gives the practical step. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men. Before you pick up the phone to the relative you have been avoiding, ask what seed you want to leave in the ground when you hang up.

after: You are responsible for the sowing, not for the timing of the harvest.
Gentleness in a hard conversation is never wasted.
days.prayer: Lord, I have a conversation ahead that I dread. Help me sow to your Spirit and not to my pride. Keep me from weariness when doing good feels useless. Give me words that are honest and kind, and let me trust you with the harvest in your own season. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What seed do you want to leave behind in the hardest conversation you face this week?

days.title: Purpose When Progress Is Slow

body.p: Verse seven is a man bargaining upward. Rams. Then thousands of rams. Then ten thousands of rivers of oil. Then his own firstborn child. Each offer is bigger, as if God must be impressed by size.
The answer is startlingly small. He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good. Not a new revelation, but something already shown. Do justly. Love mercy. Walk humbly.
There is nothing fast in that list. Justice is done one honest decision at a time. Mercy is loved over years. And walking is the slowest way to travel anywhere. God did not ask for a sprint.

When progress is slow, we are tempted to reach for the big gesture. The dramatic fast, the grand vow, the rivers of oil. Micah says the Lord is not asking for that. He is asking you to keep walking with him at walking pace.
Think of the trader in the market who has dealt fairly for twenty years and still has a small stall. Slow, yes. But each fair measure was exactly what the Lord required.

line.b: He asks for a humble walk.

after: Slow obedience is still obedience.
You already know what is good, because he has shown you.
days.prayer: Lord, I keep trying to impress you with bigger offerings when you have already shown me what is good. Teach me to do justly in small decisions, to love mercy when it costs me, and to walk humbly with you at the pace you set. Give me patience when progress is slow. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What big gesture are you offering God in place of a humble daily walk?

days.title: Purpose At the Point of Decision

body.p: James uses one of the most ordinary pictures in the Bible. A man beholding his natural face in a glass. Then, in the next verse, he walks away and forgets what he looked like.
Everyone has done this. You glance in the mirror on the way out, notice the collar is crooked, and arrive at work with it still crooked. You saw. You did nothing. The seeing did not help.
That, says James, is what hearing without doing is like. And the person most fooled is not the neighbour. It is you. deceiving your own selves.

The point of decision, then, is not usually between knowing and not knowing. Most of us know what the passage says. It is between knowing and doing, and that gap can be as short as the walk from the mirror to the door.

Verse twenty one offers the way in. receive with meekness the engrafted word. Engrafted, like a branch bound into a tree until it becomes part of it. So when you close your Bible this morning, pick one sentence and do it before lunch.

line.a: Seeing the crooked collar is not enough.

after: Knowing what to do is the beginning of the decision, not the end of it.
The mirror only helps the one who acts on what it shows.
days.prayer: Lord, I have heard so much and done so little. I do not want to deceive myself. Graft your word into me, and give me the meekness to receive it and the courage to act on it before I walk away and forget. Show me one thing to do today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What did you last see clearly in Scripture and then walk away from?

days.title: Purpose In the Waiting Room

body.p: Paul wrote this from prison, and he knew he might never see the Philippians again. So he praises them for obeying not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence.
The waiting room is a place of absence. The doctor has not come out yet. The letter has not arrived. The person who used to guide you is not there. It feels as though nothing is happening.

Verse thirteen says something is. it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do. Both. Not only the doing, which we can sometimes see, but the willing, the wanting, which is hidden even from us. God is at work on your desires while you sit in the plastic chair.

That is why verse fourteen follows so naturally. Do all things without murmurings and disputings. Waiting rooms are where grumbling grows best. Paul does not deny the wait is hard. He simply asks us not to let it turn sour.
If you are sitting in an actual hospital corridor today, waiting for news, you are not outside God's work. He is shaping your will even here, quietly, while the clock above the door moves slowly.

line.b: God is working on the wanting.

after: Absence of guidance is not absence of God.
Wait without grumbling, and let him work where you cannot see.
days.prayer: Father, I am waiting and it is hard. I cannot see you working, but your word says you are working in me, even in what I want. Keep me from murmuring. Shape my will while I wait, and give me grace to obey when no one is watching. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would change if you believed God is working on your desires while you wait?

days.title: Purpose When You Feel Small

body.p: Paul is saying goodbye. He tells the elders of Ephesus that they shall see my face no more, and a few verses later they are weeping on his neck. This is not a speech from a man who feels nothing.
Yet in the middle of it he says none of these things move me. He means the chains and troubles waiting for him in every city. They are real. They simply do not get to decide his direction.
And look at what he wants. Not greatness. Not a famous name. that I might finish my course with joy. A course is a runner's lane, marked out, specific, his own. He is not running anyone else's race.

When you feel small, it is often because you are measuring your lane against someone else's. Paul's sense of purpose rested on a ministry he had received of the Lord Jesus. Received, not invented. Small or large, it was given.
Maybe your course is a classroom of seven children in a village school, or a sick parent's bedside. It may look small from the outside. Finish it with joy. That is the whole ambition.

line.a: You do not need a larger lane.
line.b: You need to finish your own.

after: Feeling small is not the same as being unimportant.
Grief and steadiness can live in the same heart.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I feel small and my work looks small. Help me stop comparing my course with others. Give me Paul's steadiness when troubles come, and his joy in finishing what you have given me. Thank you that my ministry is received from you and not measured by anyone else. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose course are you measuring yours against?

days.title: Purpose Through an Open Door

body.p: Psalm ninety is the prayer of Moses, and most of it is about how short life is. Grass that withers by evening. Years that fly away. By the last verse you half expect despair.

Instead, Moses asks for two things in a particular order. First, Let thy work appear unto thy servants. Then, at the very end, establish thou the work of our hands. God's work first. Ours after, and only as it rests on his.

He asks for that second thing twice. yea, the work of our hands establish thou it. A man who had watched a whole generation die in the wilderness wanted his labour to last, and he knew he could not make it last himself.

An open door is exciting. A new job, a new ministry, a new city. But underneath every new door sits the question of whether anything we build there will remain. Moses does not answer by working harder. He prays for the beauty of the LORD our God to rest upon the work.
If you are walking through a new door this month, a shop you are opening on a busy street or a first lecture, say the prayer twice, as Moses did. Some prayers are worth repeating.

line.b: Ask God to make the work last.

after: Ask to see God's work before you ask him to bless yours.
What lasts is what he establishes.
days.prayer: Lord our God, my days are short and I know it. Let me see your work before I rush into mine. As I walk through this new door, let your beauty rest on what I do, and establish the work of my hands. Yes, establish it, because I cannot make it last alone. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you building that you have not yet asked God to establish?

days.title: Purpose When the Answer Is No

body.p: The verse people love is The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD. The verse that follows is the one people need. Though he fall.

Notice that it does not say if. David, writing as an old man, assumes the good man whose steps are ordered will still fall. Ordered steps include stumbles. They include doors that close and prayers answered with no.
The promise is careful. he shall not be utterly cast down. Utterly is an honest word. It admits that you may be cast down, bruised, embarrassed, grieving. It denies only that the fall will be final.
And the reason has nothing to do with the strength of the one falling. the LORD upholdeth him with his hand. A hand under you is something you usually notice only on the way down.

If the answer this week was no, the scholarship, the proposal, the result you hoped would come back clear, you may be on the ground right now. You are not utterly cast down. The hand is already there.

line.a: A no can knock you down.
line.b: It cannot knock you out of his hand.

after: Falling is not proof that your steps were never ordered.
He delights in your way even on the day it hurts.
days.prayer: Lord, the answer was no and it hurts. I feel cast down. Thank you that you do not say I will never fall, only that I will not be utterly cast down. Hold me with your hand today. Order my next steps, and help me believe you still delight in my way. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where has a no made you doubt that your steps are ordered?

days.title: Purpose In What You Already Have

body.p: Most of us read this verse looking for new directions. But it begins with the ways you are already walking. In all thy ways acknowledge him. The roads under your feet right now.

To acknowledge him is more than nodding in his direction. The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for knowing. Know him in your ways. Know him at the sink, in the accounts, in the conversation with your teenage son.

Verse five does not tell you to throw away your understanding. It says lean not unto thine own understanding. You still think, plan and reason. You just stop resting your full weight on it, the way you would stop leaning on a cracked wall.

Verse seven adds the warning that keeps this from turning into pride. Be not wise in thine own eyes. The person who already has plenty, skills, education, experience, is the one most likely to lean on it.

So before asking God for something new, look at what you already hold. The job you have, the family you have, the street you live on. Acknowledge him there. That is often where the direction comes from.

line.a: You keep asking for a new road.
line.b: He asks to be known on this one.

after: Direction often comes after acknowledgement, not before it.
Use your understanding, just do not lean your whole weight on it.
days.prayer: Lord, I trust you, but I lean so heavily on my own understanding. Teach me to know you in the ways I already walk, my work, my home, my friendships. Keep me from being wise in my own eyes, and direct my paths as you have promised. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: In which of your current ways have you stopped acknowledging him?

days.title: Purpose When Nobody Notices

body.p: The Preacher is not sentimental. His reason for doing your work with might is blunt. there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave. You will not get this day back.

Then he admits what we would rather not say aloud. the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong. Skilful people go unrewarded. Clever people stay poor. time and chance happeneth to them all.

That is a strange foundation for purpose, but an honest one. He is not promising that hard work will be noticed. He is saying do it anyway, with your might, because the work is your portion in this life, and because life will soon be over.
Verse nine makes it gentler. Enjoy the life you have with the people you love. The Preacher pairs hard work with quiet joy, not hard work with applause.

The tailor finishing hems late at night, the clerk who checks every figure though nobody reviews them, the father mending a broken chair at home. Nobody may notice. Do it with your might anyway, and then go and eat supper with the people you love.

line.b: Do it with your might anyway.

after: Life is too short for half hearted work, and too short for joyless work.
Fairness is not guaranteed under the sun, but faithfulness is still possible.
days.prayer: Lord, sometimes my work goes unseen and it feels unfair. Thank you for the honesty of your word about time and chance. Help me do what my hand finds with all my might, and help me enjoy the people and the portion you have given me while I have them. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What work have you been doing half heartedly because no one notices it?

days.title: Purpose With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: Jesus calls money that which is least. That alone is surprising. In verse eleven he calls it the unrighteous mammon and sets it beside the true riches, which are something else entirely.
Yet he does not say money is unimportant. He says it is a test. How you handle the least reveals how you would handle much. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.

That keeps purpose on the ground. It is easy to dream about faithfulness in big things, a ministry, a large business, a platform. Jesus points instead at the change in your pocket and the receipt you could quietly adjust.

The parable just before these verses is about a dishonest manager who uses money shrewdly. Jesus is not praising the dishonesty. He is saying that money, used well, can serve friendship and eternity. Small, earthly things can be handled with heaven in view.

If you work at a till, or keep the books for a church, or run a small transport business, the least is in your hands every day. Handle it faithfully. Jesus says that is how true riches come to be entrusted.

after: Faithfulness with small sums is training for true riches.
Nobody becomes trustworthy in much by skipping the least.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, you call money the least, yet I often treat it as the most. Make me faithful with the small amounts that pass through my hands. Keep me honest when no one would know. Teach me to use earthly things with heaven in view, so that I can be trusted with true riches. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you being tempted to be unfaithful in a little thing this week?

days.title: Purpose When You Must Begin Again

body.p: Just before these verses, James and John asked for the best seats in glory. The other ten were angry with them. It was, once again, a moment where the disciples had completely missed the point.
Jesus does not dismiss them. He begins again with them, patiently, from the ground up. Greatness is turned upside down. whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all.
Then he points to himself. the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister. If anyone deserved to be served, it was him. He chose the other side of the table.

And look at what happens next. They walk into Jericho, and by the side of the road sits a blind man begging. The great words about a ransom land, almost at once, on one person in the dust. That is what service looked like. The next needy person on the road.

If you have failed, if you have been chasing the wrong seat, you can begin again the way Jesus began again with his friends. Not with a grand plan. With the next person you pass, perhaps the boy selling water at the junction.

after: Beginning again often starts with serving someone small.
Jesus is patient with disciples who miss the point twice.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I have chased the wrong things again. Thank you for your patience with me. You came to minister and to give your life for many. Teach me to begin again as a servant, and open my eyes to the person by the road who needs me today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which seat have you been asking for, and who is sitting by the road?

days.title: Purpose In the Middle of the Work

body.p: Jesus says this the night before he dies, in a room full of men who will run away within hours. Henceforth I call you not servants. He calls them friends.

The difference he names is information. A servant is told what to do. A friend is told why. all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you. They were brought inside the purpose, not just handed tasks.
Then he turns their assumption around. Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you. They thought they had decided to follow him. In fact he had picked them first, on the shore and at the tax booth.

That changes the middle of the work, the long stretch when the thrill of beginning is gone and the end is not yet in sight. You are not there because you volunteered and must now prove yourself. You are there because you were chosen, and the aim is fruit that should remain.

And the command at the centre of it is plain. love one another. In the middle of a long project with tired colleagues, when tempers fray around the photocopier, that may be the fruit that lasts longest.

after: You were chosen before you chose.
The fruit that remains is often love shown in the middle of tired work.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling me your friend and not only your servant. In the middle of my work, when I am tired and the end feels far away, remind me that you chose me. Make my fruit last, and help me love the people I work beside. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Do you come to God as a servant waiting for orders or as a friend who is told why?

days.title: Purpose When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Paul writes from a Roman prison, and he knows Timothy is afraid. Standing beside a chained man was dangerous and embarrassing. So he says Be not thou therefore ashamed.
Look at how Paul describes himself. Not Nero's prisoner. me his prisoner. The Lord's. Even in chains he will not let fear name his situation for him.

Then he reaches back past every fear Timothy has. God called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, given before the world began. The calling is older than the fear. It was settled before the first threat was ever spoken.

And he reaches forward too. Christ hath abolished death. The worst thing fear can point to has already been dealt with. Paul does not pretend suffering is easy. He invites Timothy to share in it. But he refuses to let fear have the last word.

When fear speaks first, before the interview, before you tell your family about your faith, before you walk back into the clinic where the diagnosis was given, let it speak. Then answer it with something older.

line.b: Grace spoke before the world began.

after: Your calling does not depend on your courage.
Fear may speak first, but it does not have to speak last.
days.prayer: Lord, fear always seems to speak first in me. Remind me that you called me by your own purpose and grace before the world began, not by my works or my bravery. Keep me from being ashamed of you. Let me share in hard things by your power, and hold to the hope that Christ has abolished death. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is fear saying to you first today, and what older word answers it?

days.title: Purpose With an Open Hand

body.p: Paul calls Timothy a workman. Not a scholar or a celebrity. A tradesman, the kind who works with his hands and whose work can be inspected at the end of the day.

The phrase rightly dividing the word of truth carries the picture of cutting straight. A carpenter sawing timber along the line. A farmer ploughing a straight furrow. Handling Scripture well is a craft, learned slowly and done carefully.

But notice what surrounds that verse. Before it, Paul tells Timothy to charge people that they strive not about words to no profit. After it, shun profane and vain babblings. On both sides of the craft sits the danger of arguing for the sake of arguing.
That is where the open hand comes in. A workman with a clenched fist cannot cut straight. Study is meant to make you approved unto God, not victorious over your cousin at the family gathering.

So study. Open the Bible on the bus, read slowly, compare one passage with another, ask honest questions. Then hold what you learn with an open hand, ready to serve with it rather than to win with it.

after: A good workman measures twice and argues rarely.
The aim of study is God's approval, not the last word.
days.prayer: Lord, make me a workman who has no need to be ashamed. Give me patience to study your word carefully and to handle it straight. Keep me from arguing about words for no profit. Let me hold what I learn with an open hand, ready to serve others with it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Has your study of Scripture lately made you gentler, or just better at arguing?

days.title: Purpose When You Cannot See Far

body.p: The writer has just given one of the sternest warnings in the New Testament. Then, suddenly, his tone softens. But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you.

The reason he gives is remarkable. God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love. Forgetting your love would be, in his words, unrighteous. God's own justice is committed to remembering.

Look at the tenses. ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister. Past and present together. They had served, and they were still serving. The writer does not ask them to see the end, only to keep going with the same diligence they had already shown.

When you cannot see far, it helps to know that the road behind you has not been erased. The meals you cooked for the grieving, the visits to the sick, the offering given quietly when money was short, are not lost in the fog. They are held by a God who will not forget.
If you are a carer whose days blur together at home, or a Sunday school teacher wondering if any of it sticks, keep ministering. You do not have to see the end of the road. He sees all of it.

line.b: He has not forgotten the beginning.

after: God remembers what you have forgotten you did.
Keep doing tomorrow what you did with love yesterday.
days.prayer: Father, I cannot see far ahead and I am tired. Thank you that you are not unrighteous to forget my labour of love. Help me keep ministering with the same diligence, to the full assurance of hope, even when I cannot see where it leads. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What past labour of love do you need to remember God has not forgotten?

days.title: Purpose In the Honest Answer

body.p: This is a verse often handed to people in pain, sometimes too quickly. It helps to read what comes just before it. Paul has admitted that we do not even know how to pray as we should, and that the Spirit maketh intercession for the saints.
So the verse begins in honesty, not certainty. We do not know what to pray. And yet, we know that all things work together for good to them that love God. Not knowing and knowing sit side by side.
Paul does not say all things are good. Loss is not good. Betrayal is not good. He says they work together, woven into something larger by a God who has not stopped working.

Verse twenty nine tells us what the good is. To be conformed to the image of his Son. The good is not always comfort or success. It is becoming like Jesus, and sometimes that happens most deeply in the hardest places.

So if a friend sits with you in a hospital car park and you have nothing wise to say, it is fine to answer honestly. Say you do not know how to pray about this. That honest sentence is exactly where the Spirit begins to intercede.

line.a: We do not know what to pray.
line.b: We still know who is at work.

after: Honesty about pain does not cancel trust in God's purpose.
The good God works toward is that you look more like his Son.
days.prayer: Spirit of God, I do not know what to pray, and I will not pretend I do. Thank you for interceding for me according to the will of God. Help me trust that you are working all things together for good, even what is not good in itself, and make me more like Jesus through it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where do you need to admit you do not know how to pray?

days.title: Purpose When the Cost Is Real

body.p: Paul prays something enormous for the Thessalonians. That God would sanctify you wholly, spirit, soul and body, kept blameless until Christ comes. It is the kind of prayer that makes you feel the size of the gap.
Then he gives the reason it is possible. Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it. Not you will do it. He will. The one who called you is the one who completes the work.

That matters when the cost of following feels high. A calling can cost sleep, money, comfort and friendships. Paul knew that better than most. He had been driven out of Thessalonica by a mob. But the weight of finishing does not rest on the one who is called.
And then, in verse twenty five, the great apostle asks for help. Brethren, pray for us. Four words. The man who wrote the prayer needed one himself.
When the cost is real, tell someone. Send a message to a friend tonight and say you are struggling and need prayer. Paul did not think it beneath him. Neither should you.

line.b: So is the faithfulness of the one who called you.

after: He who calls you also carries the finishing.
Asking for prayer is not weakness, it is what apostles did.
days.prayer: Faithful God, the cost of following you feels heavy right now. Thank you that you who called me will also do it. Sanctify me wholly, spirit, soul and body, and keep me. Give me the humility to ask others to pray for me, as Paul did. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who could you ask to pray for you about the cost you are carrying?

days.title: Purpose For the Long Road

body.p: Two days frame this sentence. from the first day until now, and then until the day of Jesus Christ. One lies behind the Philippians, the day Lydia opened her home by the river. The other lies ahead, the day Christ returns. Between them is the long road.
Paul is confident of this very thing. Not confident in them, as if their stamina guaranteed anything. Confident that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it.

The God who starts is the God who finishes. That is the whole hope of the long road. You do not have to keep the work alive by your own strength. You only have to stay with the one who is carrying it.

And Paul writes this in chains. I have you in my heart, he says, both in my bonds and in his defence of the gospel. The long road for him included prison. His confidence did not depend on his circumstances being easy.

If you are years into a marriage, a ministry, a slow recovery or a course of study that keeps getting longer, remember both days. The first day, when he began, and the day he will finish. You are somewhere in between, and he has not let go.

line.a: He began it on the first day.
line.b: He will finish it on his day.

after: The road between the two days is long, but it is held at both ends.
Your perseverance rests on his faithfulness, not on your stamina.
days.prayer: Lord, the road is long and I am tired. Thank you that you began a good work in me and that you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. When my strength runs low, remind me that the finishing is yours. Keep me in fellowship with your people along the way. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it mean to trust God with the finishing as much as the beginning?

days.title: Purpose At the End of the Day

body.p: Joshua was taking over from Moses, a man who had spoken with God face to face. Three times in this chapter he is told to be strong and courageous. Nobody needs telling three times unless they are afraid.

The instruction about the book is physical. It shall not depart out of thy mouth. In Joshua's world, meditating meant murmuring the words aloud, going over them day and night, the way you repeat a phone number so you do not lose it.

The promise of success here is easy to twist. It is tied to this, observe to do according to all that is written therein. Prospering in this chapter means walking in God's ways and seeing his purposes done, not a guarantee of wealth or an easy life.
Then the heart of it. Have not I commanded thee? Courage is not a mood Joshua has to go and find. It is an order, and it comes with a reason. the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.

At the end of the day, when the house is quiet and tomorrow's worries start to talk, murmur a line of Scripture before you sleep. Say it over until it sits in your mouth. Then lie down knowing he goes with you into tomorrow.

line.a: Courage is not a feeling you find.
line.b: It is a word you are given.

after: Let the last words in your mouth today be his.
He goes with you into tomorrow, wherever tomorrow turns out to be.
days.prayer: Lord my God, at the end of this day I bring you my fears about tomorrow. Put your word in my mouth and keep it there, day and night. Make me strong and of a good courage, not because I feel brave, but because you have commanded it and you are with me wherever I go. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What line of Scripture could you murmur tonight before you sleep?

days.title: Purpose For What Comes Next

body.p: David does not say if trouble comes. He says Though I walk in the midst of trouble. In the midst. Not near it, not around it. Right in the middle, with trouble on every side.
And yet he expects to be revived there. thou wilt revive me. Not after the trouble ends, but while he is still walking through it.

Then comes the line that closes this month well. The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me. Perfect here means complete, bring to its finish. Whatever concerns you, the half done, the not yet, the lain awake over, he will see through.

What is striking is the last sentence. Having just stated his confidence, David still prays forsake not the works of thine own hands. Confidence and pleading sit together. He is sure, and he still asks. That is not doubt. It is how children talk to a father they trust.

As you step into what comes next, a new month, a new school term, a move to another city, carry both. The certainty that he will complete what concerns you, and the freedom to keep asking him not to let go.

line.a: He will finish what concerns you.
line.b: You may still ask him not to let go.

after: Trouble in the middle does not cancel mercy that lasts for ever.
You are the work of his hands, and he does not abandon his work.
days.prayer: Lord, I walk into what comes next with trouble on some sides of me. Revive me in the middle of it. Thank you that you will perfect what concerns me and that your mercy endures for ever. I am the work of your hands. Please do not forsake me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What concern do you need to hand over for God to complete?

days.title: Courage Before You Feel Ready

body.p: Most people start reading at verse ten, with Fear thou not. It is worth backing up one line, because the command is not the first thing God says.

Before he tells Israel not to be afraid, he tells them who they are. Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away. The courage is built on a fact that was settled long before the fear showed up.

Notice also what has not changed yet. In verse eleven the people who were incensed against thee are still there. The promise is that they shall be as nothing, and it is in the future tense. Israel is asked to stop being dismayed before the evidence arrives.

That is what courage before you feel ready looks like. It is not a feeling you wait for. It is a decision to believe the earlier sentence, chosen and not thrown away, while the later sentence is still on its way.

Maybe you are sitting outside an interview room in Lagos, or waiting for a hard phone call to connect. You do not have to feel brave first. You only have to remember who called you before you walked in.

line.a: The fear arrived in verse ten.
line.b: The choosing happened in verse nine.

after: God did not wait for you to be ready before he chose you, so you need not wait to be ready before you trust him.
Whatever is set against you today is described by God in the future tense as nothing.
days.prayer: Lord, I do not feel ready for what is in front of me. Remind me that you chose me before I was brave and that you have not cast me away. Hold me with your right hand while my feelings catch up with your promise. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would you do today if you believed you had already been chosen and not cast away?

days.title: Courage In the Next Step

body.p: God asks Joshua a question in the middle of a promise. Have not I commanded thee? It sounds almost like a parent at the door, reminding a child of something already said.

Joshua has heard it before. Be strong and of a good courage comes to him again and again in this one chapter. Fear does not always need new information. Often it needs the old word repeated until it lands.

Then look at verse ten. Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people. No long season of feeling courageous comes in between. The next thing Joshua does is give the next instruction. Courage, in this chapter, is measured by what happens after the promise.
The promise is also shaped like a road. The LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest. Not where you stand still and wait, but wherever you go. The presence is attached to the moving.

Your next step might be small. Sending the message to the landlord. Booking the clinic appointment. Telling your supervisor the figures do not add up. Joshua conquered nothing in verse ten. He only spoke to the officers, and that was enough for that day.

after: Courage is often just the next obedient sentence you say out loud.
Wherever you go today, the promise is already travelling with you.
days.prayer: Lord, you have already told me not to be afraid, and I have heard it many times. Help me stop waiting to feel strong and simply take the next step you have put in front of me. Go with me into every room and every hard conversation today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is the one next step you have been waiting to feel brave enough to take?

days.title: Courage When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: David asks two questions here and answers neither of them. Whom shall I fear? and then of whom shall I be afraid? He leaves the silence after them on purpose.

Questions like that only work when you already know the answer. Nobody. Not because nothing frightening exists, but because of what comes before each question. The LORD is my light, and then the LORD is the strength of my life.

Verse two tells us where that confidence came from, and it is written in the past tense. Enemies came upon me to eat up my flesh, and they stumbled and fell. David is remembering. His courage now is borrowed from a day that already happened.
That matters on the quiet stretches, when nothing dramatic is going on and fear fills the gap. Silence is where old worries talk loudest. David fills the quiet with memory instead.

Tonight, when the house goes still and your mind starts listing what could go wrong, try listing what already went right. Name one time God carried you. Then ask David's question again and let the silence answer it.

after: A quiet day is a good day to remember, out loud, one thing God has already done.
The questions in this psalm are meant to be left hanging, because the answer is nobody.
days.prayer: Lord, you have been my light before and the strength of my life on days I barely remember. When things go quiet and my fears start talking, bring back to my mind the times you helped me. Let my memory of your faithfulness be louder than my worry. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is one past day when God carried you that you could remember tonight?

days.title: Courage Without an Audience

body.p: The scale of this psalm is enormous. The earth may be removed, and mountains be carried into the midst of the sea. And yet the word that holds it together is small and close. Present.

A very present help in trouble. Not a distant help, not a help that turns up once a crowd has gathered. Very present. The psalm describes God as near to the person in trouble, at the moment of trouble.

Much of our bravest living happens with no one watching. The night shift. The diagnosis you have not told anyone yet. The temptation refused alone in a hotel room. Nobody claps. The psalm does not need them to. God is already in the room.
Then comes Therefore will not we fear. The courage is a conclusion, drawn from the first verse. We do not fear because God is near, not because the mountains have stopped moving.

It is also sung in the plural. Even alone, you belong to a people who have sung these words for three thousand years. Wherever you are facing something quietly today, at a desk or in a hospital car park, you are not the first and you are not by yourself.

after: The bravest thing you do today may be something nobody ever sees, and that is fine.
Courage in this psalm is a conclusion drawn from who God is, not from how calm things look.
days.prayer: God, you are my refuge and strength, and you are present in the places no one else sees. Meet me in the private trouble I have not told anyone about. Let me be faithful when there is no audience, knowing that you are near and that is enough. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What hard thing are you carrying quietly that you could bring to the God who is already present?

days.title: Courage For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: Count the word my in verse two. my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer, and it keeps going. David does not stop at one picture of God. He needs a whole row of them.

That is honest. A single day asks for more than one kind of help. A rock to stand on in the morning. A fortress when the criticism starts at work. A deliverer when the bus breaks down and the money is short. A high tower when you need to see further than the next hour.
Before any of the list, though, comes a simpler sentence. I will love thee, O LORD, my strength. The psalm begins with affection, not with strategy.

Ordinary days are where this matters. Nobody writes songs about Tuesday, yet most of life happens on one. David wrote this after a great rescue, according to its title, but the words he chose are things you lean on every day. Rocks and towers do not move. That is the point of them.
Pick one of the names for today. If the day feels shaky, make it rock. If it feels crowded, make it fortress. Say it under your breath on the walk to the shop.

line.a: One day needs many kinds of help.

after: Choose one of David's names for God and carry it into an ordinary hour.
The psalm starts with love before it starts with need.
days.prayer: Lord, I love you. You are my strength, my rock and my fortress, and today I need more than one of those. Be steady ground under me this morning and a high tower when I cannot see past the next problem. Make this ordinary day a place where I trust you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which of David's names for God do you most need on this particular day?

days.title: Courage When Plans Change

body.p: Read verses three and four slowly and listen for a change in grammar. He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me. Then, in the valley, it turns. For thou art with me.
Up to this point David has been talking about God. In the shadow he starts talking to him. The valley is where the psalm becomes a prayer.

It is also worth noticing that the valley is on the path. The same shepherd who leadeth me in the paths of righteousness is the one walking with David through the shadow of death. The hard place was not a wrong turn. It was part of the road he was being led on.

That is a comfort when plans change. The job that ended, the move that fell through, the pregnancy that did not go as hoped. A changed plan can feel like being lost. This psalm says you can be in the valley and still be on the path, with God near enough to speak to directly.

Then the table. Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies. The enemies are still there. Dinner is served anyway. If your plans have collapsed this week, speak to him rather than about him, from wherever you are sitting.

line.a: In the pasture, David speaks about God.
line.b: In the valley, he speaks to him.

after: A changed plan does not mean you have left the path.
The table was set while the enemies were still watching.
days.prayer: Lord, this is not the road I planned, and some days it feels like a valley. I do not want only to talk about you. I want to talk to you. Be with me here, comfort me with your rod and staff, and help me believe I am still on your path. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Have you been talking about God in your changed situation more than you have been talking to him?

days.title: Courage In the Work at Hand

body.p: It is striking how the righteous are described here. Not as people who stand tall or never waver. The righteous cry. That is the first thing we are told they do.
No shame is attached to it. The cry is not a failure of faith. It is the faith. and the LORD heareth follows straight after, with nothing in between, no waiting period and no test to pass.
Verse eighteen sharpens it. The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart. Nigh means near. Broken people are not sent to the back of the queue. They are the ones he stands closest to.

Courage in the work at hand often looks like this. You keep doing the job, and you cry out while you do it. The nurse finishing a double shift after a hard death on the ward. The trader opening the stall when sales have been bad for weeks. The student going back to the textbook after failing once.
You do not have to stop crying out to keep working, and you do not have to stop working to cry out. Tell him about it on the way. He hears.

line.b: The LORD hears, with nothing in between.

after: Crying out to God in the middle of your work is not weakness, it is the very thing this psalm describes.
If your heart is broken today, the psalm says that is where he stands closest.
days.prayer: Lord, I have work to do today and a heavy heart to carry while I do it. Hear my cry in the middle of the task, not only when I stop. Be near to me in my brokenness and give me strength for the next hour of work. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it look like to keep working today and cry out to God at the same time?

days.title: Courage When You Need Clarity

body.p: Verse nineteen is one of the most honest sentences in the psalms. Many are the afflictions of the righteous. Not a few. Not only for those who have wandered. Many, and for the righteous.

Some of us were taught, quietly, that trouble means we did something wrong. This verse clears that up. Faithful people suffer, often and in more than one way. The psalm says so plainly and without apology.
Then it adds the second fact with the same plainness. but the LORD delivereth him out of them all. One line holds both truths and does not let either cancel the other.

Clarity is not the same as having every answer. It is seeing what is actually true. Here two things are true together: the afflictions are many, and the deliverance is complete. The timing is not given. Some of it comes in this life and some waits for the next. The verse does not promise when. It promises that none will be left out.

If you are sitting in a clinic queue or at a kitchen table with unpaid bills, trying to work out what your trouble means, start here. It does not mean God has left. It means you are in the first half of verse nineteen.

after: Trouble is not proof that you have failed God.
The deliverance in verse nineteen covers every affliction, even though it does not give a date.
days.prayer: Lord, I am confused about what my troubles mean. Thank you that you tell the truth about suffering and do not hide it. Clear my mind of the lie that I am being punished, and help me trust that you will bring me out of every affliction in your time. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Have you been reading your troubles as a verdict on you rather than as the first half of a promise?

days.title: Courage One Choice at a Time

body.p: The well loved line about casting your burden sits right after a description of betrayal. The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart. Earlier in the psalm David says this was not an enemy but a companion, someone he once walked with to the house of God.

So the burden in verse twenty two is specific. It is the weight of being lied to by a friend. Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee. Sustain is not the same as remove. It means being held up while the weight is still real.
Then the psalm ends on a choice. After all the anger about deceitful men, the last words are but I will trust in thee. It is a decision, made in the first person, at the end of a long complaint.

Courage after betrayal rarely comes as one great act. It is a string of small choices. Not to reply to the message tonight. To pray for the person tomorrow, even through gritted teeth. To trust one new person again next month.
If someone's soft words have cut you, you do not need to resolve all of it today. Make one choice. Hand this one weight over, and say the psalm's last sentence for yourself.

line.a: The betrayal was smooth as butter.
line.b: The answer was one plain choice.

after: Being sustained does not mean the weight is gone, it means you are held up under it.
You can end a day of hurt the way David ended this psalm, with one sentence of trust.
days.prayer: Lord, someone I trusted has hurt me with words that sounded kind. I cast this burden on you, because I cannot carry it well. Sustain me while it still hurts, guard my heart from bitterness, and help me make one faithful choice today. I will trust in you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is the one choice you can make today about the person who hurt you?

days.title: Courage Under Pressure

body.p: David does not say if I am afraid. He says What time I am afraid. In other words, when. He expects fear to come and has already decided what to do with it.
The pressure he describes is constant. Mine enemies would daily swallow me up. Daily. This is not a single bad afternoon. It is the kind of pressure that wakes you up and is still there at bedtime.

Watch how the three verses move. Verse two is pressure. Verse three is fear met with trust. By verse four he is saying I will not fear what flesh can do unto me. The fearlessness comes last, not first. Trust is what carries him from one to the other.

That order is a relief for anyone who is frightened. You do not have to start at verse four. You can start exactly where David did, afraid, and still be doing the right thing. Fear is not the opposite of trust here. It is the moment trust gets used.

When the pressure comes today, the deadline, the call from the debt collector, the meeting where you know you will be blamed, say the short line from verse three. It was written for the very moment your heart starts to race.

line.b: Trust already has its answer ready.

after: You are allowed to start the day afraid, as long as you take your fear straight to God.
The fearlessness of verse four came after the trust of verse three.
days.prayer: Lord, I am under pressure and I am afraid. I am not going to pretend otherwise. When I am afraid, I will trust in you. Carry me from fear to trust, and in your time from trust to peace, one hour at a time. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: When fear arrives today, what will be the very first thing you do with it?

days.title: Courage After the Excitement Fades

body.p: David is praying from a long way off. From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee. Whether he means distance on a map or distance in his heart, he feels far from the place where God once seemed close.

Many people know that feeling after a high point passes. The conference ends, the new job becomes ordinary, the early joy of faith settles into routine. Then something hard arrives and you realise you are a long way from where you started.

Look at what he asks for. lead me to the rock that is higher than I. He does not ask for strength to climb. He asks to be led. The rock is higher than he is, which is the whole point. He cannot get there on his own and does not pretend he can.

Then verse three looks back. For thou hast been a shelter for me. When the excitement is gone, memory does the work feelings used to do. He has been sheltered before, and that history is enough to pray on.

If your faith feels flat this month, you do not need to force the old excitement back. Pray from where you are, even if it feels like the end of the earth. Ask to be led. Then remember one shelter he has already been.

line.b: The rock is still higher than I.

after: You can pray honestly from far away, and God hears it as clearly as from close by.
Asking to be led is not a lesser kind of courage.
days.prayer: God, I feel far from you and the early excitement has gone. Hear my cry anyway. My heart is overwhelmed, so lead me to the rock that is higher than I am. You have been a shelter for me before. Be that again today, in this ordinary week. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where do you need to stop climbing and ask to be led instead?

days.title: Courage In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: Psalm seventy three is a hard conversation written down. For most of it, Asaph admits something embarrassing. He envied the wicked. Their lives looked easier than his, and he nearly slipped.
By verse twenty five he has come through it, and the turn is beautiful. Whom have I in heaven but thee? It is a question asked after a long, honest argument, not instead of one.

Then comes the line that holds the day together. My flesh and my heart faileth. Both of them. His body and his inner strength are giving way, and he says so. Only then does he add but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.

Courage in a difficult conversation starts with that kind of honesty. Asaph did not tidy his feelings before bringing them. He said the envious, bitter, tired thing, and God met him in it. The strength came after the confession, not before.

If you have a hard talk ahead today, with a spouse, a pastor, a parent, or with God himself, you may feel your heart failing before you open your mouth. Say the true thing gently. Let God be the strength of your heart, because yours may not be enough, and that is allowed.

line.b: God is the strength of it.

after: Asaph's honest complaint made it into Scripture, which means God can handle yours.
Before a hard conversation you do not need a strong heart, only a God who is its strength.
days.prayer: God, my heart is failing as I think about the conversation ahead. You are my portion and the strength of my heart. Give me words that are honest and kind. Let me not hide what is true, and let me not wound with it either. Be with me when I open my mouth. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What true thing have you been afraid to say, to God or to someone else?

days.title: Courage When Progress Is Slow

body.p: The first verse of Psalm ninety one is full of staying words. He that dwelleth in the secret place, and then shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. Dwell. Abide. Nobody dwells anywhere for an afternoon.

These are words for people who stay put, which is hard when life is moving slowly. When progress is slow we want to go looking for somewhere faster. Another church, another plan, another version of ourselves. The psalm points the other way. Stay under the shadow.
Shade is not dramatic. You only notice it when the sun is fierce, and you only benefit from it if you remain inside it. Stepping in and out does little. The protection is for those who live there.

Verse two then moves from description to speech. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress. It is something said out loud, perhaps many times, perhaps on days when it does not yet feel true.

If your recovery, your savings, your marriage or your studies are moving at a crawl, slow does not mean wrong. Keep dwelling. Say the sentence again this evening, the way a farmer walks the same field each day long before anything breaks the soil.

line.a: Slow progress tempts us to move.
line.b: The psalm asks us to dwell.

after: Shade only helps the one who stays in it.
Calling God your refuge on a slow day is not pretending, it is dwelling.
days.prayer: Lord, things are moving slowly and I am tempted to run somewhere faster. Teach me to dwell in your secret place and stay under your shadow. I will say of you that you are my refuge and my fortress, even on days when I see no progress at all. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you tempted to step out of the shade because things are moving too slowly?

days.title: Courage At the Point of Decision

body.p: Pilgrims sang this psalm on the road up to Jerusalem. The hills were in front of them, beautiful and also dangerous. Robbers hid there, and so did the shrines of other gods.
So the first line is really a moment of decision. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills. Where you look when you are uncertain says a great deal about what you trust.
The answer in verse two goes past the hills to the One who made them. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth. The hills are not the help. They were made. Their Maker is the help.

At the point of decision most of us look at whatever is biggest in front of us. The offer letter, the visa interview, the person who wants an answer by Friday. Those are hills. They are real and they matter. But they are not where help comes from.

Before you decide today, look up, and then look further. Ask the God who made heaven and earth, and the embassy and the job market and the person waiting for your reply, to help you choose. He is larger than the thing you are staring at.

after: Whatever looms largest in your decision today was made by someone larger.
Look up before you choose, and then look past what you see.
days.prayer: Lord, I have a decision to make and the hills in front of me look very large. I lift my eyes, but I do not want to stop at the hills. My help comes from you, the maker of heaven and earth. Give me wisdom and peace as I choose. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What hill are you looking at today instead of looking to the One who made it?

days.title: Courage In the Waiting Room

body.p: Isaiah begins with two questions that sound almost impatient. Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard. These people knew the truth already. They had simply grown too tired to hold on to it.

That is what waiting does. It is not that we forget what we believe. The long hours wear the edges off it. So the prophet repeats the basics. God fainteth not, neither is weary. Whatever you are waiting for, he is not tired of you.

Then verse twenty nine. He giveth power to the faint. Look who receives it. Not the strong, not those who have waited well, but the faint, and them that have no might. The qualification for this gift is having nothing left.

Verse thirty removes the last excuse for shame. Even the youths shall faint and be weary. The young, the fit, the people who seemed to have endless energy, they faint too. Running out is human, not a moral failure.
If you are sitting in a waiting room today, at a hospital, an embassy, or on the bench outside a courtroom, you are allowed to be empty. That is exactly who the power is given to.

line.b: The faint are the ones who receive.

after: Being out of strength is the very condition this promise was written for.
God is not weary of your waiting, even if you are.
days.prayer: Everlasting God, you never faint and you are never weary, but I am. I have been waiting a long time and I have little might left. You give power to the faint, so I come to you faint. Increase my strength for this hour in the waiting room. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would change if you saw your tiredness as the qualification for help rather than a reason for shame?

days.title: Courage When You Feel Small

body.p: The order of verse thirty one is surprising. First they shall mount up with wings as eagles. Then they shall run, and not be weary. Then, last of all, they shall walk, and not faint.
We would probably write it the other way round, building up to the soaring. Isaiah builds down. Flying, then running, then walking. The final promise is the most ordinary one.

That is good news if you feel small. Most days are not eagle days. Most days are walking days, one foot in front of the other, to the market, to the classroom, to the bedside of someone who is ill. Isaiah saves his last word of strength for exactly that pace.

And it comes right after verse thirty, where the young men shall utterly fall. The contrast is not between big people and small people. It is between those who rely on their own reserves and they that wait upon the LORD. Waiting is the secret, not size.
If today you cannot fly and cannot run, walk. Do not despise it. Walking without fainting is the promise that was kept for last.

after: A walking day is not a lesser day in God's eyes.
The strength in this verse belongs to those who wait, not to those who are big.
days.prayer: Lord, I feel small today and I cannot imagine soaring. Thank you that your promise reaches down to walking pace. As I wait on you, renew my strength enough to keep going, step by step, through this ordinary day without fainting. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you discouraged because today feels like walking rather than flying?

days.title: Courage Through an Open Door

body.p: Isaiah does not say if. He says When thou passest through the waters, and when thou walkest through the fire. The waters and the fire are assumed. They are part of the route.

The other word that matters is through. Not around, not over, not instead of. God's people are not promised a path that avoids the river. They are promised that the rivers shall not overflow thee, and that he will be with them in the middle of it.
Before any of that, verse one gives the reason they can walk at all. I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. Before the water, a name. The one going through the fire belongs to someone.

Sometimes the door that opens in front of you leads straight into deep water. A new country where you know no one. A promotion with responsibility that frightens you. A ministry you said yes to before you knew what it would cost. An open door does not mean the room beyond it is easy.

If you are standing at a threshold today, go through. Not because the waters are shallow, but because you are called by name and you belong to him. That is what Isaiah gave his people to carry into the river.

line.b: The name goes through it with you.

after: An open door is not a promise of an easy room, but it is never a door you walk through alone.
You are called by name before you are asked to pass through anything.
days.prayer: Lord, a door has opened in front of me and part of me is afraid of what is on the other side. You have called me by name and I am yours. When I pass through the waters, be with me. Help me walk through, not around. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What open door are you hesitating at because you can already see water on the other side?

days.title: Courage When the Answer Is No
