body.p: Nahum is not a gentle book. It is a warning to Nineveh, and the verses around this one are full of fire. his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. Then, in the middle, one quiet sentence.
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble. It sits between verse six and verse eight like a small room with thick walls in a city under siege.

Notice that the trouble does not disappear. The flood in verse eight still comes. Verse seven does not cancel the storm. It tells you where to stand during it. A strong hold is a place you shelter in while something is happening outside.

That is important when the answer to your prayer has been no. The scholarship was refused. The relationship ended. The scan came back with bad news. A no does not mean God is not good. Nahum puts the goodness of God in the same paragraph as the hardest things he knows. Then he adds he knoweth them that trust in him.
You may not know why the answer was no. You are known, though. Sit in the strong hold tonight and let that be the one thing you are sure of.

line.b: The LORD is good, and he knows you.

after: God's goodness in Nahum stands right next to the storm, not after it has passed.
Being known by God is a comfort that does not depend on getting the answer you wanted.
days.prayer: Lord, the answer I prayed for did not come and it hurts. I do not understand. But you are good, a strong hold in the day of trouble, and you know those who trust in you. Hold me in that strong place while I grieve what did not happen. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Can you trust that God is good today while you are still sad about his no?

days.title: Courage In What You Already Have

body.p: Everything in verse eighteen hangs on its first word. Yet I will rejoice in the LORD. Yet, after what?

After verse seventeen, where Habakkuk lists a complete failure. No blossom on the fig tree, no fruit on the vine, nothing from the fields, the flock gone and the stalls empty. For a farming people, that is the whole economy lost.
And he rejoices. Not in the harvest, which has failed, but in the God of my salvation. What Habakkuk still has is God, and he decides that is enough to sing about.

Then the picture of the deer. he will make my feet like hinds' feet. A hind can stand on narrow rock where other animals would fall. God does not flatten the mountain. He gives Habakkuk the kind of feet that can walk on it. The last line even hands the song To the chief singer, so this was meant to be sung aloud with others, empty barns and all.

Look at what is in your hands today, even if it is small. A little rice in the pot, one friend who still calls, breath in your lungs. Courage begins by rejoicing in the God who is still there, and asking him for feet to match the ground.

line.a: The fig tree did not blossom.
line.b: Yet the song went to the choir.

after: Habakkuk's joy did not wait for the harvest to return.
God may not lower the mountain, but he can change your feet.
days.prayer: Lord, a lot in my life has not blossomed. Yet I will rejoice in you, the God of my salvation. You are my strength. Make my feet steady on the high and narrow places, and teach me to be grateful for what I already have. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What can you rejoice in today, even though some of your fields are still empty?

days.title: Courage When Nobody Notices

body.p: Verse twenty seven is one of the largest claims Jesus ever makes. All things are delivered unto me of my Father. Everything. Then, in the very next breath, he turns to the tired.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden. The one who holds all things uses that authority to call people who are worn out. He does not call the impressive. He calls the exhausted.

Labour is often unseen. The mother up at night with a feverish child. The man who supports three households from one salary and never mentions it. The quiet woman who stacks the chairs after every church meeting. Nobody notices. Jesus names them first.

And he describes himself in a way that makes it safe to come. I am meek and lowly in heart. He is not a harsh supervisor checking whether you have earned a break. The yoke he offers is shared, and the rest he promises reaches unto your souls, not only your shoulders.
If you are doing faithful work that no one sees, the most powerful person in this passage has seen it. Bring the tiredness to him today, on your break, on the bus home, before you sleep.

after: The work nobody thanks you for is labour Jesus already sees.
Rest for your soul is offered by someone gentle, so you do not have to earn it.
days.prayer: Jesus, I am tired, and much of what I carry nobody else notices. You see it. I come to you as you invited me. Take my heavy load, teach me your gentle way, and give my soul the rest I cannot find on my own. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What unseen labour do you need to bring to Jesus today?

days.title: Courage With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: Jesus says these words on the last night before the cross, at supper, with Judas already gone out into the dark. It is a farewell. Peace I leave with you is the language of someone leaving something behind, the way a parent leaves an inheritance.

He knows exactly what is coming, for himself and for them. In the next breath he says plainly, I go away. This is not a peace that pretends nothing bad will happen. It is offered with full knowledge of the arrest, the trial and the scattering.
That is what not as the world giveth means here. The world's peace usually depends on the trouble being removed. His does not. It is given in the same breath as the bad news.

He also tells them how it will last. the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, will bring all things to your remembrance. Peace will often come back to them through memory, through recalling what Jesus said.

Courage with both feet on the ground is not pretending things are fine. It is holding his peace while looking straight at what is real. Before your next hard task, ask the Spirit to remind you of one thing Jesus said, and stand on it.

line.a: The world's peace waits for trouble to leave.
line.b: His peace is given while trouble is still coming.

after: Jesus gave his peace on the worst night of his life, so it is strong enough for yours.
Let the Spirit remind you of one word Jesus said, and stand on it today.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want your peace, not the kind that depends on everything going well. Keep my heart from being troubled or afraid. Holy Spirit, bring the words of Jesus to my remembrance when I need them most, and help me stand on solid ground. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it look like to have peace today without pretending the hard thing is not there?

days.title: Courage When You Must Begin Again

body.p: Jesus tells his friends that they are about to fail him. ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone. Within hours it happens exactly as he said.

Then, without a pause, he speaks of peace. These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. He is giving them words to come back to after they have run. The peace was prepared before the failure.
And he uses a surprising tense. I have overcome the world. Not I will. He says it before Gethsemane and before the cross, as if it were already done. For him, it was settled.

Beginning again is one of the hardest kinds of courage. You failed someone, or you walked away from God, or you made the same mistake for the hundredth time. Shame tells you to stay scattered. Jesus saw the scattering coming and still said be of good cheer.

If you need to start over today, you do not start from nothing. You start from words he spoke to you before you fell. Open your Bible where you left off, or kneel by the bed you got out of without praying, and begin again.

after: Jesus prepared the way back before his friends had even left.
You can begin again from what he said, not from what you did.
days.prayer: Jesus, I have scattered from you more than once and I am ashamed. Thank you that you knew and still spoke peace to me. You have overcome the world. Help me be of good cheer and begin again with you today, right where I am. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What has kept you from beginning again, and does the peace Jesus spoke reach it?

days.title: Courage In the Middle of the Work

body.p: Verse thirty is a chain of four links. Predestinated, called, justified, glorified. And every one of them is in the past tense, including the last.

That is strange. Glory has not arrived yet for the Romans Paul is writing to. They are still suffering, still waiting. Yet he writes them he also glorified as though it were finished. In God's mind, the end of the work is as certain as the beginning.

So when Paul asks What shall we then say to these things? he is speaking to people in the middle. Not at the start, full of energy, and not at the finish, but in the long tiring stretch where the work is real and the outcome is not yet seen.

His answer argues from the larger thing to the smaller. He that spared not his own Son, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? This is not a promise of every wish. It is a promise that the God who gave the greatest gift will not leave you short of what you need to reach home.

Halfway through a building project, a degree, or a hard season of raising children, it is easy to wonder if it will ever be finished. Paul is so sure of the ending he writes it in the past tense. Pick up today's portion of the work with that in mind.

line.b: God writes the end in the past tense.

after: God speaks of your glory as if it were already done.
The One who gave his Son will not leave you short of what you truly need for the road.
days.prayer: Father, I am in the middle of things and the end feels far away. Thank you that you have called me, justified me, and will finish what you started. You did not spare your own Son for me. Help me trust you for the rest of the road. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What part of your life feels stuck in the middle, and how would it change if you believed the end was certain?

days.title: Courage When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Before Paul's great line, he quotes a lament. For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. It comes from Psalm forty four, a song of people who felt God had abandoned them.
Paul lets the frightening voice speak first. He does not skip over it or soften it. Sheep for the slaughter is how some believers in Rome actually felt.
Then one word. Nay. It is almost abrupt, like someone standing up in the middle of a conversation to disagree. Fear has had its say. Now comes the answer.

Notice where the victory happens. in all these things, not out of them or after them. The persecution is still there. And the source is a person, not a mood. through him that loved us. Paul's courage rests on having been loved, in the past tense, at the cross.

When fear speaks first today, and it often does, before your feet touch the floor or the moment you pick up your phone, let it finish its sentence. Then answer it with Paul's one word, Nay, and remind yourself whose love you are standing in.

after: You do not have to silence fear before you answer it.
The victory is in these things, not after them.
days.prayer: Lord, fear often speaks first in my mind, and it is loud. Teach me to answer it with your truth. In all these things I am more than a conqueror through you who loved me. Let your love be the last word in my heart today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What does fear usually say first to you in the morning, and how will you answer it?

days.title: Courage With an Open Hand

body.p: The verse before the call to be strong is about a plan that fell through. Paul wanted Apollos to visit Corinth. his will was not at all to come at this time. Paul does not argue. He reports it and trusts that Apollos will come when he shall have convenient time.
That is an open hand. Paul was an apostle with real authority, yet he let a fellow worker say no without bitterness.

Then come four short commands, almost like orders to a soldier. Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. To quit yourselves like men means to act with maturity, not like children. It is firm language.

But Paul will not let strength stand alone. The very next line is Let all your things be done with charity. All of it. Courage without love becomes stubbornness. Standing firm without kindness becomes a fist. Paul wants spines that are straight and hands that are open.

Where do you need to be strong today without clenching? Perhaps in a family meeting about money, or with a colleague who has refused to help you. stand fast in what is right. Hold everything else loosely, and let love shape the way you do it.

line.b: Do all of it with charity.

after: Paul let Apollos say no and still called the church to stand firm.
Strength that is not done in love is not the courage this letter asks for.
days.prayer: Lord, make me strong and steady in my faith, but keep my hands open. Where I want to control others, teach me to let go as Paul did. Let everything I do today, even the firm things, be done with love. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you being strong with a clenched fist instead of an open hand?

days.title: Courage When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Paul calls himself and his friends earthen vessels. Clay jars. The kind you find in any market, cheap and easily cracked, used for everyday storage.

He says this deliberately. The treasure is the gospel, and it is kept in containers that look unimpressive that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. The weakness of the jar is part of the plan.
Then he lists four pairs. Hard pressed yet not crushed. Hunted yet not abandoned. Knocked down yet not finished. And one of them is surprisingly honest. we are perplexed, but not in despair.

Perplexed means confused, not sure which way to turn. An apostle admits it. He does not always know what is happening or what comes next. Faith does not remove the confusion. It stops the confusion from becoming despair.

If you cannot see far ahead this week, you are in good company. You do not need a five year plan to be faithful. Clay jars do not see the road. They are carried. Do the next right thing in front of you, and let the power be God's.

after: Confusion is not the same as despair, and Paul knew the difference.
A clay jar does not need to see the road to carry the treasure.
days.prayer: Lord, I cannot see very far ahead and I am confused about what comes next. I am a clay jar, easily cracked. Let your power show in my weakness. Keep me from despair while I am perplexed, and help me do the next right thing. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you perplexed right now, and how can you keep it from turning into despair?

days.title: Courage In the Honest Answer

body.p: Paul prayed the same prayer three times. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. We are never told exactly what the thorn was. We are told that he asked, and asked again, and asked a third time.
The answer was honest, and it was not the one he wanted. My grace is sufficient for thee. The thorn stayed. God did not remove it. He explained what he would do with it instead.

There is kindness in that honesty. God did not leave Paul guessing. He gave him a reason. my strength is made perfect in weakness. The weakness would become the very place where the power of Christ would rest.

Paul's response is honest too. He does not pretend the thorn is pleasant. He lists infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses. But he chooses to glory in them, because of who rests on him there.

Some prayers will be answered the way Paul's was. You may be in a hospital corridor tonight, praying for the third or the thirtieth time. It is right to keep asking. And if the answer comes back as grace instead of removal, it is still an answer, and his grace will be enough for this day.

line.b: God answered with grace, not removal.

after: Asking God again for the same thing is not a lack of faith, because Paul did it.
Grace that is sufficient is grace that is enough for today, even if the thorn remains.
days.prayer: Lord, I have asked you many times to take this away. I will keep asking, and I will also listen for your answer. If you choose to give me grace instead of removal, make that grace enough, and let the power of Christ rest on me in my weakness. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: If God answers your repeated prayer with grace rather than removal, will you receive it as an answer?

days.title: Courage When the Cost Is Real

body.p: The passage on the armour of God follows straight on from instructions about the household and the workplace. Verse nine is addressed to masters. forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven.

Then Paul says Finally, and turns to strength. The order matters. The battle he is about to describe is not only far away in some unseen realm. It is fought in how a boss treats workers, how children speak to parents, how husbands love wives. The armour is for ordinary rooms.

And the enemy's method is described in one phrase. the wiles of the devil. Wiles are schemes, tricks, slow pressure. Not usually a frontal attack, but a quiet suggestion to cut a corner, to threaten instead of reason, to give up on a hard marriage.

Doing right in those places has a real cost. The manager who refuses to cheat staff loses a bonus. The employee who will not falsify the report is passed over. Paul does not promise it will be cheap. He says be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Not ours. His.
The goal is modest and brave at once. that ye may be able to stand. Today, wherever the pressure comes, at the office or across the dinner table, aim simply to still be standing at the end of it.

line.a: The armour is for ordinary rooms.
line.b: The aim is simply to stand.

after: The schemes against you will mostly be quiet, so your faithfulness can be quiet too.
You have a Master in heaven who sees how you treat people when it costs you.
days.prayer: Lord, doing what is right is costing me something real. Make me strong in you and in the power of your might, not my own. Help me see the quiet schemes for what they are, and give me grace to stand at work and at home today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where is the quiet pressure to compromise strongest for you right now?

days.title: Courage For the Long Road

body.p: Verse thirteen is often lifted out on its own and written on exam folders and football shirts. Read in place, it is about something quieter. Paul has just said I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound.

The all things he can do are mostly the things of a long life. Being full and being hungry. Having plenty and having nothing. I am instructed, he says, which means he learned it slowly, over years, through prisons and shipwrecks and seasons of plenty.
So I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me is first of all a sentence about contentment. Christ gives Paul strength to be the same man in a full season and an empty one.

Then verse fourteen adds a tender detail. Notwithstanding ye have well done, that ye did communicate with my affliction. Paul has just said Christ is enough, and in the same breath he thanks the Philippians for helping him. Christ's strength did not make their gifts unnecessary. It often came through them.
On the long road you will have full months and lean ones. Learn what Paul learned, one season at a time. And when a friend sends help, receive it as part of how Christ strengthens you.

line.a: Paul learned to be hungry and full.
line.b: Christ was his strength in both.

after: Contentment is something you learn over years, not something you feel in a moment.
Accepting help from others is not a failure to trust Christ.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, teach me what you taught Paul, to be steady whether I have plenty or very little. Strengthen me for the long road, not only for one big moment. Thank you for the people you have sent to share my troubles, and help me receive their help with gratitude. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you using this verse for a single big moment, or for learning contentment over a long road?

days.title: Courage At the End of the Day

body.p: Paul tells Timothy to stir up the gift of God, which is in thee. The picture is of a fire that has burned low. The gift has not gone out. It just needs someone to blow on the embers.

Timothy seems to have been naturally timid, and Paul knew it. So he reminds him where the fire came from. by the putting on of my hands. It was given on a particular day, and the Giver has not taken it back.

Then the famous line. For God hath not given us the spirit of fear. Fear is real, but it is not what God gave. What he gave was power, and of love, and of a sound mind. Love sits between the other two, as if to keep power gentle and a sound mind warm.

Paul writes this as his prisoner, in chains. He is not asking Timothy to be brave from a comfortable distance. He is asking him to share in suffering according to the power of God, not according to his own reserves.

At the end of a long day, or at the end of this month, your fire may be low. That is normal. Before you sleep tonight, stir the embers. Thank God for one gift he has given you, and ask him to fan it again tomorrow.

line.b: The gift was never taken back.

after: A low fire is still a fire, and God's gift in you has not gone out.
Fear is real, but it is not what God gave you.
days.prayer: Father, it has been a long day and my fire is burning low. Thank you that you have not given me a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind. Stir up the gift you have placed in me, and give me rest tonight and courage tomorrow. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What gift of God in you has burned low and needs stirring tonight?

days.title: Prayer Before You Feel Ready

body.p: David does not begin with a speech. He begins with the voice of my cry, which is the sound a person makes before they have found any words at all.

Then he says when: in the morning, twice in a single verse. Morning is the hour when nobody feels ready. The face is unwashed, the mind is still slow, and yesterday's worry is already sitting on the edge of the bed.

The word direct carries the picture of setting things in order, the way wood was laid out on an altar before the fire came. David arranges his prayer, and then he does the second thing, the one we usually skip. He will look up. He waits to see what God does with it.
Readiness is not the entry fee. A cry is enough to begin, and the order can come after. God hears the voice before he hears the arrangement.
Tomorrow, before you reach for anything on the pillow, say one honest sentence to him. Then, somewhere between the bath and the front gate, glance up. Expect him in the hours that follow.

after: A rough prayer said in the morning is still a prayer said in the morning.
Somewhere in the day, look up, and expect to be answered.
days.prayer: my King, and my God, I do not feel ready, and I am coming anyway. Hear the voice of my cry before I have found good words. Help me set my day in order before you this morning, and then give me eyes to look up and notice where you are answering. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would you say to God tomorrow morning if you stopped waiting until you felt ready?

days.title: Prayer In the Next Step

body.p: Psalm 19 begins with the whole sky speaking, the heavens declaring and each day pouring out speech to the next. It ends with one man asking about his own mouth.

He asks for two things to be acceptable: the words of my mouth, which everyone can hear, and the meditation of my heart, which nobody can. He does not separate the public from the private. He wants both in the same condition.
Notice the word sight. Words are usually heard, but he asks for them to be acceptable in thy sight. God sees the thought before it becomes a sentence, and he sees the sentence we decided not to say.
Just before this he prays against presumptuous sins, the ones we walk into with our eyes open. Most of those begin as a thought we allowed to sit too long, and then a word.

So the next step is small. It is the next thing you say in the meeting, the next message you send your brother, the next thought you let settle while you wait at the bus stop. He calls God my strength, and my redeemer, because he knows he will need both.

line.a: The next step is usually a sentence.
line.b: Let it be one he can look at.

after: What you think in the queue becomes what you say at the counter.
God is strength for the word you have not said yet and redeemer for the one you already said.
days.prayer: O LORD, my strength and my redeemer, keep me back from the sins I choose with my eyes open. Let the words I say today and the thoughts I keep to myself be acceptable in your sight. Where I have already spoken badly, redeem it, and give me a better next sentence. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which thought have you let sit so long that it is about to come out of your mouth?

days.title: Prayer When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: The setting is loud. An army encamped, war rising on every side. You would expect the next line to be a request for the enemy to leave.

Instead David says, One thing have I desired of the LORD. The one thing is not the end of the war. It is to dwell in the house of the LORD, to look at his beauty, and to ask him questions in his temple.
That is a quiet desire in a noisy psalm. And when trouble comes, the help he describes is quiet too. God will hide him in the secret of his tabernacle. Not a parade. A hidden room.
Some seasons of prayer feel like that room. Nothing dramatic is happening, no answers are arriving, and the way feels silent. It is easy to think silence means absence. David treats it as shelter.

If your prayers lately have been plain and still, sitting on the edge of the bed with a cup of tea going cold, you may not be forgotten. You may be hidden. The house is still the house when nobody is shouting in it.

line.a: Quiet is not the same as empty.
line.b: Sometimes it is the secret room.

after: Ask for the one thing today, and let the other things wait their turn.
A hidden season can also be a held season.
days.prayer: Lord, when the way is quiet and I hear nothing back, let me still desire the one thing. Let me want you more than I want the silence to end. Hide me in your secret place, set me on the rock, and teach me to behold your beauty even when nothing seems to be happening. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: If you could ask God for only one thing this month, would it be him?

days.title: Prayer Without an Audience

body.p: A deer does not pant for show. It pants because it has been running, and the water is the only thing on its mind.
The psalmist borrows that picture for prayer: so panteth my soul after thee, O God. There is no crowd in the image. Just an animal and a stream, and a need that nobody else can feel on its behalf.

Thirst works like that. You can describe it to a friend, but they cannot drink for you. Prayer without an audience begins here, when you stop thinking about how the prayer sounds and start thinking about what you lack.

His question is when shall I come and appear before God. He wants to appear, but before one person only. Not before the church, not before the family, before God. And it is the living God he wants, someone who answers, not the memory of someone.
Try it tonight in your room, with the light off and nothing to prove. Say what you are thirsty for. Say it the way you would ask for a glass of water.

line.a: Nobody can be thirsty for you.
line.b: Nobody needs to watch you drink.

after: The truest prayers are often the ones no one else would find impressive.
Bring God your thirst, not your performance.
days.prayer: Living God, my soul is thirsty, and I am tired of praying as if someone were listening over my shoulder. Let me come before you alone, with nothing to prove. I am not asking to sound holy. I am asking for water, and you are the water I need. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: When you pray, who else are you secretly hoping will hear?

days.title: Prayer For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: Before Be still there is a great deal of noise. Bows snapping, spears cut in pieces, chariots burning. Verse nine is God ending wars across the earth.

Then God himself speaks, and the first thing he says is be still. It is not advice from a calm person to a nervous one. It is the voice of the one who has just put the weapons down, telling everyone else they can put theirs down too.

Most of us save this verse for a quiet retreat. It belongs just as much on a Tuesday, when no war is ending and the weapons are smaller: a deadline, an unpaid bill, a child who will not get dressed for school.

Stillness here is not doing nothing. It is knowing something, know that I am God, and letting that knowledge slow the hands for a minute. Then the chorus: The LORD of hosts is with us. Us. The whole tired congregation, not just the calm ones.
So on an ordinary morning, standing at the stove while the beans boil, stop for the length of one breath. Remember who has already done the fighting.

line.a: Be still is not a mood.
line.b: It is a fact about who is God.

after: Stillness can fit inside a single minute, even on a busy day.
The God of Jacob is a refuge for people who are ordinary and tired.
days.prayer: Lord of hosts, on this ordinary day my hands are full of small battles. Let me be still long enough to know that you are God and I am not. Break the bows I keep picking up. Be my refuge in the kitchen, at the desk and on the road. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What small weapon are you holding today that God has already told you to put down?

days.title: Prayer When Plans Change

body.p: David wrote this after his own life went off course, and not by accident. The heading of the psalm ties it to Bathsheba and to Nathan's visit. The future he had planned now contained a sin he could not undo.

He does not ask God to fix things. He asks, Create in me a clean heart, O God. Create is the word from the first page of the Bible, the word for making something where there was nothing. He knows repair will not be enough.

Then, renew a right spirit within me. A right spirit is a steady one, a spirit that can stand up straight again. And under it all is a fear: Cast me not away from thy presence. He is less afraid of losing the kingdom than of losing God.

Plans change for many reasons. Some are storms you did not cause. Some, like David's, are your own doing. Either way the prayer has the same shape. Not, give me back my old plan, but, make something new in me that can live in the new one.
If you are sitting in a parked car outside the office where the news was bad, or outside a house where you did wrong, this is the prayer for that seat.

line.a: You may not get the old plan back.
line.b: You can be given a new heart.

after: God does not only patch what broke; he is able to create.
When a plan is lost, his presence is the thing to hold on to.
days.prayer: God, my plans have changed, and some of it is my own fault. I do not ask you to rewind the year. Create in me a clean heart, and renew a steady spirit within me. Whatever else I lose, do not cast me away from your presence. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you asking God to restore your old plan, or to create something new in you?

days.title: Prayer In the Work at Hand

body.p: The heading of this psalm places David in the wilderness of Judah. When he writes about a dry and thirsty land, where no water is, he is describing the ground under his feet.
He begins with possession: O God, thou art my God. Before he asks for anything, he says whose he is. Then early will I seek thee, the first hours of the day given before the heat sets in.

What is striking is where he looks for God. Not back at the temple, though he remembers it. He has seen thee in the sanctuary, and he wants to see the same power out here, in the dust, where the work of surviving is.

Many of us keep God for the sanctuary hours. Sunday is for seeing him, and Monday is for the job. David will not accept that split. The God of the sanctuary is the God of the desert, and he wants to see him in both.
So the prayer of the work at hand is prayed in the workshop, at the till, in the long afternoon on the farm. Before the first task, say whose you are. Then look for him in the dry place.

line.a: The sanctuary showed him who God is.
line.b: The desert is where he needed it.

after: Seek him early in the work, before the heat of the day.
The ground you are standing on is a place God can be seen.
days.prayer: O God, you are my God, here and not only on Sunday. The work in front of me today feels dry. Let me seek you early, before the pressure comes, and let me see in this ordinary place the same power and glory I have seen in worship. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where in your work today do you most need to see what you have seen in worship?

days.title: Prayer When You Need Clarity

body.p: Clarity often arrives as a comparison. This psalm offers two of them, and both are blunt.

For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. One day near God outweighs a thousand elsewhere. Then the second: he would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than live comfortably in the tents of wickedness.
A doorkeeper stood at the threshold. Not at the centre, not in the best seat, just at the edge where people came in. The psalmist would take the edge of God's house over the middle of anywhere else.

When a decision feels foggy, it is often because we are weighing things that look the same size. The psalm helps by putting them on the right scale. Which choice keeps you nearer the house, even at the door? Which one is a tent, roomy but wrong?

The last verse says no good thing will he withhold from the upright. That is not a promise of everything you want. It means what he keeps back was not good for you to have. If two offer letters are on the table at midnight, ask which one is the doorway.

line.a: Clarity is a matter of scale.
line.b: One day near him outweighs a thousand away.

after: The edge of God's house is better than the centre of a wrong one.
What he withholds, he withholds for your good.
days.prayer: LORD God, my sun and shield, I cannot see clearly which way to go. Put my choices on the right scale. Let me prefer the door of your house to the comfort of a wrong tent, and help me trust you with whatever you choose not to give me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which option in front of you looks roomy but is really a tent you should not live in?

days.title: Prayer One Choice at a Time

body.p: In the middle of this psalm sits a small prayer that most of us need more than we admit: unite my heart to fear thy name.
It assumes a heart can be in pieces. Part of it wants God, part wants approval, part just wants to be left alone. David does not pretend otherwise. He asks for the pieces to be gathered.

Look at what comes before and after. Before it, Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth. He asks to learn and promises to walk. After it, I will praise thee, O Lord my God, with all my heart. All of it. A united heart is one that can finally praise without holding anything back.

A divided heart is not healed in one evening. It comes together the way a scattered household comes together, one decision at a time. You choose the truth in one conversation. You choose it again at lunch.
When you are standing in the market deciding whether to tell the trader she gave you too much change, that is the uniting happening. Small, unseen, one choice.

line.a: A divided heart cannot walk straight.
line.b: So he asks for it to be made one.

after: Each honest choice gathers one more piece of you toward God.
You do not need a whole heart before you start, only the next right step.
days.prayer: Lord, you are God alone, and my heart keeps splitting into many loyalties. Teach me your way and I will walk in your truth, one choice at a time. Unite my heart to fear your name, so that one day I can praise you with all of it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where is your heart most divided right now?

days.title: Prayer Under Pressure

body.p: Count the verbs in verse six. O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker. Each one goes lower than the last. Worship, then bow, then kneel, until the body is close to the ground.

Pressure pushes the other way. It tightens the shoulders, lifts the chin, makes us stand guard over our own lives. The psalm suggests that the answer to being pressed down is to go down willingly, before the one whose hands formed the dry land.
The reason given is gentle. We are the sheep of his hand. Not only of his field, of his hand, close enough to be carried.

Then the verse breaks off: To day if ye will hear his voice. The psalm goes on to warn against hardening the heart as Israel did in the wilderness, when the pressure of thirst made them quarrel with God. Pressure can harden a person or it can bend one. Today is when that is decided.

If the pressure is a hospital bill, or a manager waiting for your answer, find somewhere for two minutes, a stairwell, a quiet corner, and lower yourself. Kneel if you can. Let the body say what the mind is too tight to say.

line.a: Pressure tells you to stand guard.

after: Going low before God is not defeat; it is relief.
Today, while the pressure is on, keep your heart soft enough to hear him.
days.prayer: LORD my maker, the pressure on me is heavy and I have been standing stiff against it. I bow down. I kneel before you. I am a sheep of your hand, so carry what I cannot carry. Today, keep my heart soft enough to hear your voice. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is the pressure you are under making your heart harder, or bending it toward God?

days.title: Prayer After the Excitement Fades

body.p: People reach for this psalm at the start of things. Harvest services, dedications, the first Sunday in a new building. Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands.

But the middle verb is an unglamorous one. Serve the LORD with gladness. Serve is a word for daily labour, the kind done in the same place by the same hands for years. The psalm puts gladness inside service, not only inside celebration.

And when it gives the reason, the reason is not a feeling. Know ye that the LORD he is God. Know. Then the fact underneath everything: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves. We did not make ourselves, so we do not have to keep ourselves excited either.

Excitement fades from every good thing. The new job, the new church, the first months of marriage, the season when prayer felt warm. What is left is the knowing. We are his people and the sheep of his pasture, whether or not we feel it this week.
So if you are sweeping the same church floor you swept last year, or opening the shop again before dawn, you can still bring a song. Not because it is thrilling. Because you know whose you are.

line.b: Knowing whose you are is a foundation.

after: Gladness can live in a routine as well as in a celebration.
You did not make yourself, and you do not have to hold yourself up.
days.prayer: LORD, the excitement I once felt has gone quiet, and I miss it. Teach me to serve you with gladness anyway, in the plain work of this week. Remind me that you made me, and not I myself, and that I am still one of the sheep of your pasture. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What do you still know about God now that the feeling has faded?

days.title: Prayer In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: A difficult conversation does not give you time to look things up. Your sister is crying, or your colleague has just raised his voice, and whatever you say next will come from what is already inside you.
That is the logic of Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee. Hiding is something done ahead of time. You store water before the dry season, not during it.

The man who wrote this was not careless. He had sought God With my whole heart, and still he prays, O let me not wander from thy commandments. Wholehearted people wander too, especially when they are hurt and want to win.

And he ends as a student: teach me thy statutes. Even with the word hidden in him, he knows he has more to learn. That is a good posture for a hard talk. Not the expert who is sure, but the learner who is listening.
Before you knock on that door, or return the call you have been avoiding, take one line of Scripture with you. Say it quietly in the corridor. Let it be the thing you reach for when the heat rises.

line.a: You cannot fetch water in the middle of a fire.
line.b: Hide the word before you need it.

after: What you have stored is what you will speak when you are pressed.
Go into the hard conversation as a learner, not a judge.
days.prayer: Lord, there is a conversation ahead of me that I dread. Hide your word in my heart so that I do not sin against you or against the person in front of me. When I am hurt, do not let me wander. Teach me your statutes even while I am speaking. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which verse will you carry into the conversation you have been avoiding?

days.title: Prayer When Progress Is Slow

body.p: Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. The wondrous things are already there. He is not asking God to add them. He is asking to see what has been on the page all along.
That is worth hearing when progress feels slow. Often the problem is not that nothing is happening. It is that our eyes are fixed on the one thing that is not moving, and miss the many that are.

He also says, I am a stranger in the earth. A stranger walks slowly. He does not know the streets, he has to ask directions, he gets lost and turns back. The psalmist accepts that about himself and asks only, hide not thy commandments from me. Let me keep seeing the way, even if I walk it slowly.
His first request is modest too: that I may live, and keep thy word. Not that he may succeed quickly. That he may stay alive long enough to keep going.
If you have prayed for the same change in yourself for years, reading in the same chair every evening, ask for new eyes rather than a new chapter. There may be wonders on the slow page.

line.a: The wonders were already on the page.

after: Slow is not the same as stuck.
A stranger who keeps asking directions still arrives.
days.prayer: Lord, I am tired of how slowly I change. Open my eyes to see what you are already doing, the wonders I keep walking past. I am a stranger here and I walk slowly. Do not hide your commandments from me, and keep me living and keeping your word. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What might God already be doing that you have not had eyes to see?

days.title: Prayer At the Point of Decision

body.p: The lamp in this verse is not a floodlight. It was a small clay lamp with a wick in oil, the kind you could hold in one hand. It lit the ground near your sandals and not much more.

So when the psalmist says Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, he is describing a modest kind of guidance. Enough light for the next step. Then, as you walk, enough for the one after that. It is also a light unto my path, but the path is shown by walking it.
At a point of decision we usually want the whole road lit. Where will this lead in five years, what will it cost, who will be pleased. Scripture rarely gives that. It gives the step.

The verses either side add two things. Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way. The word clears away the wrong options first. Then, I have sworn, and I will perform it. Some decisions were already made the day you promised to follow him. You are only keeping that promise in a new place.
Standing at a junction, the admission letter in one hand and your family's opinion in the other, ask what the lamp shows of the next step. Take that one.

line.b: He gave you the next step.

after: Enough light for one step is enough to start walking.
Many decisions were settled the day you said yes to him.
days.prayer: Lord, I am standing at a decision and I want to see the end of the road. Give me light for my feet instead. Show me which ways are false so I can turn from them, and help me keep the promise I already made to follow you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What does the lamp show you about the next single step?

days.title: Prayer In the Waiting Room

body.p: David is not patient in this prayer, and he does not pretend to be. Hear me speedily, O LORD: my spirit faileth. He is at the end of himself, and he says so in the first line.

Then he asks for something very particular: Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning. It sounds like a man who has had a long night. He wants the first thing he hears when light comes to be God's kindness.

Waiting rooms are like nights. The clock on the wall seems slower than other clocks. Names are called that are not yours. Every door that opens might be news. In that kind of waiting, the soul does not need a lecture. It needs to hear love, early.

He gives his reasons plainly: for in thee do I trust, and for I lift up my soul unto thee. He is not trusting because he feels calm. He is trusting because he has nowhere better to put his soul. And at the end, I flee unto thee to hide me. Waiting can become a hiding place if it is waiting in him.
If you are sitting on a plastic chair in a hospital corridor tonight, you can pray this almost word for word. Ask to hear his lovingkindness when morning comes, whatever the doctor says.

line.b: Ask for kindness at first light.

after: It is not faithless to ask God to hurry.
Lift your soul to him while the clock is slow.
days.prayer: LORD, my spirit is failing in this waiting. Hear me quickly. Do not hide your face from me. When morning comes, let the first thing I hear be your lovingkindness. I lift up my soul to you because I have nowhere else to put it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it mean to hear God's kindness first tomorrow morning, before any other news?

days.title: Prayer When You Feel Small

body.p: Wisdom is speaking in this chapter, standing where the roads meet and calling to anyone passing by. In verse sixteen she lists who relies on her: By me princes rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth.

If you feel small, that line might make it worse. Princes, nobles, judges. Important people making important decisions. But the next verse widens the door. I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me. No title is required. Only love and seeking.

The wisdom that guides rulers is available to the woman frying akara at the roadside, to the student in the back row, to the cleaner who arrives before the managers. The only condition is that you look for it, and look early, before the day has filled your hands.

Even the riches she offers are a different kind: durable riches and righteousness. Not wealth that can vanish in a bad month, but the kind that lasts because it is joined to doing right. The small often hold more of that than the great.
Feeling small is not the same as being shut out. Seek her tomorrow at first light, in whatever corner you wake up in.

line.b: So can anyone who seeks it early.

after: God does not ration wisdom by rank.
Durable riches are the ones that survive a bad year.
days.prayer: Lord, I feel small beside the people who seem to run things. Remind me that your wisdom loves those who love it, and is found by those who seek it early. I am seeking now. Give me what lasts, the riches of righteousness, rather than what fades. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where in your small corner do you most need wisdom this week?

days.title: Prayer Through an Open Door

body.p: These words were written in a letter. Jeremiah sent it to the exiles in Babylon, people carried away from home and told by false prophets they would be back soon. Jeremiah told them the truth. Seventy years. Build houses. Plant gardens. Pray for the city.

Then comes this: Then shall ye call upon me, and ye shall go and pray unto me, and I will hearken unto you. The word then matters. The promise is not that the door opens tomorrow. It is that God is listening the whole time it stays closed.

And the seeking he asks for is not casual: when ye shall search for me with all your heart. Searching is what you do for something lost, turning out drawers, looking under the bed. God says, look for me like that, and I will be found of you. He lets himself be found.
Only after that does he speak about roads home: I will turn away your captivity. The open door comes from the God who was found, not the other way round.
If you are in a place you did not choose, a city far from home, a job you feel stuck in, begin by searching for him there. Doors open from inside that search.

after: God hears in exile as clearly as he hears at home.
Search for him as you would search for something precious you have lost.
days.prayer: LORD, I am in a place I did not choose and the door looks shut. Teach me to search for you here with all my heart. Thank you that you hear me even before anything changes. Let yourself be found by me, and in your time bring me where you want me to be. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you searching for the open door more earnestly than you are searching for God?

days.title: Prayer When the Answer Is No

body.p: Jesus says something unsettling about the people who prayed on street corners. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. They wanted to be seen, and they were seen. Their prayer got exactly what it was aiming at.
Sometimes a yes is the poorest answer there is. To be admired by people for an afternoon and miss the Father altogether is a yes nobody should want.

The alternative is the closet, the small inner room, when thou hast shut thy door. There you pray to thy Father which is in secret. Not a judge, not a machine, a Father. And Jesus warns against vain repetitions, praying as if many words could force an answer out of heaven.

That room is where a no can be heard without despair. A no from a machine would mean it was broken. A no from a Father who seeth in secret means he has seen something we have not. It still hurts, and Jesus does not ask us to pretend otherwise. But it is spoken by someone who loves us and is still in the room.

If you have been asking for months and the answer seems to be no, take it somewhere quiet, a bedroom with the door closed, the bathroom if that is all you have. Say it was hard. Then stay a while with the Father who saw.

line.a: A no from a machine means it is broken.
line.b: A no from a Father means he saw something.

after: You cannot talk God into an answer by saying more.
The Father who says no is still in the room with you.
days.prayer: Father, I asked and the answer seems to be no, and it hurts. I will not try to wear you down with many words. I bring it into the quiet room instead. You see in secret, so you see this too. Help me trust that you saw what I could not. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Can you tell your Father honestly how the no feels, without trying to change his mind with more words?

days.title: Prayer In What You Already Have

body.p: Verse seven is famous on its own. Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. The verse before it is quoted far less, and it is a little strange.

neither cast ye your pearls before swine. Jesus assumes his listeners are already carrying something holy, something precious enough to be trampled. Before he tells them to ask for more, he tells them to take care of what they have.

That changes how the asking sounds. It is not a beggar at a gate with nothing. It is a child who has already been given pearls, coming back to the same Father for bread. For every one that asketh receiveth. Every one. Those already holding gifts are invited to keep asking.

Gratitude and asking are not opposites. The person who notices what is already in their hands, a roof, a friend who calls, a mind that still works, often asks more freely, because they know the kind of Father they are asking.

Tonight, before you list what you need, put your hands on what you have. The plate in front of you. The child asleep in the next room. Name them as gifts. Then ask, seek and knock from inside that gratitude.

line.a: You are not asking with empty hands.
line.b: There are pearls in them already.

after: Look after what is holy before you ask for more.
Asking from gratitude sounds different from asking from fear.
days.prayer: Father, I have come to you so often with empty-handed asking that I have forgotten what you have already given. Thank you for the pearls in my hands today. Help me guard what is holy. And from here, let me ask, seek and knock as a child who knows you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What precious thing has God already given you that you have been treating carelessly?

days.title: Prayer When Nobody Notices

body.p: The evening before, the whole town of Capernaum had gathered at the door. And he healed many that were sick of divers diseases, and cast out many devils. If anyone had a reason to sleep in, it was Jesus.

Instead, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed. Mark gives none of the words. No crowd saw it. The most important hour of the day happened where nobody could praise it.

The only people who noticed were the disciples, and only because they wanted him back. And Simon and they that were with him followed after him. The sense is that they hunted for him. The crowds were waiting, and Jesus was missing.

What the town saw was healing. What it did not see was the dark hour that came before. That is often how it is. The visible work rests on an invisible one, and the invisible one is easy to skip because nobody will know.

If your praying happens at five in the morning on a mat beside the bed, while the house is asleep and the street is still quiet, nobody may ever notice. Jesus kept that same hour. It was enough that the Father was there.

line.b: Nobody saw the hour before it.

after: The hidden hour holds up the visible day.
Prayer that nobody notices is still prayer the Father keeps.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, you rose before day to pray where no one could see you. Give me a love for the hidden hour. When nobody notices my prayers, let it be enough that the Father does. Strengthen the unseen part of my life so that the seen part can stand. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would your prayer life look like if no one ever found out about it?

days.title: Prayer With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: Jesus says her name twice. Martha, Martha. People repeat a name when they love someone and want them to stop for a moment and really hear. It is not the voice of a teacher scolding. It is closer to a friend putting a hand on a shoulder.

Martha is not wrong to cook. Someone had to feed a room full of guests, and Luke tells us she was the one who welcomed Jesus into the house. The problem is the word many. thou art careful and troubled about many things. Her mind is pulled in a dozen directions.
Against the many he sets one: But one thing is needful. Mary has chosen it, and Jesus says it shall not be taken away from her. The meal will be eaten and forgotten. The listening will stay.

Prayer with both feet on the ground does not mean abandoning the work. It means letting the one thing hold the many things in their proper place. Martha could have sat for ten minutes and then cooked with a quieter heart.
If you are in the kitchen tonight, pot on the fire, phone buzzing, guests on their way, hear him say your name twice. Then sit, even for a short while, before you stand again.

line.a: Many things will always be waiting.

after: Jesus does not despise the work; he gives it its proper size.
What you receive while listening cannot be taken away.
days.prayer: Lord, you know my name and you know how many things I am anxious about. Say it to me twice today until I stop. Help me choose the one thing needful before I return to the many. Let the work of my hands come from a quiet heart. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are the many things pulling at you, and when will you sit for the one?

days.title: Prayer When You Must Begin Again

body.p: These disciples were not new to prayer. They were Jewish men who had heard the psalms since childhood and kept the set hours of prayer. And still, after watching Jesus, one of them asks, Lord, teach us to pray.
Notice when he asks: as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased. He waited. He watched Jesus pray all the way to the end, and something in what he saw made his own praying feel unfinished.

That is permission for anyone who has prayed for years and feels they have forgotten how. You are allowed to start over. Grown disciples did. They even mention that John taught his followers, as if to say, everyone else seems to know, and we want to learn too.

Jesus does not hand them a technique. He gives them a first word: Our Father which art in heaven. Beginning again starts there. Not with getting better at prayer, but with remembering who you are speaking to, and that he is ours, not only mine.
If your prayers have gone stale, say the Lord's Prayer slowly on the bus tomorrow, one line between each stop. Treat it as a first lesson. Many saints went back to it at the end of their lives.

line.a: They had prayed all their lives.
line.b: They still asked to be taught.

after: Beginning again is not failure; it is discipleship.
Every fresh start in prayer can begin with the word Father.
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to pray. I have done it for years and somewhere along the way it went dry. I want to start again like a learner. Let me begin with you as our Father, hallow your name, and want your kingdom and your will more than my own. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What has made your praying feel unfinished lately?

days.title: Prayer In the Middle of the Work

body.p: This conversation happened at a well, around noon, beside a water jar. The woman had come to do a chore. She was not on her way to worship. She was in the middle of the work.

She had asked a question about places: this mountain, or Jerusalem? Jesus answers by lifting worship off the map. the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth. Not here or there. Spirit and truth, wherever a person is standing.

Then he adds the most surprising line: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. We think of ourselves as the ones looking for God. Here God is the one looking, and he came looking at a well in the heat of the day.
Her reply shows she is still thinking of later: when he is come, he will tell us all things. Jesus is about to tell her that later is now. The one she is waiting for is sitting at the well.

So worship does not wait for the end of the shift. It can happen while you lift crates in the warehouse or carry water for the house, if it is done in spirit and in truth. The Father may already be looking for you there.

line.b: The Father came looking for a worshipper.

after: Worship is not tied to a building; it is tied to spirit and truth.
The hour you are in is the hour God is seeking you.
days.prayer: Father, I am in the middle of my work, and I did not expect to meet you here. Thank you that you seek worshippers in ordinary places. Let me worship you in spirit and in truth while my hands are busy, honest about who I am and open to who you are. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where in your daily chores could you worship in spirit and in truth today?

days.title: Prayer When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Jesus said this on the last night, after supper, with Judas already gone out into the dark. The disciples were frightened. Something terrible was coming and they could feel it.
Before he gives them anything to do, he tells them what they already are. Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you. Clean first. The command comes second.

And the command is the gentlest possible: Abide in me, and I in you. Abide means stay. Remain. Do not leave. Fear always speaks first and it speaks loudly, telling you to run, to fix, to control. Jesus speaks after it, quietly, and says stay.

A branch does not strain to produce grapes. It stays joined to the vine and the life moves through it. for without me ye can do nothing sounds harsh until you hear it in a frightened room. It means you do not have to carry this alone, because you were never able to.
When fear wakes you at three in the morning with a list of disasters, let it speak, and then answer it with his words. I am clean. I will stay. Then lie back down as a branch, not a soldier.

after: You are made clean before you are made fruitful.
Staying joined to Christ is the work fear keeps interrupting.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, fear spoke first again today, and it was loud. Thank you that you have already made me clean by your word. Help me abide in you instead of running. I cannot bear fruit by myself, so keep me joined to you, the vine. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: When fear speaks first, what does it usually tell you to do instead of staying with Christ?

days.title: Prayer With an Open Hand

body.p: Paul does not start with a demand. He starts with I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God. Therefore points back over eleven chapters of grace. The asking only comes after all that giving.
What he asks for is specific: that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice. Bodies. Not only thoughts or good intentions. Hands, feet, eyes, the tongue, the hours of the day.

A living sacrifice is a strange idea. The old sacrifices were offered once and that was the end. A living one stays on the altar while it is still breathing, which means it can climb off. So the offering has to be made with an open hand, again and again, each time you notice it has closed.

Then the second verse: be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. Paul does not say transform yourself. He says be transformed. An open hand is not a fist straining to change. It is a hand held out, letting God do the renewing.

Try it with your actual hands. Before work starts, open them on your lap, palms up, in the danfo or at your desk. Say, these are yours today. It will feel small. It is where Paul would have you begin.

line.a: A closed fist keeps what it holds.
line.b: An open hand can be filled.

after: Mercy comes first; offering yourself is the reply.
When you notice you have climbed off the altar, simply climb back on.
days.prayer: God of mercy, you have given me so much before asking anything of me. I present my body to you today, my hands, my words and my hours. When I take them back, help me open my hand again. Renew my mind, and let me prove your good and perfect will. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which part of your body or your day do you find hardest to hold out to God?

days.title: Prayer When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Romans 12 reads like a list, and verse twelve is three short items in it. Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer. Each is only three words long, as if Paul knew they would be said under strain.
Hope, by its nature, is about what cannot yet be seen. You do not hope for the thing already in your hand. So rejoicing in hope is joy about a horizon you cannot see past.

Patience in tribulation is the middle step. It does not say happy in tribulation. It says patient, which means staying under the weight without giving up. And continuing instant in prayer means keeping at it steadily, the way someone keeps a lamp burning through a long night.

Notice what surrounds those three. Before them, Not slothful in business. After them, Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality. When you cannot see far ahead, Paul does not tell you to stare harder at the future. He points you to the work in front of you and the neighbour at your door.
If the next year is fog, cook a little extra and take it to the widow down the road. Then pray again tonight. The near things are what you can see. Do those, and keep your hope for the far ones.

line.b: You can see the person at your door.

after: Hope is joy about a horizon you cannot yet see past.
When the future is fog, do the near good thing and keep praying.
days.prayer: Lord, I cannot see far ahead and it frightens me. Teach me to rejoice in hope, to be patient under what I am carrying, and to keep on praying. While the future stays hidden, show me the near need I can meet today, and give me a welcome for whoever comes to my door. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is one near need you can meet today while the far future stays unclear?

days.title: Prayer In the Honest Answer

body.p: After the long description of armour, the helmet and the sword, Paul does not add another piece. He adds a way of wearing all of it: Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit.

Then comes a small, honest request. And for me. The apostle who wrote so much of the New Testament asks the church to pray for him. And he names exactly what he lacks: that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly.

Paul wrote this from prison, an ambassador in chains, as he says a verse later. You might expect him to ask for release. He asks for words, and for courage to say them. He admits that boldness does not come naturally even to him.

That is what an honest answer in prayer often looks like. Not a list of needs dressed up to sound spiritual, but the real thing. I am afraid to speak. I need words. Please pray for me. It takes humility to say that to the people you lead.
Tomorrow, when someone at work or in your fellowship asks how they can pray for you, tell them the true thing. Not the polite version. Paul did, and the church has been praying with him ever since.

line.a: Paul asked for words, not freedom.
line.b: He was honest about what he lacked.

after: Telling people your real prayer request is a kind of courage.
Prayer is not one more piece of armour; it is how the armour is worn.
days.prayer: Lord, I often give people the polite version of what I need. Make me honest like Paul. Give me words when I must speak, and the boldness to open my mouth for what is true. Help me pray always, for myself and for all your people, with perseverance. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: If someone asked how to pray for you today, what would the honest answer be?

days.title: Prayer When the Cost Is Real

body.p: Paul wrote this letter in chains, not knowing whether he would live or die. When he says Be careful for nothing, he is not a man without trouble. The cost of following Christ was sitting on his wrists.

So the instruction is not, stop caring. Careful here means anxious, full of care. The alternative he offers is not denial but speech: in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. Every thing. Including the costly things.

Look at what he does not promise. He does not say God will remove the cost or grant every request. He promises that the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds. Keep is a soldier's word. It means to stand guard.

This peace does not explain the situation. It passes understanding, which means it often makes no sense to the people watching. It simply stands at the door of your heart while the hard thing goes on.

If obedience has cost you a promotion, a friendship, or your family's approval, name that to God, with whatever thanks you can honestly find. Then let his peace stand guard at the door while you go to work tomorrow.

line.a: He did not promise the cost would go.
line.b: He promised a guard at the door.

after: Bring the costly thing to God by name, with whatever thanks you can find.
The peace of God can stand guard even where nothing has been explained.
days.prayer: Lord, following you has cost me something real, and I feel it today. I bring it to you by name, with the thanks I can honestly give. I do not ask you to explain. I ask your peace to keep my heart and mind through Christ Jesus. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What has following Christ cost you that you have not yet told him about plainly?

days.title: Prayer For the Long Road

body.p: Colossians 4 opens with a word to masters about treating servants fairly, and then, with no change of tone, Paul says, Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving. Prayer sits among the duties of an ordinary household, next to paying people what is right.
Continue is a long road word. It assumes you will get tired, that some days prayer will feel like walking uphill in the heat. The instruction is not to feel strongly. It is to keep going.

Watch adds something. It is the word for staying awake. You think of the disciples in Gethsemane, asked to watch and falling asleep. A long road dulls the eyes. Watching means praying with your attention switched on, noticing what God is doing along the way.

And thanksgiving keeps it from turning grim. Paul is in chains, for which I am also in bonds, and still he wants thanks to run alongside the asking. He asks for a door of utterance rather than a door out of prison.

On a long road you do not pray once and arrive. You pray in the morning queue for water, at the end of a twelve hour shift, and again next month when nothing has changed. Keep your eyes open. Give thanks for the mile you just walked.

line.a: A long road makes the eyes heavy.
line.b: Watch, and give thanks for each mile.

after: Continuing in prayer is mostly a matter of not stopping.
Thanksgiving keeps a long prayer from turning bitter.
days.prayer: Lord, this road is long and I am tempted to stop praying. Help me continue. Keep me awake to what you are doing, and give me thanks for the small mercies along the way. Open doors for your word, even where I feel bound. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What have you stopped watching for because the road has been long?

days.title: Prayer At the End of the Day

body.p: Two of these verses are among the shortest in the Bible. Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. You could write them both on the back of your hand.

Without ceasing cannot mean speaking words every second. Paul made tents, travelled, argued and slept. It means prayer that is never fully switched off, a conversation you keep returning to all day, like calling out now and then to a friend in the next room.

The end of the day is when that conversation becomes visible. Lying down, you can look back and see where you spoke to God and where you forgot. That is not a reason for guilt. It is a chance to pick the thread up again.

Then verse eighteen: In every thing give thanks. In, not for. Paul does not ask you to thank God for the argument or the bad diagnosis. He asks you to find something to thank him for inside it. And he says plainly, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.

Tonight, before sleep, walk back through the day from morning to now, the bus, the office, the meal, the call. In each, find one thing to thank him for. Then tell him you will take up the conversation again in the morning.

after: The day ends, but the conversation with God does not have to.
Look back tonight and find one gift hidden in each hour.
days.prayer: Father, the day is ending. I look back and see where I talked with you and where I forgot you. Thank you for what you gave me in every part of it, even the hard parts. Keep the conversation open while I sleep, and wake me ready to continue it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where in today did you forget to speak to God, and what can you thank him for in that hour?

days.title: Prayer For What Comes Next

body.p: James puts a tender promise inside a severe paragraph. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Around it are instructions to submit, to resist the devil, and then one of the hardest lines in the letter, let your laughter be turned to mourning.

The people he is writing to are not at their best. He calls them ye sinners and ye double minded. They have been fighting each other and praying with wrong motives. And it is to them, not to the polished, that the invitation is given. Come near. He will come near too.

The mourning is not meant to crush them. It is the honest sorrow of people who have seen what their divided hearts have done. You cannot draw near while pretending nothing is wrong. Clean hands and a purified heart begin with tears more often than with smiles.

That is a good word for what comes next. A month of prayer is ending. Another will begin, and you will not be perfect in it. But the pattern is simple. You take one honest step toward God, and he meets you with his own.
So tomorrow, wherever you wake, in a crowded room in Lagos or a quiet flat far from home, take that step. Confess the thing you already know. Then expect him to draw near.

after: The invitation to come near is given to sinners, not to the finished.
Honest sorrow is often the first step into God's nearness.
days.prayer: God, as one month ends and another begins, I want to draw near to you. I am double minded, and I know it. Cleanse my hands and purify my heart. Let me grieve what needs grieving, and then meet me as you promised you would. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What honest step toward God are you ready to take next?

days.title: Wisdom Before You Feel Ready

body.p: Most of us wait to feel ready before we take God seriously. We want to understand first, and then we will fear him. Proverbs puts it the other way round.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Beginning. Not the prize handed out at the end of a long course, but the first step through the door. Solomon has just promised to help the reader understand proverbs and dark sayings, the riddles of life, and before he explains a single one, he says where understanding starts.
That means you do not have to be wise to begin. You have to be willing to bow. Reverence comes before the answers, and it is often what makes the answers make sense when they arrive.

Then the very next line turns homely: My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother. The fear of God is learned at a kitchen table long before it is learned in a library.

If you are facing a decision this week and feel unqualified, you are not disqualified. Start where Proverbs starts. Kneel by the bed before you open the spreadsheet, and let the first thing you bring to the choice be honour for the God who sees it.

after: You do not need all the knowledge to start. You need the beginning of it, and the beginning is bowing.
Some of the wisest things you know were said to you by a parent who never read a book on wisdom.
days.prayer: Lord, I keep waiting until I feel ready, as if readiness were the entry fee. Teach me to start with reverence instead. Before I plan, before I argue with myself, let me bow before you, and help me listen to the good instruction you have already placed around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What decision are you postponing until you feel ready, when what it needs first is reverence?

days.title: Wisdom In the Next Step

body.p: He layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous. The picture is of a storehouse. Grain put by in a good season so that there is bread in a lean one.

That changes how we think about the next step. We tend to imagine God handing out guidance on the spot or not at all, and we panic when nothing comes in the moment. Proverbs says he has been laying it up already, before you knew you would need it.

Notice where it comes from: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding. Wisdom here is spoken. It is not a feeling that arrives in the chest but a word that has been said, and much of it is already written down for you.

And it comes with protection: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly. A buckler is a small shield, the kind you carry close. Not a fortress you hide inside, but cover for someone who is still walking.

So the next step may not need a new revelation. It may need you to go back to the store. The passage you read last month, the counsel your pastor gave, the verse your grandmother repeated over the cooking pot. Open the cupboard before you decide it is empty.

line.a: You are asking for bread today.
line.b: He stored it up long ago.

after: Guidance is often not missing. It is stored where you have not looked lately.
Walk the step you can see, and trust the small shield on your arm.
days.prayer: Father, I keep asking for fresh direction as if you had never spoken. Thank you for the wisdom you have laid up for me. Help me go back to what you have already said, and give me courage to take the next step while you shield me as I walk. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What wisdom has God already stored up for you that you have stopped returning to?

days.title: Wisdom When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: Lean is a body word. You lean on a wall when your legs are tired, on a stick when the path is rough, on a friend at a funeral. Leaning is what you do with your weight.

Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. Solomon does not tell us to throw our understanding away. He tells us not to put our full weight on it. Think, plan, consider, but do not rest your whole self on the thinking.
That matters most when the way is quiet. When God seems to say nothing, our own understanding gets loud. It fills the silence with theories about what he must be doing and why he has not answered.
The promise that follows is not that he will explain. It is that he shall direct thy paths. Direction is something you often see only by looking back. A quiet road can still be a directed one.

If you are on a bus home tonight with no word about the job, the marriage, the move, practise leaning differently. Say to God what you know and what you do not. Then lay your weight on him, not on your guesses, and acknowledge him in the small ways you can still see.

line.a: Your understanding can walk beside you.
line.b: It was never built to carry you.

after: Silence from heaven is not the same as absence from heaven.
Notice where you are resting your weight today, and shift it.
days.prayer: Lord, the way is quiet and my mind is filling the silence with fears. I will still think and plan, but I do not want to lean my whole life on my own reasoning. I lean on you. Direct my paths even when I cannot see that you are doing it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you leaning your full weight on your own understanding right now?

days.title: Wisdom Without an Audience

body.p: Be not wise in thine own eyes. We usually worry about looking foolish in front of others. Proverbs worries about something quieter, looking wise in front of ourselves.

Your own eyes are the audience that never leaves. They watch every choice and they are easily impressed. Most self-deception does not happen on a stage. It happens alone, in the private speech we give ourselves about why this shortcut is fine.
