The cure is twofold and plain: fear the LORD, and depart from evil. Turn your attention to the one whose opinion is true, and then walk away from the thing you were justifying.

Look where the passage says the benefit lands: health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones. The navel and the marrow. Places nobody sees. This is not a promise that faithful people never fall ill. It is a picture of wholeness reaching the hidden centre of a person, the very place where unconfessed things ache.

Wisdom without an audience looks like the office worker who corrects an expense claim nobody would have checked. Or the student who hands back the leaked exam paper unread. No one claps. Something deep in the bones is quieter afterwards.

line.a: The hardest audience to fool is God.

after: Your private reasons deserve as much honesty as your public ones.
The good you do unseen still reaches the marrow.
days.prayer: Lord, I am very good at convincing myself. Show me where I have been wise in my own eyes. Give me the reverence to care more about your view than mine, and the courage to turn from what I have been excusing, even when nobody else would ever know. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What have you been calling wise in your own eyes that you would hesitate to explain to God?

days.title: Wisdom For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: With all thy getting get understanding. The phrase assumes something. It assumes you are already getting.

Getting is what most days are made of. Getting the children to school, getting stock for the shop, getting the rent together, getting a reply from the client. Solomon does not tell his son to stop all that and go up a mountain. He says, in the middle of all your getting, get this as well.

That is good news for an ordinary day. Wisdom is not reserved for retreats. It is gathered at the same time as everything else, the way a trader in a busy market keeps one ear on the customer and one eye on the scale.

And wisdom is spoken of as a person here, someone you love and embrace: Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her, and she shall keep thee. You do not just study her. You keep company with her, and she keeps you.

Pick one ordinary errand today. Between the traffic and the shopping list, ask what understanding this moment could give you. Patience with the slow cashier, honesty about the price, attention to the person in front of you. Get that along with the groceries.

line.a: You are getting things all day.
line.b: Get understanding while you are at it.

after: Wisdom does not ask you to leave your errands. It asks to come along.
The most ordinary day still has something to teach the person who is listening.
days.prayer: Lord, my days are full of getting, and most of it is necessary. In the middle of it all, help me get understanding too. Let me not rush past what you want to teach me in traffic, at work, in the kitchen. Keep me close to your wisdom, and let her keep me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Among all the things you are trying to get this week, where does understanding rank?

days.title: Wisdom When Plans Change

body.p: When plans change, we look outward. The visa refused, the contract cancelled, the wedding postponed. We study the circumstances, which is natural. Proverbs points us to a different place.
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life. The issues are the outflows, the springs. Whatever life comes out of you will come from the heart, not from the plan.

Plans are things you hold. The heart is something you keep, the way a watchman keeps a gate. You can lose a plan in one phone call. You can lose a heart slowly, through bitterness that is allowed in a little each night.

Notice what comes straight after: Put away from thee a froward mouth, and perverse lips put far from thee. The heart and the mouth sit side by side. When things fall apart, the mouth is often the first sign of what the heart has let in. Complaint becomes cynicism, and cynicism becomes a way of talking about God.
If your plans changed this week, grieve them honestly. Then guard the gate. Watch what you say about it at the dinner table, because the children are listening and so is your own soul.

line.a: Plans can be cancelled from outside.
line.b: The heart is lost or kept from within.

after: You may not control what changed, but you can keep watch over what it does to you.
Listen to your own words today. They will tell you how the gate is holding.
days.prayer: Lord, my plans have shifted and I feel unsteady. I bring you the disappointment honestly. Help me guard my heart so that bitterness does not move in. Set a watch over my mouth, and let what flows out of me still be life for the people around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What has a change of plans been doing to the way you speak?

days.title: Wisdom In the Work at Hand

body.p: One line appears twice in three verses: but a prating fool shall fall. Proverbs rarely wastes words, so when it repeats itself, it wants us to notice.

A prating fool is a chatterer. Someone whose mouth is always running ahead of his hands. In the first verse he is set beside The wise in heart who will receive commandments. The wise person takes the instruction and gets on with it. The fool talks about it.
Every workplace knows both. The colleague who explains in every meeting what should be done, and the one who quietly does it. Proverbs says the talker will fall, not always quickly, but surely.

In between sits a lovely line: He that walketh uprightly walketh surely. Surely means securely. The honest worker does not need to remember which story she told to whom. Her footing is simple because her ways are straight.

Look at the task in front of you today, the report, the farm, the stall, the ward round. Receive the instruction you have been given and do it well, without announcing it. Let your work speak more than your commentary on the work.

after: Straight paths are easier to walk because there is nothing to keep track of.
Do one task today without telling anyone about it.
days.prayer: Lord, I can talk a great deal about what I will do. Make me someone who receives instruction and acts on it. Give me integrity in my work, so that I walk securely and have nothing to hide. Quiet my need to be seen working, and let me simply work well. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is there a task you have talked about more than you have done?

days.title: Wisdom When You Need Clarity

body.p: When we are confused, we usually reach for more words. We talk it through, then talk it through again, and the phone call becomes an hour, and we feel no clearer at the end.

In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise. Proverbs is not against conversation. It is against volume. The more we say, the more room there is for exaggeration, for blame, for the half truth that slips out because we were tired of listening to ourselves.
The verse before names two ways words go wrong: hiding hatred behind polite lips, and spreading slander. Both happen most easily when we are talking a lot and thinking little.

Then comes the image: The tongue of the just is as choice silver. Choice silver has been refined. The dross has been burned off. A just person's words are fewer because they have been through the fire first.

If you need clarity about something, try subtraction. Before you ring a third friend, sit on the edge of the bed and write down in three sentences what is actually true. Say those to God. Clarity often comes not from saying more but from saying less, and saying it to him.

line.a: More words, more room for sin.
line.b: Fewer words, more room for light.

after: Refined silver is mostly a matter of what was taken away.
Say less today, and mean all of it.
days.prayer: Lord, when I am anxious I talk and talk and still feel lost. Teach me to refrain my lips. Burn away the careless words, the gossip, the exaggeration, and make my speech like refined silver. Give me the clarity that comes from being quiet before you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would you say about your situation if you could use only three honest sentences?

days.title: Wisdom One Choice at a Time

body.p: In the multitude of counsellors there is safety is quoted often, usually on its own. Here it sits between two other sayings, and they explain it.

Before it: A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. After it comes a warning about standing surety for a stranger, guaranteeing a debt for someone you do not really know.

Put together, the three verses describe one choice we make again and again: whom do we let in? Counsel brings safety only if the counsellors keep confidences. And a promise made to a stranger can cost you dearly. Good counsel is not about numbers alone. It is about trustworthy people.
This is how wisdom usually works. Not one grand decision but many small ones about who hears your business, whose advice you weigh, whose loan you sign.

Before you share your trouble at the next fellowship meeting, or sign for a cousin's friend at the bank, pause. Ask whether this person has a faithful spirit. Choose two or three who have kept your secrets before, and bring them the matter. That is one choice, and it shapes the next.

after: The people you confide in are part of your wisdom.
Be the kind of counsellor who keeps the matter covered.
days.prayer: Lord, help me choose well whom I trust. Give me friends of a faithful spirit, and make me one. Keep me from careless promises and from spreading what was told to me in confidence. Guide me one choice at a time, through people who love you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who are the two or three people of faithful spirit you would trust with your hardest decision?

days.title: Wisdom Under Pressure

body.p: A fool's wrath is presently known. Presently, in the older English, means at once. Immediately. The same minute.
That is the mark Proverbs gives the fool under pressure. Not that he gets angry, everyone does, but that his anger shows up the moment it is felt. No delay between the spark and the shout.

The prudent person is described in contrast: a prudent man covereth shame. He covers it. He holds the insult for a moment before deciding what to do with it. That might mean answering later, or not at all, or dealing with it privately rather than in front of the whole office.
The verse before adds a quieter thought, that a man is satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth. What we say under pressure does not vanish. It grows into something we will later have to eat.

Pressure has a way of shrinking time. The boss's message lands, the child spills the drink, a driver cuts in front of you on the expressway. Wisdom makes a little space. Take a breath. Ask yourself whether this needs saying now. The delay is not weakness. It is where prudence lives.

line.a: The fool's anger arrives on time.
line.b: The wise one makes it wait.

after: A pause of a few seconds can save a relationship of many years.
Whatever you say under pressure today, you will meet again later.
days.prayer: Lord, I react so quickly when I am pressed. Put a space between what I feel and what I say. Help me cover what should be covered and speak only what will bear good fruit. When the pressure rises today, steady me with your Spirit. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: How much time usually passes between your anger and your words?

days.title: Wisdom After the Excitement Fades

body.p: The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul. The degree is finished, the house is bought, the baby is home. For a while the sweetness carries you.

Then the excitement fades, as it always does, and ordinary life resumes. What shapes you now is not the achievement but the company. The next verse makes that turn: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise.
Walketh is a slow word. It is not about one dramatic meeting with a mentor. It is about whose pace you match over months, whose jokes you laugh at, whose habits rub off on you without your noticing.

The warning is serious: a companion of fools shall be destroyed. Rarely in a day. Usually by small agreements, an evening here, a shrug at sin there, until the drift has carried you a long way from where you began.

When the celebration is over, look at who is walking beside you. The friends from the old season may still be the right ones, or they may not. Find a wiser person and ask to share a lunch break or a walk after church. Sweet moments pass. Companions stay.

line.b: The company you keep does not.

after: Your friendships are quietly writing the next chapter of your life.
Walk a little way with someone wiser today.
days.prayer: Lord, thank you for the good things you have let me reach. Now that the excitement has settled, help me choose my companions well. Bring wise people alongside me, and give me humility to learn from them. Keep me from drifting with those who mock your ways. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose pace have you been matching since the last big season of your life ended?

days.title: Wisdom In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: There is an unsettling phrase in this passage: the fool rageth, and is confident. Rage and confidence in the same breath. The angrier he gets, the surer he is.
Most of us have been that person in a hard conversation. Heat rising, certainty rising with it. The two feed each other until we cannot imagine being wrong.

Proverbs sets two other people beside him. One is the simple who believeth every word, the one who takes in whatever is said without testing it. The other is the prudent man who looketh well to his going. He watches his steps.

A difficult conversation needs that kind of watching. You listen without swallowing everything whole. You speak without letting anger pose as conviction. And the wise man feareth, and departeth from evil. A little holy caution is not cowardice. It is the right posture when emotions are high.

Before the conversation with your spouse tonight, or your landlord, or the elder at church, notice your confidence level. If it is rising with your temperature, slow down. Ask one question before you make one point. Look well to your going.

after: Feeling sure and being right are not the same thing.
In every hard conversation, watch your step as well as your point.
days.prayer: Lord, I have mistaken my anger for certainty too often. Give me the wisdom to watch my steps in hard conversations. Help me not to believe everything I hear, nor to rage when I feel wronged. Let me listen first and speak with care. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: In your next difficult conversation, how will you tell the difference between conviction and anger?

days.title: Wisdom When Progress Is Slow

body.p: A soft answer turneth away wrath. The verb is gentle. A soft answer does not crush anger or win the argument in one blow. It turns it, the way you turn a heavy cart, a little at a time.

That is why soft answers can feel useless. You speak kindly once and the other person is still angry. You do it again a week later and see little change. Grievous words get faster results. They stir up anger immediately, and it can feel like something is happening.
But turning is still moving. A relationship can be slowly rotated away from war by many small, mild replies.

The second verse adds a detail worth noticing: The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright. Knowing the right thing to say is not the same as using it rightly. The fool also has knowledge. He just pours it out, all at once, without care for timing or tone.

If you are in a long, slow situation, a teenager who is shut away, a colleague who resents you, a mother in law who will not warm, keep giving the soft answer. Count progress in degrees, not miles. You may look up in a year and find the cart is facing a different way.

after: Slow progress in love is still progress.
Use what you know rightly today, not just loudly.
days.prayer: Lord, I want to see change quickly and I am tired of being gentle without results. Give me patience to keep answering softly. Help me use what I know with care and good timing. Turn hard hearts slowly, including mine, and let me trust you with the pace. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where have you given up on soft answers because they seemed to work too slowly?

days.title: Wisdom At the Point of Decision

body.p: Without counsel purposes are disappointed. Purposes are plans. Disappointed is a strong word here. It means broken, frustrated, brought to nothing.

The verse does not say plans without counsel are slightly weaker. It says they tend to fall apart. And the opposite: in the multitude of counsellors they are established. Given footing. Made to stand.

The point of decision is exactly where we are least inclined to ask. We have thought it through, we are excited or frightened, and asking feels like slowing down. Sometimes we avoid counsel because we suspect what it will say.

Verse 23 offers a reward for those who ask, and for those who answer: a word spoken in due season, how good is it! One sentence at the right moment can save a family years of trouble. Most of us can remember a word like that, and who said it.

Before you sign, resign, propose or relocate, sit down with two or three people who love God and love you. Tell them the whole plan, including the part you are tempted to leave out. Then listen. The decision is still yours. But it will stand on firmer ground.

line.a: A plan you will not show anyone
line.b: is a plan you are afraid to test.

after: Counsel is not weakness at the moment of decision. It is foundation.
Someone near you may be carrying the word in due season.
days.prayer: Lord, I am close to a decision and part of me wants to rush past asking anyone. Give me humility to seek counsel and honesty to share the whole picture. Speak through wise people, and let my plans be established, not broken, because I listened. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What part of your plan are you tempted to leave out when you ask for advice?

days.title: Wisdom In the Waiting Room

body.p: Commit thy works unto the LORD. The Hebrew word behind commit has the sense of rolling. Roll your works onto the LORD, the way you roll a heavy load off your back onto a cart that can carry it.

Waiting rooms are where we feel the weight most. The hospital corridor before the doctor comes out. The bench at the embassy. The hour before the exam results are posted. There is nothing left to do, and that is what makes it heavy.

The verses before this one are humbling. Even the answer of the tongue is from the LORD. And while All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes, the LORD weigheth the spirits. He sees what we cannot see, including in ourselves.

That is a comfort in a waiting room. The outcome does not rest on our ability to read the situation correctly. It rests with one who weighs everything truly. Committing our works to him does not guarantee the result we want. It means we stop carrying what was never ours to hold.
And the promise is about our thoughts: they shall be established. Settled. Not every answer arrives, but the mind can stop spinning. Roll it over. Then sit, and breathe, and wait with him.

line.b: You can roll it onto him.

after: Waiting is lighter when you are not also holding the result.
He weighs what you cannot measure.
days.prayer: Lord, I am waiting and I feel the weight of what I cannot control. I roll it onto you now, the outcome, the fear, the endless what ifs. You weigh all things rightly. Settle my thoughts while I wait, and stay with me in this room. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you still carrying in the waiting that you could roll onto the Lord today?

days.title: Wisdom When You Feel Small

body.p: Pride goeth before destruction is one of the most famous lines in Proverbs. It is usually read as a warning to the proud. One verse later comes a word for everyone else.

Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud. Notice the small word with. It is not only about having a humble spirit in private. It is about where you stand and whose company you keep. Lowly people. People with no spoil to divide.
Feeling small often comes from comparison. The classmate with the car, the cousin abroad, the colleague who was promoted first. We look at those who are dividing the spoil and feel left behind.

Proverbs says, gently, that you may be standing in the better place. Spoil divided among the proud has a way of ending in a fall. And The highway of the upright is described simply as departing from evil and keeping your way. Nothing grand. Just steady.
If you feel small today on the walk home from a job that pays little, consider who is walking beside you. There is honour in that road. Jesus himself chose it, and he still walks it with the lowly.

line.b: The lowly have the better road.

after: Small is not the same as lost.
Look around at the lowly people near you. You are in good company.
days.prayer: Lord, I feel small and I keep comparing myself with others. Teach me that a humble spirit among humble people is better than a share in proud gains. Keep me on the highway of the upright, and let me find your nearness in low places. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose spoil have you been envying, and what might the lowly road be giving you instead?

days.title: Wisdom Through an Open Door

body.p: Verse 28 has a gentle humour in it. Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise. Proverbs is almost smiling. If you cannot be wise yet, you can at least be quiet.

But the verse before it is the real lesson: He that hath knowledge spareth his words. Spareth is a money word. You spare what is valuable. The person who knows much does not spend his words freely, because he understands what they are worth.
An open door tempts us to speak. The new job, the first visit to the in laws, the chance to lead a group. We want to prove we belong, so we fill every silence.

Wisdom walks through the door more slowly. It watches how the place works. It learns names. It asks questions before offering opinions. And it is marked by an excellent spirit, which the Hebrew pictures as a cool spirit, calm rather than anxious to impress.

If a door has opened for you, thank God for it. Then spend your first weeks spending words carefully. Let people discover what you know over time. You will be trusted with more because you did not rush to show it all.

line.a: An open door invites you to talk.

after: The words you save today are not wasted. They are stored.
Ask one more question than you planned before giving your view.
days.prayer: Lord, thank you for the door you have opened. Keep me from rushing to prove myself. Teach me to spare my words, to listen and learn, and to carry a calm spirit into this new place. Let my quietness be wise and not fearful. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: In the new place God has opened for you, are you spending your words or sparing them?

days.title: Wisdom When the Answer Is No

body.p: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. We do this with people. We also do it with God.

When the answer to a prayer is no, the temptation is to answer back before we have heard the whole matter. He does not care. He is punishing me. It was all pointless. The reply forms before the listening is done.

Proverbs calls that folly, and it is. But it does not stop there, and it does not pretend the no is painless. Verse 14 asks an honest question: a wounded spirit who can bear? The book of wisdom admits there are wounds that strength cannot carry.

Both things are true at once. Do not answer too quickly, and do not pretend you are not hurt. A refusal, whether from a university, a doctor, a fiancee or from heaven, can wound the spirit deeply. The wise response is not to deny the wound. It is to stay long enough to hear what else is being said.

If you have received a no, tell God how it hurts, plainly. Then wait before you write the story of what it means. You may not hear the full reason in this life. But you will hear more than you would have if you had answered first.

after: Do not let the first interpretation of a disappointment become the last one.
Even the wise admit that some wounds are too heavy to carry alone.
days.prayer: Father, you closed this door and I am sore from it. I will not dress the pain up as something else. Keep me from deciding too quickly what this means about you or about me. Carry the wounded part of my spirit that I cannot carry, and help me keep listening. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What story have you already told yourself about a recent no, before you finished listening?

days.title: Wisdom In What You Already Have

body.p: Hear counsel, and receive instruction. Receive is a hands word. You receive what someone else is holding out to you. Instruction in this verse is not something you invent. It is something handed over.

Most of us already have more of it than we use. A father's advice about money. A teacher who told you the truth about your temper. A sermon you nodded at years ago. Wisdom is often not the next thing to find but the last thing you were given.
And the purpose is long range: that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end. Some instruction does not make sense until later. You carry it for years before you need it.

Verse 21 keeps us humble: There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand. Our schemes are many. His counsel is one, and it holds. The instruction we have received from him and through faithful people outlasts our clever plans.

Today, instead of searching for fresh advice, go back to something you were already told. Find the old notebook, call the aunt who prayed for you, reread the chapter you underlined. Ask what you were handed that you have left unopened.

line.a: You keep asking for new counsel.
line.b: Some of it is already in your hands.

after: The counsel of the Lord does not expire with the season it was given.
Your latter end is being prepared by what you receive now.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been given so much wise instruction, and I have used so little of it. Help me receive what has already been handed to me. Let your counsel stand over all my many plans, and make me wise in my latter end. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What counsel were you given years ago that you have not yet put into practice?

days.title: Wisdom When Nobody Notices

body.p: Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD. The picture comes from the market. A trader keeps two stones in his bag, a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling. Customers never see the switch.
That is the point. Divers weights are a sin nobody notices. They live in a pocket. And Proverbs uses one of its strongest words for them. Abomination. God sees the bag.

The verse before is about a different hidden thing: Say not thou, I will recompense evil. Revenge is often planned in silence too. A quiet resolve to pay someone back when the moment comes. Nobody hears it but you.

Instead: wait on the LORD, and he shall save thee. Not, he will punish them for you. He will save you, which may include saving you from becoming the kind of person who keeps a light stone in the bag.

When nobody notices, ask what you are carrying in your pocket. A padded invoice. A measuring tin at the market that runs a little short. A grudge saved for later. Take one of them out today, before anyone has to find it. God already has.

line.b: They have never fooled the Lord.

after: Integrity is what your scale weighs when nobody is checking.
Hand your grudge to God before it becomes your weight.
days.prayer: Lord, you see every hidden weight and every grudge I keep in silence. Make me honest in the small unseen measures of my work. When I want to repay evil, help me wait on you instead, and save me from becoming what I resent. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What hidden weight are you carrying that only you and God know about?

days.title: Wisdom With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want. The contrast is not between workers and lazy people. It is between the diligent and the hasty. Both are busy. One is patient.

Haste looks like ambition. It promises shortcuts. The scheme that will double your money in a month, the deal that has to be signed tonight. Proverbs says it tends toward want. The next verse names the worst version: The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro. Wealth gained by lies is smoke in the wind.

Diligence is less exciting. It plans, measures, saves a little and keeps going. These are proverbs, observations about how life usually works, not promises that every careful person will be rich. Many faithful people stay poor. But diligence keeps your feet on the ground while haste lifts them off it.
Verse 4 adds that even the plowing of the wicked is sin. Hard work alone is not virtue. What matters is the heart behind the plough.
If someone is pressing you to decide quickly about money this week, slow down. Ask for time. Sleep on it. A good opportunity will usually survive a night of prayer.

line.b: Diligence keeps you on the road.

after: Anything that cannot wait for you to pray probably should not have your savings.
Faithful slowness is not failure.
days.prayer: Lord, protect me from haste dressed up as opportunity. Give me a diligent heart that plans honestly and works steadily. Keep me from any gain that comes through lies, and teach me contentment whether I have much or little. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where is haste pushing you to decide before you have prayed?

days.title: Wisdom When You Must Begin Again

body.p: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches. Chosen. A good name is not something you are simply born with or lose forever. It is chosen, again and again, in each decision.
That matters if you are starting over. Perhaps a business failed, or a marriage ended, or you did something that people still talk about. You may feel that your name is gone.

Proverbs does not pretend reputation is easy to rebuild. But it does say the name is worth more than what you might be tempted to grab instead, great riches, silver and gold. And it is made of choices. Which means today's choices count.

The second verse is quietly radical: The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all. In the market, the church, the bus queue, they stand side by side. Neither the riches you lost nor the riches someone else has define who you are before God. He made you both.

Beginning again rarely starts with a big announcement. It starts with paying back a small debt, keeping a small promise, arriving on time at the new job. Each one adds a letter to the name you are choosing. Write one today.

line.a: You cannot buy back a name.
line.b: You can choose it again today.

after: Reputation is rebuilt the same way it is built, one honest choice at a time.
The God who made the rich and the poor has not finished with you.
days.prayer: Lord, I am starting again and I feel the weight of what went wrong. Help me choose a good name over quick gain. Give me patience for the slow rebuilding of trust, and remind me that you made me and have not discarded me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is one small choice today that would add to the good name you are choosing?

days.title: Wisdom In the Middle of the Work

body.p: Three verbs build this passage. A house is builded, then established, then its chambers be filled. Wisdom, understanding, knowledge, each with its own stage.

Building is exciting. People come to see the foundation and the walls going up. Filling is lovely too, the furniture, the photos, the guests. But established is the middle stage, and it is the least noticed. It means made firm. Set right. Strengthened so it will stand.

Most of life is spent in the middle. The marriage that is past the wedding and not yet at the anniversary photos. The business that is open but not yet steady. The faith that has started but has not yet been tested by a long trouble.

Proverbs says that middle work is done by understanding. Not by excitement, not by noise. By slowly learning how things really work and adjusting. And it is set against verse 2, people whose heart studieth destruction. They study too. They are just studying the wrong thing.

If you are in the middle of something today, the third year of a course, the tenth year of a ministry, the fourth month of a recovery, take heart. The unseen strengthening counts. Study the work in front of you with as much care as the wicked study harm.

after: The middle of the work is where the house learns to stand.
Ask what you need to understand, not just what you need to finish.
days.prayer: Lord, I am in the middle of the work and it feels slow and unseen. Give me understanding to strengthen what has already been built. Keep me faithful in the unglamorous stage, and fill the rooms in your time. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What in your life is in the establishing stage, and what understanding does it need from you?

days.title: Wisdom When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Iron sharpeneth iron sounds pleasant on a fridge magnet. In real life it is noisy. Iron against iron throws sparks. Something is taken off both blades.

The verse continues: so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend. Countenance means face. This kind of sharpening happens face to face. Not by message, not behind the back, but looking at each other.
That is exactly where fear speaks first. Fear says do not raise it, he will be offended, she will walk away, it is not your place. So we keep our blades apart and both grow dull.

The verse before says that trying to hide a quarrel is like trying to hide the wind. Some things cannot be hidden. Conflict avoided is not conflict removed. And verse 18 reminds us that the patient keeper of the fig tree eats its fruit. Friendship that survives sharpening bears fruit later.

Is there a friend you have been avoiding a hard conversation with? Fear may be speaking first, but it does not get the last word. Ask to sit down together over tea. Speak gently, face to face. Let both of you leave a little sharper.

after: Sparks are not always a sign that a friendship is failing.
Some conversations are only possible face to face.
days.prayer: Lord, I am afraid of the hard conversation and I keep avoiding it. Give me courage to speak face to face, gently and honestly. Make me a friend who sharpens and who can be sharpened, and guard the friendship through the sparks. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which friend have you been keeping at a distance because sharpening would mean sparks?

days.title: Wisdom With an Open Hand

body.p: Nearly everyone agrees with this famous list in theory. A time to be born, a time to plant. The line that stops people is the last phrase of verse 2: a time to pluck up that which is planted.

Not weeds. Not a mistake. That which is planted. Something you put in the ground on purpose, perhaps with prayer, perhaps with tears. And the Preacher says there is a time when even that is pulled up.

This is hard wisdom. A ministry you started may need to end. A house you built may need to be sold. A role you loved may need to be handed to someone younger. None of this means the planting was wrong. It means a time to every purpose under the heaven includes endings.

The open hand is not indifference. A farmer who uproots a finished crop still loves the field. He simply knows the season has turned. Holding on beyond the season does not keep the crop alive. It only keeps the ground from the next planting.

Look at what you are gripping tightly. Ask God honestly whether its season is still now. If it is, keep tending it. If not, grieve it, thank him for it, and open your hand. The ground is his, and so is the next season.

line.a: Everything you plant is a gift.
line.b: Nothing you plant is yours forever.

after: Letting go of something good can be an act of faith, not failure.
An open hand is still a loving one.
days.prayer: Lord, there are things I planted with love that I am afraid to release. Show me which season I am in. Give me grace to tend what is still mine to tend, and to open my hand over what you are bringing to an end. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What did you plant with love that may now be in its season of plucking up?

days.title: Wisdom When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Verse 7 is a man bargaining. thousands of rams? ten thousands of rivers of oil? Then, desperately, his own firstborn? The offers keep rising, as if God were a hard seller who needs a higher price.
The answer in verse 8 begins with words that change everything: He hath shewed thee, O man. Past tense. Already shown. What God wants is not hidden at the end of a long negotiation.

to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God. Three things, and none of them requires you to see far ahead. You can do justly in this transaction. You can love mercy toward this neighbour. You can walk humbly with God for the next mile.

When the future is fogged in, we are tempted to bargain like the man in verse 7. Big promises, dramatic sacrifices, anything to make God show us the road. Micah's answer is gentle and firm. He has already shown you what matters most.

You may not know where you will be in five years. You can still pay your workers fairly on Friday, forgive the neighbour who reversed into your gate, and pray humbly before bed. That is enough light to walk by.

line.a: You were looking for a map.
line.b: He had already given you a path.

after: God is not asking for a bigger offering. He is asking for a humbler walk.
Justice, mercy and humility can all be done within sight.
days.prayer: Lord, I cannot see far and I am tempted to bargain with you for clarity. Thank you that you have already shown me what is good. Help me do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with you today, in the small part of the road I can see. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What big offering have you been trying to make when God asked for something simpler?

days.title: Wisdom In the Honest Answer

body.p: The wise man in Jesus' story does not avoid the storm. And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house. Every word of weather falls on the wise man's house first.

That is the honest answer to a question many believers carry quietly. If I obey, will I be spared? Jesus does not say so. The house on the rock is beaten by the same rain as any other. The difference is not the weather. It is what happens after: it fell not.

And the difference begins long before the clouds. The wise man is the one who heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them. Hearing alone is not the rock. The verse just before is sobering: some who did many things in his name hear the words I never knew you. Activity is not the same as obedience, nor the same as knowing him.
So the honest answer is both hard and kind. You will face storms. Doing what Jesus says will not prevent them. It will give you a foundation that holds while they last.
If the rain is falling on your house now, a diagnosis, a debt, a grief, do not assume you built badly. Check the foundation, yes. But remember the wise man got wet too.

line.a: Obedience does not stop the rain.

after: A storm is not proof that you built on sand.
Do one thing Jesus said today, not just hear it.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to be the one who hears your words and does them. I will not ask you to keep every storm away, but I ask you to be my rock when it comes. Keep me honest about whether I am obeying or only listening. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which of Jesus' sayings have you heard many times but not yet done?

days.title: Wisdom When the Cost Is Real

body.p: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost? The first act of the builder is not digging. It is sitting down.

Jesus says this to large crowds following him, many of them excited by miracles. Just before, he has said that whoever does not bear his cross cannot be his disciple. He is not trying to thin the crowd for its own sake. He is asking them to sit down and think.

Counting the cost is not a lack of faith. It is honesty. Following Jesus may cost you a friendship, a promotion, the approval of your family, comfort, money. Pretending otherwise sets people up for the shame of verse 29, a foundation laid and nothing more, while all that behold it begin to mock him.
Yet the tone is not grim. A builder who sits down to count does so because he wants the tower. The cost is real because the thing is worth building.

Find a quiet chair this evening. Write down honestly what following Jesus is costing you right now, or may cost you soon. Do not hide it from him. Then tell him again that you want to finish. He knows the sum, and he does not ask you to pay it alone.

after: Faith that has sat down and counted is stronger than faith that never looked.
The cost is real because the tower matters.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to follow you all the way, not just to the foundation. Help me sit down honestly and count what it will cost. Give me grace to bear my cross, and strength to finish what you have called me to build. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is following Jesus costing you right now that you have not admitted to him?

days.title: Wisdom For the Long Road

body.p: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not. Upbraideth not. He does not scold.

That small phrase matters on a long road. Early on, asking God for wisdom is easy. By the fifth year of the same struggle, the same illness, the same difficult child, we begin to feel embarrassed. Surely he is tired of hearing about this. Surely I should know by now.
James says no. God gives liberally, which means generously, without measuring. And he does not reproach you for asking again. The tenth request is welcomed like the first.

The verse before explains why the road is long: let patience have her perfect work. Patience is doing something in you that a shortcut could not. The aim is that you would be perfect and entire, wanting nothing, whole and mature.

Then James asks for faith, nothing wavering. Not faith that has no questions, but faith that keeps coming to the same God rather than drifting between him and other answers. If you are on the long road this morning, standing at the bus stop with the same prayer as last year, pray it again. He is not annoyed with you.

line.a: You think you have asked too often.
line.b: He has never once scolded you.

after: God's generosity does not run out on the long road.
Patience is working on something you cannot yet see.
days.prayer: Father, I have asked you for wisdom about this many times and I still need it. Thank you that you do not scold me for asking again. Give me your wisdom generously today. Let patience do its full work in me, and keep my faith steady. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What have you stopped asking God about because you felt you had asked too many times?

days.title: Wisdom At the End of the Day

body.p: Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath. One swift and two slows. James is giving us a ratio.
Evenings test it. You come home tired, the house is loud, someone asks a question for the third time. Speaking is fast. Anger is faster. Hearing has quietly gone to sleep.

Notice the word that opens verse 19: Wherefore. It points back to verse 18, where God begat us with the word of truth. We were born by a word God spoke. People made by his patient word are being shaped to listen and be patient too.

Then James is honest about anger: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Our anger often feels righteous. We are defending what is right. But it does not produce the right thing. It produces more anger, and children who learn to shout.

Tonight, at the dinner table or in the car home, try the ratio. Listen to the end of the sentence before you answer. Let one irritation pass without comment. Speaking slowly will not feel heroic, but it may be the most godly thing you do all day.

after: A tired evening is where the ratio of James is tested most.
You were made by a word spoken in patience.
days.prayer: Father, the end of the day finds me tired and quick to react. Make me swift to hear the people in my home, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Remind me that my anger does not produce your righteousness. Shape me by your word of truth. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who in your home needs you to be swift to hear tonight?

days.title: Wisdom For What Comes Next

body.p: The wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable. James lists eight qualities, but he puts one of them first on purpose.

Pure comes before peaceable. That order protects us. Peace is easy to fake. We can keep things calm by avoiding the truth, by flattering, by going along with what is wrong. Heavenly wisdom will not buy peace with impurity. It is clean first, and then it makes peace.

The rest of the list is lovely: gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Easy to be intreated means open to reason, willing to be persuaded. Wisdom from above can change its mind.

The contrast in verse 16 is honest. Where envy and rivalry rule, there is confusion and every evil work. Many decisions go wrong not because people lack information but because envy is quietly steering.

This month has been about faithful choices. What comes next will need the same kind of wisdom, and James ends with a farmer's promise: the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace. Sown, not harvested. Whatever you choose this week, in the shop, the meeting, the family gathering, sow it cleanly and peacefully. The fruit comes later.

line.b: Peace sown in purity bears fruit.

after: Ask first whether a choice is pure. Then ask whether it is peaceable.
What you sow in peace today, someone will eat from later.
days.prayer: Lord, as I face what comes next, give me the wisdom that is from above. Make me pure first, then peaceable, gentle and open to correction. Keep envy from steering my choices, and let me sow peace wherever I go, trusting you with the harvest. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is there a peace you are keeping that is not pure?

days.title: Grace Before You Feel Ready

body.p: The psalm opens with a congratulation. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven. David does not say blessed is the man who has improved, or the man who has finally stopped. He says blessed is the one who has been forgiven, and he says it first.

Look at how many words he uses for the problem. Transgression, sin, iniquity. Then three ways God deals with them: forgiven, covered, not counted. It is as if he wants to leave no corner of the trouble untouched.

There is only one condition in these two verses, and it is not readiness. It is honesty. in whose spirit there is no guile. Guile is the tidy version of yourself you present before you feel worthy to come. God is not asking for that version. He is asking for the true one.

Many of us wait. We want to feel sorry enough, clean enough, steady enough, and then we will ask. David knew what that waiting did to him; a few lines later he speaks of bones that grew old while he kept silent.
So on the bus this morning, or at the kitchen sink, you do not need to rehearse. Tell him plainly what happened. The blessing in this psalm was spoken over people who were not ready either.

line.a: You do not have to be ready.

after: God blessed the forgiven before he said a word about the improved.
You can bring the true version of today, not the tidy one.
days.prayer: Lord, I keep waiting until I feel ready to come to you, and the waiting has made me tired. I bring you the true version of me, with the things I have hidden and the things I have explained away. Forgive, cover, and do not count them against me, as you did for David. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you waiting to feel before you will tell God the truth?

days.title: Grace In the Next Step

body.p: David begins this prayer with God, not with himself. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness. The measure he appeals to is not his track record. It is the character of the one he is talking to.

That matters because his track record at that moment was terrible. The heading of the psalm names Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba. He had been found out. If he had begun with himself, he might never have reached the second line.

Notice also the word throughly. Wash me throughly. It is an old spelling, but the meaning is plain enough. He does not want a surface rinse. He wants to be scrubbed all the way through, the way you wash a garment that has carried a stain for too long.

The next step after failure is rarely a grand plan. It is usually a sentence. Have mercy. Wash me. Cleanse me. David does not yet know how the rest of his life will go, but he knows who to speak to first.
If you are sitting with your phone, thumb hovering over a message you are ashamed of sending, start where David started. Not with what you deserve, but with what God is like.

line.a: Your record is a poor place to begin.
line.b: His lovingkindness is a better one.

after: The first step back is usually a sentence, not a plan.
Ask to be washed all the way through, not only to look clean.
days.prayer: God, I do not want to begin with my excuses or my record, because both are weak. I begin with your lovingkindness and the multitude of your tender mercies. Wash me all the way through, not just where people can see. Show me the one next step I need to take, and give me courage for it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: When you fail, do you start by talking about yourself or about what God is like?

days.title: Grace When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: Most of the work God does in a person happens where nobody is looking. David says it directly: thou desirest truth in the inward parts. And then, in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.
The hidden part. Not the platform, not the public apology, not the visible change people can comment on. The quiet place inside where you tell yourself the story of what you did.

Hyssop was a small, bushy plant. Priests dipped it in water or blood and shook it over whatever needed cleansing. Nothing about it was impressive. It was a humble tool for a holy job, and David asks to be touched by it.

Then comes the most honest line in the passage. the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice. David does not pretend the season was painless. He says God broke something. He also says those same bones will one day rejoice, which is a strange and tender hope.

If your faith feels quiet right now, if no one would guess anything is happening, that may be exactly where God is at work. Sweeping the shop floor at closing time, you can still pray for joy and gladness to come back.

line.b: It is where the hidden part is healed.

after: God often does his deepest work where no one claps.
Broken bones can learn to rejoice, though not all at once.
days.prayer: Father, you want truth in the hidden part of me, and that is the part I guard most. Come into the quiet place where I tell myself stories. Cleanse me with whatever humble means you choose. Where something in me has been broken, let it hear joy and gladness again in your time. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What story are you telling yourself in the hidden part that God wants to make true?

days.title: Grace Without an Audience

body.p: David is not preaching here. He is speaking to his own soul; the psalm opens with him telling his soul to bless the Lord. These lines are a man reminding himself, in private, of what God is like.

He will not always chide. Chiding has an end. Whatever correction God brings, it is not a permanent tone of voice. neither will he keep his anger for ever. Keep is the word of someone storing something away, and God refuses to store it.

Then the past tense. He hath not dealt with us after our sins. This is not a promise about tomorrow. It is a report about yesterday. Look back over your life, David is saying, and compare what you actually received with what you earned.

Grace without an audience works the same way. Much of the mercy God shows you no one else will ever see. The accident that did not happen. The cruel word you nearly said. The debt that was quietly reduced. There was no crowd for any of it.
Try what David did. On your walk to the market or in the queue at the bank, talk to your own soul. Remind it of three times God did not deal with you as you deserved.

line.a: God does not store his anger.

after: Much of God's mercy to you happened without witnesses.
Your soul sometimes needs to be reminded by you, out loud.
days.prayer: Lord, you have not dealt with me after my sins, and I forget that so quickly. Thank you for the mercies no one saw, the ones I did not even notice. Teach my soul to remember. When I expect you to keep your anger, remind me that you chose to let it go. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Can you name three times God did not give you what you had earned?

days.title: Grace For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: David could have said as far as the north is from the south. He did not. North and south have ends; you can stand at a pole. East and west never meet. Keep walking east and you will never arrive at a point where it turns into west.
That is the distance he means. so far hath he removed our transgressions from us. Not a long way. An unmeasurable way.

But the passage does not stay up in the sky. Verse 13 comes down into a house. Like as a father pitieth his children. Pity here is not looking down on someone. It is the ache a parent feels watching a child struggle with something too heavy for small arms.

Ordinary days are where we most need both pictures. On a Tuesday nothing dramatic happens. You simply remember the sharp thing you said on Sunday, or the old failure you thought was buried. It comes back while you are ironing a shirt.
When it comes back, picture the horizon, then picture a father bending over a tired child. Both are true of how God has handled your sin. You do not need to walk east to fetch it back.

line.a: North and south have an end.

after: A forgiven sin is not waiting somewhere to be collected.
God looks at your weakness the way a good father looks at a tired child.
days.prayer: Father, old failures come back to me on ordinary days, while I am working or cooking or lying awake. Remind me how far you have removed them. Let me feel your pity, the kind a father has for a child, and stop me from walking east to bring them back. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which old failure do you keep going back to collect?

days.title: Grace When Plans Change

body.p: The famous invitation sits in an unexpected place. Just before it, God gives a list of hard, practical commands: relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. Just after it, he speaks of being willing and obedient.

So Come now, and let us reason together is not a soft moment set apart from life. It comes right in the middle of God calling his people to change direction. The cleansing and the new direction arrive in the same breath.
Scarlet and crimson were dyes that held fast. Cloth dipped in them did not wash out. Isaiah chooses the most permanent stain he knows and says God can make it white.

Notice too that God says reason, not shout. He invites conversation, as though the people are allowed to bring their side. When plans change, when the life you planned is interrupted by your own choices or by someone else's, God does not stop speaking to you. He asks you to sit down with him.

If you are holding a letter that ended a job, or a plan that collapsed at the last moment, read verse 17 again. Grace often turns you outward. There is still a widow to plead for, still a fatherless child nearby, still good to learn.

line.a: God does not wash you and leave you idle.
line.b: He cleans you and hands you work.

after: The stain that will not wash out is the one God specialises in.
A changed plan can still have a widow in it to help.
days.prayer: Lord, my plans have changed, and some of the reason is my own doing. Thank you that you still invite me to come and reason with you. Make what is scarlet in me white. Then turn my eyes outward, to someone oppressed or alone, so that this new season is not only about me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who near you needs the help you could give in this changed season?

days.title: Grace In the Work at Hand

body.p: God turns the language of work upside down here. Israel was meant to serve him. Instead he says, thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities. The servant made the master do the labour.
It is a startling picture. God, tired. Not because he is weak, but because carrying a stubborn people is real work, and he names it honestly.

And then, without waiting for Israel to repair anything: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake. The repetition is deliberate. I, even I. Nobody else is doing this. Not the priests, not the sacrifices they never brought.
For mine own sake is the hinge. God forgives because of who he is, not because Israel finally turned up with sweet cane. That is good news for anyone who measures their standing by their output.

At your desk, behind the counter, in the middle of a long shift, you may feel your worth rising and falling with your work. The work matters. But your forgiveness was never part of the job description. It was done by someone else, for his own name.

line.a: You were meant to serve him.

after: God's forgiveness is not a wage for good work.
The one who blots out sin also chooses not to remember it.
days.prayer: God, I have wearied you with my sins and then tried to make up for it with effort. Thank you that you blot out my transgressions for your own sake. Let me do the work in front of me as a forgiven person, not as someone trying to earn back your favour. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you working today to be forgiven, or because you already are?

days.title: Grace When You Need Clarity

body.p: Micah's own name is a question. It means, roughly, who is like the Lord. Near the end of his book he turns his name into worship: Who is a God like unto thee.

The verse before is dark. Nations licking the dust, creeping out of their holes like worms, afraid. Micah has seen judgement clearly. He does not soften it. That is why the question that follows lands with such force.
Who is like this God? Not because he is fierce, but because he delighteth in mercy. Delight is a strong word. It is not reluctant permission. It is pleasure. God does not pardon with a sigh.

Clarity often comes from asking a better question. When you are confused about what to do next, about a relationship, about a decision you regret, it helps to stop asking what is wrong with me for a while and ask Micah's question instead. Who is God, and what does he enjoy?

Sitting in traffic with your thoughts spinning, try saying it slowly. Who is like you, Lord, who passes over my wrong? The answer will not solve everything. It will tell you which direction is safe to face.

line.a: Clarity begins with a better question.
line.b: Who is a God like you?

after: God pardons with pleasure, not with a sigh.
When your thoughts spin, ask who God is before you ask what is wrong with you.
days.prayer: Lord, my thoughts are crowded and I cannot see clearly. I will ask the question Micah asked. Who is like you, who pardons and passes by and delights in mercy? Turn my eyes from my confusion to your character, and let that be the place I decide from. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Do you believe God enjoys showing you mercy, or only allows it?

days.title: Grace One Choice at a Time

body.p: In the middle of verse 19 there is a word that does not belong to a single moment. he will subdue our iniquities. Subdue is what you do to something that is still fighting.

Forgiveness and subduing are not the same thing. The guilt is thrown away all at once, into the depths of the sea. But habits, reflexes and old appetites still push back. God promises to deal with those too, and that work takes time.

Micah also changes who he is addressing halfway through. He begins with he, describing God, then switches to thou, speaking to him directly. Description turns into conversation. Faith often grows like that: we talk about God for a while, and then we find ourselves talking to him.

Verse 20 roots all of it in old promises, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old. The God who subdues your sin is the same God who kept his word to Abraham across centuries. He is patient with slow work.

So when you make the right choice at the cooker tonight, or hold your tongue in a tense meeting, that is not you earning forgiveness. It is God subduing, one choice at a time, what he has already forgiven.

line.a: The guilt is gone at once.
line.b: The habit is subdued in time.

after: God forgives instantly and changes you patiently.
Each small right choice is part of his subduing work.
days.prayer: God, thank you that my guilt is cast into the depths of the sea. But some of my old habits are still fighting. Subdue them, one choice at a time. Give me patience with the slow work, the same patience you showed Abraham and Jacob over so many years. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which habit do you need God to subdue, not just forgive?

days.title: Grace Under Pressure

body.p: Of all the beatitudes, this one has the plainest shape. Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. The reward matches the virtue exactly. Mercy given, mercy received.

Jesus places it between hunger and purity, between those who hunger and thirst after righteousness and the pure in heart. Mercy sits between wanting what is right and seeing God clearly, as though it were the bridge between them.

That position matters. People who hunger for righteousness can become hard. They want things fixed, wrongs punished, standards kept. Jesus seems to know the danger, and he sets mercy right beside that hunger as its companion.

Pressure tests this more than anything. When the deadline is close, the house is noisy, and someone makes a mistake that costs you, mercy does not come naturally. Irritation does. Under pressure we discover how much mercy we actually carry.

Think of a nurse at the end of a twelve hour shift, patient after patient asking the same question. Mercy there looks like answering kindly one more time. It is not dramatic. It is simply the bridge between wanting things right and treating people well.

line.a: Hunger for what is right can turn hard.

after: The mercy you show under pressure is the mercy you really have.
God gives mercy to the merciful, and he starts by giving it to you.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want what is right, and sometimes that makes me harsh with people. When I am under pressure today, give me mercy for the person who slows me down or gets it wrong. Let me remember how much mercy I have received, and pass some of it on. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where does pressure make you least merciful?

days.title: Grace After the Excitement Fades

body.p: Jesus builds this command in four steps, each harder than the last: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.

Love is the general posture. Blessing is a word spoken. Doing good is an action. Praying is the most private of all, done where the enemy will never see it or thank you. The command moves inward, toward the heart.
Then he gives a reason drawn from the weather. he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good. God does this every morning. It is not a single gesture of reconciliation. It is a habit.

Forgiving someone can feel stirring at first. There is a moment of release, perhaps tears, perhaps a conversation that goes well. Then the feeling fades, and you still share an office or a family compound with them. The person has not changed. That is where this passage really begins.

Tomorrow when the sun comes up over your street, notice who else it is shining on. The neighbour who reported you. The relative who spoke against you. God is giving them the same light. Pray for them once, quietly, before you leave the house.

line.a: Forgiveness has a feeling at first.
line.b: After that it has a habit, like the sun.

after: Pray for one difficult person where they will never know you did.
God sends rain on the unjust, and he sends it every season.
days.prayer: Father, the feeling I had when I forgave has faded, and the person is still the same. Help me keep loving, keep blessing, keep doing good. Teach me to pray for them in private, the way your sun rises on everyone without asking who deserves it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who is the person you forgave once but now need to forgive daily?

days.title: Grace In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: Forgiveness sits in a surprising place in the Lord's Prayer. Just before it is bread. Just after it is temptation. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.

The order suggests that forgiveness belongs with the ordinary needs of a day. You need food. You need to be forgiven. You need to forgive. All three show up every day whether you plan for them or not.

And the word Jesus chooses is debts. A debtor is someone who owes you. That is exactly how an offence feels: the person took something, and now they owe you an apology, an explanation, or at least some suffering of their own.

To forgive a debtor is to cancel what is owed. It does not mean the debt was imaginary. It means you stop collecting. This is what makes difficult conversations so hard. We often walk into them as collectors.

Before you sit down with your brother, your spouse, or your manager to talk about what went wrong, pray this middle line slowly. You are about to ask for forgiveness and offer it in the same conversation. Go in as someone who has also been released from a debt.

after: You can talk about what happened without trying to collect on it.
The prayer for bread and the prayer for pardon are said in one breath.
days.prayer: Our Father, give me bread for today, and forgive my debts as I forgive the people who owe me. I have a hard conversation ahead. Help me go in as someone who has been forgiven much, not as a collector. Guard my words, and lead me away from the temptation to win. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you entering your next hard conversation as a collector or as a forgiven debtor?

days.title: Grace When Progress Is Slow

body.p: Jesus finishes the prayer with Amen, and then he goes back. Of all the lines he has just taught, he chooses one to explain further. Not bread, not temptation, not the kingdom. Forgiveness.

For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. Then comes the hard mirror of it in verse 15. He clearly expected this to be the line his disciples would struggle with most.
He was right. Most believers can say the Lord's Prayer by heart. Fewer find it easy to live the middle of it. Forgiveness is often slow. You forgive on Monday and find the anger back by Thursday.

These verses are not a threat designed to frighten you into instant perfection. They describe a connection. A heart that refuses to release others is a heart closed to receiving release itself. The door that lets mercy out is the same door that lets it in.

If your progress is slow, if you are still angry with your father or with the friend who took the money, keep praying the line. Say it on the walk to work even when you do not feel it. Slow forgiveness is still forgiveness in motion, and Jesus took the time to come back to it.

line.a: Jesus added a footnote to one line only.
line.b: He knew it would be the hardest.

after: Mercy goes out and comes in through the same door.
Slow forgiveness is still moving.
days.prayer: Lord, you came back to this line because you knew I would struggle with it. I am still struggling. I want to forgive, and then the anger returns. Keep my heart open, so that your forgiveness can reach me and flow through me, even if it moves slowly. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which forgiveness in your life is moving slowly but still moving?

days.title: Grace At the Point of Decision

body.p: Peter's question follows straight after a promise. where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them. Jesus has just described his people gathered. Peter immediately thinks of what happens when people gather: they hurt each other.

Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Seven was a generous number. Peter was not being stingy. He was trying to set a reasonable limit, a point at which he could finally decide he had done enough.

Jesus does not give him a bigger limit. Until seventy times seven is not really a number to reach. Nobody is keeping a tally up to four hundred and ninety. It is a way of saying the counting itself is the problem.
Every decision about forgiveness can quietly turn into a calculation. How many times has he done this? Is this the last straw? Jesus answers by taking the calculator out of Peter's hand.

When you stand at that point again, in the corridor after the meeting or outside your sister's door, you will be tempted to count. Ask instead what Jesus was really asking Peter. Not how many, but whether you will keep being the kind of person who forgives.

after: The gathered church is also where forgiveness gets tested.
Ask who you are becoming, not how many times it has happened.
days.prayer: Jesus, I keep a count of the times people have hurt me, and I am close to my limit with someone. Take the counting out of my hands. At this point of decision, help me choose to be someone who forgives again, without pretending the hurt is small. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose offences are you still counting?

days.title: Grace In the Waiting Room

body.p: Jesus answers Peter's arithmetic with a story. Verse 23 begins with Therefore, and what follows is a parable about a king which would take account of his servants.

Peter had asked how often to forgive. Jesus moves the conversation to a royal accounting, where the first servant owes the king far more than he could ever pay. Before you can settle how often to forgive others, you need to see the size of your own account.
The answer to how often is hidden inside how much. Someone who knows what he has been released from finds it hard to keep a tight count on anyone else.

Forgiveness often happens in a kind of waiting room. You have decided to release someone, but your feelings have not caught up. The person may not have apologised. Nothing visible has changed. You sit there, so to speak, waiting for your heart to be called in.

If you are literally in a waiting room today, at a clinic or an embassy or a bank, use the time. Think about the account God has settled for you. Then think of one person whose smaller debt you are still holding. The king's mercy came first. Yours is allowed to follow, even at the pace of a slow queue.

after: The size of your own debt makes it harder to count someone else's.
Your feelings are allowed to catch up with your decision.
days.prayer: Lord, I have decided to forgive, but my heart is still in the waiting room. Show me again the size of the debt you cancelled for me. Let that settle my accounts with others, slowly if it must be slow, but truly. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Have you looked at how much you were forgiven before deciding how often to forgive?

days.title: Grace When You Feel Small

body.p: Verse 24 is one of the boldest prayer promises in the gospels. Jesus has just spoken of a mountain thrown into the sea. Then, without a pause, he turns to something that seems very small by comparison. And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any.
Mountains, and then a grudge. Jesus seems to think the grudge is the bigger obstacle.

Notice the posture. When ye stand praying. Forgiveness is not something you finish before prayer begins. It is something that comes up in the middle of it. You are standing there, asking God for something large, and a face comes to mind.

When you feel small, it is tempting to think your private resentments do not matter. You are not a pastor or a leader. Who cares what you hold against your neighbour? Jesus cares. The quiet grudge in an ordinary believer is exactly what he addresses here.

Next time you stand to pray, in a church service or beside your bed, and someone's name rises up uninvited, do not push it away. That interruption may be the most important part of the prayer. Release them there, standing, and then go on asking.

line.a: You came to pray about a mountain.

after: The face that interrupts your prayer may be the point of it.
No believer is too small for their grudges to matter.
days.prayer: Father, when I stand to pray, faces come to mind that I would rather ignore. I feel small, and I tell myself my resentments are minor. Show me they matter to you. Help me forgive while I am still standing in your presence, and then let me pray with a clear heart. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose face comes to mind when you stand to pray?

days.title: Grace Through an Open Door

body.p: The word therefore in verse 36 points backward. Be ye therefore merciful only makes sense after the line before it: he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
That sentence is worth reading slowly. God is kind to the unthankful. Not only to the poor, not only to the sorry, but to the people who take his kindness and never say thank you.

Jesus also says lend, hoping for nothing again. Anyone who has lent money to a relative knows how rare that is. We lend, and we hope. We watch for the repayment. We remember the date. Jesus asks his followers to open the door and let it stay open.

Mercy here is not soft. It is costly, practical, and often unthanked. And it rests entirely on the character of God. We are not merciful because people deserve it. We are merciful because that is what our Father is like, and children take after their father.

If someone owes you and has never acknowledged it, you may not be able to forget the amount. But you can decide to stop watching the door. Let the loan become a gift in your heart, and leave the rest with the One who is kind to the unthankful, including, at times, you.

line.a: God is kind to the unthankful.
line.b: So his children can be too.

after: Mercy that waits to be thanked is still waiting for something.
Children grow to look like their Father.
days.prayer: Father, you are kind to the unthankful, and I have been unthankful more often than I know. Make me merciful like you. Help me lend without watching for the return, and forgive without waiting for gratitude. Keep the door of my heart open. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who have you been kind to who never said thank you, and can you let that go?

days.title: Grace When the Answer Is No

body.p: Before the yes in this passage there are two nos. Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned. Only then comes the positive command, forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
The order is wise. Most forgiveness begins by refusing something. Refusing to pass the final sentence on someone. Refusing to write them off. The nos clear the ground for the yes.

Then Jesus paints a picture from the market. good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over. Anyone who has bought rice or garri by the cup knows the difference. Some traders level the cup with a finger. Others press it, shake it, and pile it until it spills into your bag.
God gives the generous way. And Jesus says the measure we use will be the measure used for us. A tight, levelled heart toward others tends to find life measured back with the same tightness.

Sometimes the answer you need to give is no. No to the gossip about your colleague. No to the verdict you have already formed about your in-law. When you say those nos, you are making room in your own cup for a measure that runs over.

line.b: God shakes it down and fills it again.

after: Forgiveness often starts with refusing to pass a final sentence.
The cup you use for others is the cup you carry yourself.
days.prayer: Lord, help me say no to judging and no to condemning, so that I can say yes to forgiving. I have levelled the cup for others and expected you to fill mine to overflowing. Make me generous in mercy, the way you are generous with me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What verdict about someone do you need to say no to?

days.title: Grace In What You Already Have

body.p: Jesus is talking to Simon the Pharisee, but in verse 48 he finally turns to the woman. And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven. Up to that point everything had been said about her. Now it is said to her.
That shift matters. She had heard him defend her to the host. But being defended is not the same as being spoken to. Jesus wanted her to hear it with her own ears, face to face.

Look at what each person had. My head with oil thou didst not anoint, he tells Simon. Simon had oil. It was his house, his feast, his servants. He simply did not use what he had for Jesus. The woman brought what she had, ointment, tears, her hair, and poured it out.
Neither of them needed something new. The difference was not in their resources but in their love. And Jesus ties that love to forgiveness: to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.

You may feel you have little to offer God. But you already have something. A voice, a kitchen, a spare hour, a small sum. Love does not wait to have more. The woman used what was already in her hands, and she went home having heard words spoken directly to her.

line.a: Simon had oil and kept it.
line.b: She had ointment and poured it.

after: Jesus does not only speak about the forgiven, he speaks to them.
Love works with what is already in your hands.
days.prayer: Jesus, I have often kept what I had, like Simon, and called it caution. Let me love much, because I have been forgiven much. Take what is already in my hands today and use it. And speak your forgiveness to me directly, so I can hear it for myself. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What do you already have that you have been keeping back from Jesus?

days.title: Grace When Nobody Notices

body.p: The son had a speech prepared. Verse 19 gives the end of it: make me as one of thy hired servants. He practised it on the road, probably many times.
But when he finally speaks in verse 21, the speech stops short. He says he has sinned. He says he is not worthy. The line about the hired servant never comes. Something in between interrupted him.
That something was his father, who saw him when he was yet a great way off. Nobody else on that road noticed a thin, ashamed figure walking home. The father did. He must have been watching.

Then the verbs pile up. Saw, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck, kissed. Running was not considered dignified for a man of his age. He did not care. He covered the distance so his son would not have to walk it alone.
