Perhaps you feel no one notices your slow return to God. You are back at prayer, back at church, trying again in small ways, and nobody has said anything. The Father has seen you from a great way off. He has interrupted plenty of rehearsed speeches before, and he may yet interrupt yours.

after: Someone noticed you on the road before you reached the door.
You do not need to finish the speech for the welcome to begin.
days.prayer: Father, I have rehearsed what I will say to you, how I will ask to be only a servant. Thank you that you see me from a great way off and run. When I feel nobody notices my small steps back, remind me that you were watching the road. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What speech are you rehearsing that the Father may not let you finish?

days.title: Grace With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: Earlier in the story Jesus had stooped down and written on the ground. Now Jesus had lifted up himself. He stands, and for the first time in the whole scene he and the woman are alone. The crowd that dragged her there has drifted away.
Her only words in the entire account are three. No man, Lord. That is all. No defence, no explanation. She simply reports what she sees: nobody is left to accuse her.

Then Jesus says the one thing no accuser could. Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more. The order matters. First, no condemnation. Then, go. The pardon is not a reward for future behaviour. It is the ground she will stand on as she walks away.

Go is an ordinary word. He sends her back into her life, into streets where people knew her story, into the same town. Grace did not lift her out of the world. It put her back in it, with both feet on the ground and a different future.
You may wish forgiveness came with a new city. Usually it does not. You go back to the same office, the same street, the same family table. His words go with you. You can walk on them.

line.a: Grace does not lift you out of your life.
line.b: It sends you back into it, uncondemned.

after: The pardon comes first and the walk comes after.
Ordinary streets are where forgiven people practise sinning no more.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, you lifted yourself up and spoke gently to a woman everyone else had used. Speak to me the same way. Let me stand on the ground of no condemnation as I go back to my ordinary places today. Help me walk there differently, without pretending the past did not happen. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where do you need to walk today as someone who is not condemned?

days.title: Grace When You Must Begin Again

body.p: Paul starts with a very human calculation. Hardly anyone would die for a righteous man, he says. Perhaps, for a really good man, some would even dare to die. He is describing the outer limit of human sacrifice.
Then the turn. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Not when we were good. Not when we were righteous. While we were yet sinners.
The word yet is small and full of hope. It means still, at that time, before anything changed. Christ did not wait for the turnaround. He went to the cross in the middle of the mess.
Verse 9 then reasons forward. Much more then. If he loved us at our worst, how much more will he keep us now that we are justified. Paul is arguing from the hard case to the easy one.

Beginning again is frightening because we assume we must first be different. But the love of God was shown while we were still the old version. If you are starting over this week, after a relapse, a failed course, or a broken promise, start from verse 8. You do not have to become someone else before you come back.

line.a: He did not wait for you to change.
line.b: He died while you were yet a sinner.

after: God's love was proved at your worst, so your worst cannot disprove it.
Much more then is how Paul reasons about your future.
days.prayer: Father, I am beginning again, and part of me thinks I must be better first. Thank you that Christ died for me while I was yet a sinner. Let that be the ground I stand on this week. Much more now, keep me and carry me forward. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What do you think you must become before God will take you back?

days.title: Grace In the Middle of the Work

body.p: Two small words open this chapter: therefore now. Paul has just finished chapter 7, where he describes his own struggle with sin in painful detail. He does the thing he hates. He fails to do the thing he wants.
Then, without resolving every struggle, he writes There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. Not later, when the struggle is over. Now, in the middle of it.

Notice also the shift in verse 2. Verse 1 speaks of them. Verse 2 says hath made me free. Paul moves from the general to the personal. It is as if he states the truth for everyone and then checks that it includes him.

Most of life is lived in the middle. The work is not finished, the character is not complete, the habit is not broken. People often believe condemnation lifts only at the end, once they have earned it. Paul says the verdict comes before the work is done.

On a building site, a half finished wall is not a failure. It is a wall in progress. If you are in the middle of a hard season of change, you are not condemned for being half built. Read verse 2 with your own name in it, then pick up the next block.

after: No condemnation is a present tense word.
Put your own name into verse 2 and read it again.
days.prayer: Lord, I am in the middle of the work, still struggling, still unfinished. Thank you that there is now no condemnation for me in Christ Jesus. Not after I finish, but now. Let that freedom steady my hands as I keep building today. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Are you waiting to finish before you believe you are not condemned?

days.title: Grace When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Paul is remarkably honest in verse 18. He does not simply say live peaceably with everyone. He adds two conditions first. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you.

If it be possible. Paul knew it would not always be. Some people will not make peace. Some situations are not safe. Scripture does not ask you to pretend otherwise, or to place yourself in harm's way to keep a calm surface.

As much as lieth in you. Your part is your part. You cannot control the other person's response. You can control whether you return evil for evil, whether you provide things honest, whether you leave vengeance to God.

Fear often speaks first in conflict. Fear says strike back before they strike again. Fear says if you do not avenge yourself, no one will. Paul answers that fear directly. Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. Someone is keeping the account, and it is not you.

When the landlord shouts, or the colleague takes credit again, you may still need to speak up or seek help. But you can do it without revenge in your heart. Do what lies in you. Leave the rest to the one who judges rightly.

line.b: Your part of it always is.

after: You are responsible for your side of the peace, not theirs.
Leaving vengeance to God is not weakness, it is trust.
days.prayer: Lord, fear tells me to strike back first and protect myself at any cost. Help me do what lies in me to live at peace, and give me wisdom where peace is not possible or safe. Take vengeance out of my hands, and let me trust you to repay. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What part of this conflict truly lies with you?

days.title: Grace With an Open Hand

body.p: Before Paul writes the famous line about the new creature, he writes something about how we see other people. Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh.

Paul had once judged Jesus that way, as a troublemaker from Nazareth, a failed messiah. He admits it: though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more. His way of seeing changed completely.

That change touches how he sees everyone. If any man in Christ is a new creature, Paul cannot keep holding people to their old version. The brother who lied, the friend who betrayed, the young man who was reckless: if they are in Christ, the old file is not the full truth about them.

This is what forgiveness with an open hand looks like. A closed hand grips the record. An open hand lets God rewrite it. old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. Behold means look. Paul is asking you to look again.

You may have someone in your church or your extended family you have quietly filed under their worst moment. This week, look again. Ask God to show you what he has made new in them, and let go of the file.

line.a: A closed hand holds the record.
line.b: An open hand lets God rewrite it.

after: People in Christ are more than their worst moment.
Behold means look again, so look again at someone.
days.prayer: Lord, I have known some people only after the flesh, by their failures and their past. Open my hand. Let me see them the way you see those who are in Christ, as new. And help me receive that same new seeing for myself. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who have you filed under their worst moment?

days.title: Grace When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Paul uses a striking phrase in verse 20. as though God did beseech you by us. Beseech means to beg, to plead earnestly. God, through his messengers, is pleading.
That is not how we usually picture it. We imagine the sinner pleading and God deciding. Here it runs the other way. God is the one asking, and the message is simple: be ye reconciled to God.
Verse 19 explains what makes the plea possible. not imputing their trespasses unto them. God has chosen not to count the debt against the world. He has made the first move, all of it.

Then he hands the message to ordinary people. we are ambassadors for Christ. An ambassador lives far from the king who sent him. He cannot see the throne room. He carries the message anyway, trusting the one who sent it.

When you cannot see far ahead, when the future is blurred and you are unsure what God is doing, you still know the message you carry. In the shop, at the school gate, on the long ride home, you represent a God who pleads rather than demands. You do not need to see the whole road to deliver that.

line.a: You may not see the throne.

after: God is the one pleading, and he pleads through people like you.
An ambassador does not need to see far to speak clearly.
days.prayer: Father, I cannot see far ahead, and I do not understand all you are doing. But I know you have reconciled me to yourself and not counted my trespasses. Make me a faithful ambassador today, carrying your plea gently to the people around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Do you picture God as pleading with people, or as waiting for them to plead?

days.title: Grace In the Honest Answer

body.p: Paul does not say God forgives us out of his riches. He says according to the riches of his grace. The difference is worth noticing. A rich man can give out of his wealth and hardly feel it. To give according to his wealth means the gift matches the size of the fortune.

So the forgiveness of sins is not a small donation from a large account. It is measured to the full scale of God's grace. That is the honest answer to the question many people carry quietly: is there enough for me?

Verse 6 adds another phrase: he hath made us accepted in the beloved. The beloved is Christ. We are not accepted on our own, as separate cases to be reviewed. We are accepted inside someone God already loves completely.
And verse 8 says this grace has abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence. God's generosity is not careless. It is wise. He knows exactly what he is forgiving.

If someone asks how you can be sure God has forgiven you, you do not need a clever reply. You can answer honestly. Not because I have done well, but because his grace is rich, and I am in the beloved. Say it once to yourself in the mirror before you leave the house.

line.a: Out of his riches would be generous.
line.b: According to his riches is complete.

after: You are accepted inside someone God already loves.
God knows exactly what he is forgiving, and he forgives it wisely.
days.prayer: Father, I have wondered whether there is enough grace for me. Thank you that you forgive according to the riches of your grace, not out of leftovers. Thank you that I am accepted in the beloved. Help me answer honestly when doubt asks how I can be sure. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: When doubt asks whether you are forgiven, what is your honest answer?

days.title: Grace When the Cost Is Real

body.p: Paul makes a list of things to put away: bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, and then with all malice. They move from the inside out. Bitterness sits in the heart. Wrath and anger rise up. Clamour is the noise. Evil speaking is the words. Malice is what remains underneath.
Then he gives three things to put on. be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another. Six out, three in. The getting rid of is harder than the taking on.
And the reason comes in the past tense. even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. For Christ's sake means at Christ's cost. God's forgiveness was not free to him. It was paid for.

That is why Paul can ask so much. He is not pretending forgiveness is cheap. It costs you your right to be bitter, your right to the last word, your right to tell the story your way. The cost is real. It is also smaller than the one already paid for you.

If you are holding something against a family member, bitterness may feel like the only thing keeping you safe. Paul is not asking you to pretend it did not hurt. He is asking you to begin putting it away, one layer at a time, starting with the words you say about them.

after: Start putting bitterness away with the words you say about them.
Forgiveness is not pretending it did not hurt.
days.prayer: Lord, forgiving this person will cost me my right to be bitter and my right to the last word. That feels like a lot. Remind me what my forgiveness cost you, for Christ's sake. Make me kind and tenderhearted, one layer at a time. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which of the things in verse 31 is hardest for you to put away?

days.title: Grace For the Long Road

body.p: Paul talks about character the way you talk about clothes. Put on therefore, he begins. Then, in verse 14, above all these things put on charity. Clothes are put on daily. Nobody dresses once for the rest of their life.

Look closely at the order in verse 13. Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another. Forbearing comes first. It means putting up with each other, bearing with the small irritations that are not sins at all, just differences.

Much of a long marriage, a long friendship, or a long time in the same church is forbearing. The way someone chews. The way they always arrive late. The opinion they repeat every Sunday. None of it needs forgiving. It needs patience.

Then, when real wrong comes, forgiving. And the standard is high. even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. Paul gives the reason inside the instruction. You were forgiven first. That is the cloth everything else is cut from.

The long road wears clothes out. Some mornings you will have to put on kindness again because yesterday it tore. That is normal. Get dressed again. Charity, Paul says, is the bond that holds the rest together.

line.a: Most of a long road is forbearing.

after: Not every irritation needs forgiving, but most need patience.
You will need to put kindness on again tomorrow, and that is fine.
days.prayer: Lord, I am on a long road with people I love and people I find difficult. Help me forbear the small things and forgive the real wrongs, as Christ forgave me. Each morning, help me put on kindness and patience again, and above all, love. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you treating as a wrong that only needs forbearing?

days.title: Grace At the End of the Day

body.p: The promise in verse 9 is guarded on both sides by a warning. If we say that we have no sin, verse 8 begins. If we say that we have not sinned, verse 10 begins. Saying is the problem on either side. Confessing is the remedy in the middle.
To confess is to agree with God about what happened. Not to explain it, not to shrink it, simply to say yes, that was wrong, and it was mine.

Then John describes God in an unexpected way. he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins. We might expect merciful, or kind. John says just. Forgiveness is not God bending the rules. Because Christ has dealt with sin, forgiving the one who confesses is the right thing for God to do.
And there are two gifts, not one. To forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Forgiveness deals with the guilt. Cleansing deals with the stain left behind.

At the end of the day, lying in bed with the hours running back through your mind, you do not have to pretend it was clean. Name what went wrong, plainly. God is faithful, which means he will be there tomorrow night too. Then sleep. The confessing was your part; the forgiving is his.

line.a: Saying we have no sin fools only us.

after: Confession is simply agreeing with God about what happened.
God forgives because it is just, not only because he is kind.
days.prayer: Father, at the end of this day I will not pretend I have no sin. I confess what I said, what I did, and what I failed to do. Thank you that you are faithful and just to forgive me and to cleanse me. Let me sleep tonight as someone washed. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What from today do you need to name plainly before you sleep?

days.title: The Room He Painted Yellow

body.p: A friend of mine painted a small bedroom yellow. He and his wife had been trying for a child for two years, and one Saturday he decided he was tired of the room being a place where suitcases went to die. He bought the paint. He did the skirting boards properly. He put up a shelf.
That was four years ago. The room is still yellow, and it is still empty. I have stayed in that house. You walk past the door on the way to the bathroom and you can feel it.
I used to think that room was a sad thing. I have come to think it is one of the bravest things I have seen.

Luke gives us Simeon in a handful of verses and then he is gone. We are never told how long he waited. We know only that it was long enough for the text to mention his death in the same breath as his hope — that he would not see death before he had seen. He was old. He had been holding this a long time.

What strikes me is that Luke does not describe him as passing time. He describes him as waiting for the consolation of Israel. The waiting had a direction. It was aimed at something. And when the moment finally came, Simeon was in the temple, which is to say he was standing exactly where a man waiting for that particular thing would need to be standing.
He did not miss it. After all those years, he did not miss it, because the waiting had kept him in position.

after: There is a kind of waiting that empties you out, and there is a kind that keeps you standing where you need to be standing. Most of us do not get to choose what we are waiting for. We do get to choose which kind of waiting it will be.
The yellow room is not a monument to disappointment. It is a man standing in the temple.
days.prayer: Father, you know the thing I have been holding for a long time now. I am not asking you to explain the delay. I am asking you to keep me in position — awake, expectant, standing where I would need to be standing if today were the day. Let the waiting shape me instead of hollowing me out.
days.question: What have you stopped preparing for?

days.title: What Hannah Said On The Way Home

body.p: Hannah goes up to the house of the Lord and prays so hard that her lips move without sound, and the priest watching her concludes she is drunk. It is worth sitting with how badly she was misread by the one man in the building whose job was to read people.
She corrects him. Not angrily — she just tells him plainly what she is doing. And Eli, to his credit, changes his mind in a single sentence and blesses her.

Read that last line slowly, because everything in it happens before anything changes. Hannah is not pregnant. She has no promise with a date on it. She has a blessing from a man who thought she was drunk ninety seconds ago.

And she eats. That detail is not decoration. She had refused food; the grief had reached her appetite, the way it does. Now she eats, and her face is different, and she goes home to the same house and the same silence she left.

Something lifted in the temple that had nothing to do with the outcome. She had said the true thing out loud to God, and the weight of carrying it alone came off her before the thing she asked for ever arrived.

after: We tend to assume the burden lifts when the situation resolves. Sometimes it lifts the moment we stop performing and say the actual thing.
Hannah went home to nothing new. She just did not go home alone with it any more.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been carrying this quietly and calling it faith. Today I want to say it plainly to you instead — not a tidy version, the real one. Take the weight of holding it by myself, even if the circumstance stays exactly as it is tonight.
days.question: What have you been too composed to say to God?

days.title: The Man Who Kept Opening The Window

body.p: The flood is over. That is the part we remember. What we forget is that Noah has no way of knowing it is over, and no way to find out except to open a window and let a bird go.
The raven does not come back. The dove does, because there is nowhere yet to land. So he waits.

Seven days. He does not send the dove again the next morning, which is what I would have done, and probably what you would have done. He waits a full week inside a dark boat with the animals and does nothing, and then he tries again.
The second time the dove comes back with a leaf. The third time it does not come back at all, which is the real answer — the bird has found somewhere to live.
Three attempts, two weeks of silence in between, and no guarantee at any point that the next attempt would be different from the last.

after: Faithfulness in a waiting season is rarely dramatic. It is usually the willingness to try again on a schedule that nothing external is rewarding yet.
The window opened three times. Only the third one meant anything, and he could not have known that on the first.
days.prayer: God, I am tired of trying and getting the same answer back. Give me the patience of a week I did not choose, and the courage to open the window one more time when it comes round. Let me keep doing the small faithful thing while I cannot see the ground.
days.question: What have you given up trying because it came back empty?

days.title: It Will Not Lie

body.p: Habakkuk is a short book by a man who is furious with God and says so. He is not asking a theoretical question. He is watching his country come apart and he wants to know why the God he believes in is not doing anything about it.
Then he does something I find remarkable. He says he will stand on his watchtower and wait to see what God will answer him. He complains, and then he stays put for the reply.
There is a contradiction in that verse that is not a mistake. Though it tarry, wait for it — so it will be late. Because it will surely come, it will not tarry — so it will not be late.
Both are true, and they are true from different positions. From where Habakkuk stands it is unbearably slow. From where it was appointed, it is exactly on time.
The verse does not ask him to stop feeling the delay. It asks him to hold his experience of lateness and God's appointment together without letting go of either one.

line.a: Though it tarry, wait for it.

after: You are allowed to find this slow. Habakkuk did, and God answered him rather than correcting him.
What you are not asked to conclude is that slow means never.
days.prayer: Lord, this feels late to me, and I am not going to pretend otherwise in your presence. Hold me steady between what I can see and what you have appointed. Let me wait like a man on a watchtower rather than a man walking away.
days.question: Where have you started reading slow as no?

days.title: Two More Years

body.p: Joseph is in prison for something he did not do. He interprets a dream correctly for a fellow prisoner, and he asks for one thing in return: when you get out, remember me. Mention my name to someone.
The man gets out. Everything Joseph said would happen happens exactly as he said it.
The chapter ends there. The next chapter opens by telling us it was two full years.
Two years is not a literary device. It is seven hundred and thirty mornings of waking up in a prison you should not be in, having done the right thing, for a man who owed you and forgot.

Nothing in the text suggests Joseph handled this beautifully. It simply does not tell us. What it tells us is that the forgetting was real, the delay was long, and the position he was eventually given required him to be exactly where he was when the call came.

after: Being forgotten by someone who owed you is its own particular wound, and it is worse when you did the right thing to earn the debt.
The two years were not empty. They were just unexplained until much later, and Joseph lived every one of them without the explanation.
days.prayer: Father, someone forgot me, and I have been quietly keeping the account. I am handing you the ledger. Keep me from bitterness in the long gap between what I did and what came of it, and hold me steady where you have placed me.
days.question: Who owes you something you have stopped expecting?

days.title: Four Words After Four Hundred Years

body.p: Israel has been in Egypt for four centuries. Generations were born into it, worked in it, and died in it without ever seeing anything else. There is no record of a prophet during that stretch. No promise renewed, no visitation, nothing.
Then a king dies, and the people groan. Not pray, in the first instance. Groan.
Four verbs land in two verses: God heard, God remembered, God looked, God knew. They are stacked deliberately, like someone laying out evidence.

Remembered is the strange one, because it implies a period of not remembering, which cannot be what it means. In Hebrew it is less about recall and more about acting on something long held. God moved on a promise he had been holding since Abraham.
Which means the four hundred years were not silence in the sense of absence. They were silence in the sense of a covenant being kept without commentary.

after: The groan is what starts the chapter's engine, and a groan is not an eloquent prayer. It is the sound a person makes when words have run out.
That sound was enough.
days.prayer: God, I do not have the language for this one any more. You have heard the sound I make when I have run out of words. Remember what you have promised, look on where I actually am, and let me know that you know.
days.question: What have you stopped bringing to God because you cannot phrase it?

days.title: He Stayed Two Days

body.p: The sisters send word that Lazarus is ill. They do not ask Jesus to come; they simply tell him who is sick, and they identify him by a relationship — he whom thou lovest. They assume that is enough information.
It is. And what he does with it is not what anyone in the story expects.
The hinge of that sentence is the word therefore. He loved them, therefore he stayed where he was. Not although. Therefore.

Every instinct I have wants that to be a translation problem. It is not. John has written the delay and the love into the same clause on purpose, and he has left it there for two thousand years for us to trip over.
Martha says it to his face when he finally arrives: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. She is right. That is the hard part. She is completely right, and he does not argue with her.

after: This does not make delay painless and the text never pretends it does. Jesus weeps at the tomb of a man he is about to raise.
It only rules out one conclusion: that the waiting is evidence you are not loved.
days.prayer: Jesus, I have been reading your silence as distance. Teach me that the delay and the love are not two different things in your hands. Come when you come, and until then keep me from deciding what your quietness means about me.
days.question: What have you concluded about God's love from his timing?

days.title: Her Hap Was To Light

body.p: Ruth is a widow supporting an older widow in a country that is not hers. She goes out to glean, which means walking behind the harvesters and picking up whatever they drop. It is the legal provision for people with nothing, and it is as undignified as it sounds.
She has to choose a field. She does not know the owners. She picks one.

Her hap was to light on. Her chance. The narrator writes it as luck, flatly, with no halo on it — and then spends the rest of the book showing you that this field is the hinge on which a family line turns, and eventually a king, and eventually the genealogy in Matthew chapter one.
The writer knew exactly what he was doing. He gives you the moment as Ruth experienced it — an arbitrary choice on a hard morning — and lets you find out later what it was.
She did not feel providence. She felt tired, and she picked a field.

after: You are unlikely to recognise the important day while you are inside it. It will feel like an ordinary decision made without enough information.
Keep going out to the field.
days.prayer: Lord, most of my choices are made tired and without enough information, and I cannot tell which ones matter. Work through the ordinary ones. Let me be faithful in the field I picked this morning even though it feels like nothing.
days.question: What are you doing that feels too small to count?

days.title: How Long

body.p: Psalm 13 is six verses long. It is the shortest complete emotional journey in the Bible, and it begins with a man asking God how long four times in two verses.
For ever is an accusation. He does not soften it, and nobody edited it out. The songbook of Israel opens this psalm by permitting a worshipper to tell God to his face that this has gone on too long.
Then verse five turns without warning: but I have trusted in thy mercy. There is no new information in between. Nothing has been resolved. The enemy is still there, the sleeplessness is still there.
What has happened is that he has said the whole complaint out loud, in God's direction, and having said it he finds he is still standing on something.
The complaint did not disqualify the trust. It cleared the ground for it.

after: Six verses. Four accusations and one 'but'. The 'but' is only load-bearing because the accusations were honest.
Prayer that has been pre-edited for tone is not more spiritual. It is just quieter.
days.prayer: Lord, how long. I am saying it because your own songbook taught me I am allowed to. And having said it, I am still here, and still yours, and still trusting your mercy with nothing new to go on.
days.question: What would you say to God if you stopped editing it?

days.title: They Shall Walk

body.p: This is the verse people put on gym walls, and they usually stop at the eagles. Read the whole line and notice the order it goes in.
Mount up with wings. Run. Walk. That is descending order, and it is descending on purpose. If you were writing an inspirational poster you would end on the eagles.

Isaiah ends on walking, and he attaches the strangest promise to it: and not faint. Not shall run and not be weary — that comes earlier. The final clause is about the person who is no longer soaring or running, who is just putting one foot down after the other.
That is the hardest of the three and he knows it. Anyone can be carried through a crisis on adrenaline. Sustaining an unremarkable walk through year four of something is a different order of grace.
The eagles are for the day it lifts. The walking is for all the other days, and the promise covers those too.

after: If today is not a soaring day, you have not fallen out of the verse. You have reached the part of it that was written for you.
Walking counts.
days.prayer: God, I am not soaring and I am not running. I am walking, and some days barely. Renew my strength at the pace I am actually moving, and let me not faint in the ordinary middle of this.
days.question: Where have you decided that walking means failing?

days.title: He Wanted A Bigger Moment

body.p: Naaman is a commander of an army and a leper. He arrives at Elisha's door with horses, chariots and a small fortune, expecting the encounter his position warrants.
Elisha does not come out. He sends a servant with a message: go and wash seven times in the Jordan.

Behold, I thought. That is the whole problem in three words, and it is unusually honest of the text to record it. He had a picture of how his healing would look. The prophet standing there, a hand moving over the place, the name of God called out loud.

What he got was an errand, delivered second-hand, involving a river he considered inferior to the ones back home. His servants have to talk him into it, and their argument is devastating: if he had asked you to do something great, would you not have done it?
He goes down. Seven times, which means six times coming up out of the water unchanged, with the men watching.

after: Sometimes the delay is not God's. It is the distance between the answer offered and the answer we had pictured.
The seventh time was the same river as the first.
days.prayer: Lord, I have been holding out for the version of this I imagined, and refusing the one in front of me. Show me where my picture is the obstacle. Give me the humility to go down into the ordinary water.
days.question: What has God offered that you rejected for being too small?

days.title: In The City, Doing Nothing

body.p: The resurrection has happened. The disciples have seen him, eaten with him, been commissioned by him. Every reason to move is now in place, and the whole book that follows is about movement.
And the first instruction of the book of Acts is to stay put.
Wait for the promise. That is what they do for roughly ten days — in a room, in a city, with the most urgent news in human history and explicit orders not to go anywhere with it yet.
Luke tells us what they did with the time. They prayed, they stayed together, and they attended to one piece of unfinished business among themselves. That is it. No campaign, no strategy document.
The waiting was not a pause before the mission. It was the first act of obedience the mission required, and everything after it depended on them getting that part right.

after: Some seasons of stillness are not God withholding the work. They are the work, and moving early would cost you the thing you are moving with.
Ten days in a room, and then the whole world.
days.prayer: Father, I am ready to move and you have not said go. Keep me in the room. Let me use this stillness for prayer and for putting things right with people, instead of burning it on impatience.
days.question: What are you about to start early?

days.title: Quietly

body.p: Lamentations is a funeral song for a destroyed city, written by someone who watched it happen. It is five chapters of grief with almost no relief in it.
The exception sits in the middle of chapter three, and it is famous — his mercies are new every morning. What is less quoted is the line that follows a few verses later.
Quietly wait. Not passively, and not silently in the sense of having no feelings — this is a book of loud feelings. Quietly in the sense of without frantic motion.

The man writing this has every reason to be doing something. His city is rubble. And he has concluded, from inside the rubble, that hoping and quietly waiting is a good thing rather than a wasted thing.
That conclusion is worth more coming from him than it would be from someone comfortable.

line.a: It is good that a man

after: There is a difference between quiet waiting and numb waiting. One is aimed at God. The other has simply stopped.
He wrote this in the ruins, which is the only place it could have been proved.
days.prayer: Lord, calm the frantic part of me that thinks stillness is neglect. Let my waiting be quiet and aimed at you, not numb and aimed at nothing. Your mercies are new this morning and I am taking today's.
days.question: Is your waiting quiet, or has it just gone numb?

days.title: Now Let Thy Servant Depart

body.p: We started this fortnight with Simeon in the temple, waiting for something he had been promised he would live to see. This is the day it happens.
A poor couple comes in with a baby and the cheaper of the two permitted offerings, which tells you their income. Nothing about the scene announces itself. Simeon takes the child in his arms.
Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace. He is not asking to die. He is saying that the thing which held him at his post has been delivered, and he can stand down.
The word Luke uses is the one for releasing someone from duty. Simeon has understood his whole long wait as a watch he was keeping, and he is now formally asking to be relieved of it.
He held it. That is the detail I cannot get past. He did not see it from a distance or hear about it from someone else. He got to put his arms around it.

line.a: He did not just see it.

after: Not every wait ends like this, and the Bible is honest enough elsewhere to say so. But some do, and they end quietly, in a room with nobody important in it.
It arrived carried by strangers who could only afford two birds.
days.prayer: Father, keep me at my post. And when the thing comes — carried in by people I do not recognise, looking smaller than I imagined — give me the eyes to know it, and the arms to hold it, and the peace of a servant released.
days.question: Would you recognise it if it arrived looking ordinary?

days.title: Endurance In the Waiting Room

body.p: Paul does not say we glory in tribulations because they feel good. He gives a reason, and the reason is a single word: knowing. He glories because he knows something about what trouble does while it lasts.
Look at the verb. Tribulation worketh patience. It works. It is not idle, even when you are. The long weeks of waiting look like nothing is happening, but Paul says something is being made in them.

Then the chain runs on, patience, experience; and experience, hope. The old word experience means something closer to proven character, the kind of person who has been tested and found still standing. Nobody gets that by reading about it. It is made in rooms where you sit and wait for your name to be called.
And notice where the whole thing begins. Verse two says we already stand in grace. The waiting does not earn the standing. You are held before the trouble starts and all the while it goes on.

If you are in a clinic corridor this week, or waiting for a visa letter, or for a result that will not come, the plastic chair you are sitting on is not wasted time. Something is at work in you that you cannot see from where you sit.

after: The hours you spend waiting are not subtracted from your life with God.
You can be still and still be growing.
days.prayer: Father, I do not enjoy waiting, and I will not pretend I do. But you say trouble is working something in me, so let it work. Make me patient, then proven, then hopeful, in that order and at your pace. Hold me in the grace where I already stand. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you waiting for right now, and what might it be working in you?

days.title: Endurance When You Feel Small

body.p: There is a particular fear that comes with hoping. It is the fear of looking foolish. You told people you were trusting God, and then the thing did not happen, and now you feel small in front of them.
Paul answers that fear directly: hope maketh not ashamed. The hope he is talking about will not leave you red faced at the end. It will not turn out to have been a joke at your expense.

But look at the reason he gives. It is not that every hope comes true on schedule. It is because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts. Shed abroad means poured out, spilled generously, the way water finds every corner of a jar. The ground of hope is not the outcome. It is a love already given.

And it is given by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. You did not climb up to reach it. It came down to you. People who feel small often think they must grow before God will take them seriously. Paul says the love is already inside, poured in by God himself.
So the next time you sit in a church pew or a staff meeting feeling like the least important person in the room, remember that the love of God was poured into you, not measured out by your size.

line.a: Feeling small is not the same as being forgotten.
line.b: The love was poured, not rationed.

after: Hope in God may be delayed, but it will not be made a fool of.
You do not need to feel large to be full of his love.
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, I feel small today, and sometimes foolish for hoping. Remind me that the love of God is already poured into my heart, not because I grew enough to deserve it but because you gave it. Let my hope rest on that love and not on how things look this week. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you afraid that hoping will make you look foolish?

days.title: Endurance Through an Open Door

body.p: Paul asks a question that sounds almost like a riddle: what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? Once the door is open and you can see through it, you stop hoping. You simply walk.
Which means hope only lives on this side of a door you cannot see past. If you could see the outcome, you would not need patience. Then do we with patience wait for it.

Then comes the sentence that makes this bearable. Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities. Paul admits something most of us are embarrassed to say out loud: we know not what we should pray for as we ought. Even our praying, while we wait, comes out wrong.

And the answer is not a better prayer method. It is the Spirit praying alongside us with groanings which cannot be uttered. Some nights there are no words, only a sigh into the pillow at three in the morning. Paul says the Spirit is in that sigh too.

Perhaps you are standing at a door that may open and may not, a job, a marriage, a move abroad. You do not have to know how to pray about it correctly. You only have to keep waiting near the door and let the Spirit carry what you cannot say.

line.a: You cannot hope for what you already see.
line.b: So the waiting is where hope lives.

after: When you do not know what to ask for, you have not stopped praying.
A groan offered to God is not a failure of faith.
days.prayer: Spirit of God, I do not know what I should pray for, and I am tired of pretending I do. Help my weakness. Pray in me when my words run out, and give me patience to wait at a door I cannot see through. Let my sighs reach the Father through you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would you say to God about this if you did not have to get the words right?

days.title: Endurance When the Answer Is No

body.p: Paul's list here moves fast, one short phrase after another, like instructions pinned to a kitchen wall. Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer.

Notice what sits on either side of those three. Before them comes work: Not slothful in business. After them comes the table: Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality. Endurance is set in the middle of an ordinary week, not on a mountain.

That matters when God's answer is no. A no can make you want to stop everything. Stop praying, stop serving, close the door and sit in the dark. Paul's list does not allow it. Keep praying, he says, instant, which means constantly, without letting go. And keep the pot on the fire for visitors.
This is not a way of pretending the no does not hurt. Patient in tribulation assumes there is tribulation. It simply refuses to let one closed door close every other door in the house.

If you heard no this month, from a hospital, an embassy, an employer, or from God in the silence, you may still cook for someone this weekend. You may still pray tomorrow morning. Those small faithful things are what endurance looks like from the outside.

line.a: A no can close one door.
line.b: It does not have to close the house.

after: Prayer after a no is not denial. It is trust that has been hurt and stays anyway.
Someone may need your table even in the week your heart is heavy.
days.prayer: Lord, you said no, and I do not fully understand why. Keep me from shutting down. Help me to keep praying, to keep working honestly, and to keep my door open to people who need it. Let my hope stay alive even while it aches. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Has a recent no made you close doors God never asked you to close?

days.title: Endurance In What You Already Have

body.p: The order of these two verses is the whole lesson. First the gift: thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Then the command: be ye stedfast, unmoveable. The word that joins them is Therefore.

Paul does not say be steadfast so that you might win. He says you have been given the victory, so be steadfast. Endurance flows out of something you already hold, not toward something you are trying to grab.

These lines close the great resurrection chapter. Paul has just spoken of death losing its sting. If death itself is defeated, then a hard season at work or a slow year in ministry is not the final word either.

And there is one more thing you already have. Ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Not you hope, not you suspect. You know. Paul expects believers to carry that knowledge into dull, unseen work and to keep always abounding in it.

Think of the woman who has kept the same market stall for twenty years, opening the shutters before dawn, greeting the same faces. Faithfulness in small things done for the Lord is not thrown away. It counts, because the victory under it is already secure.

line.a: You are not working toward the victory.

after: Nothing done in the Lord is wasted, even the parts nobody thanks you for.
Steadiness comes easier when you remember what you have already been given.
days.prayer: Thank you, God, for the victory you have already given me through Jesus. Let me work today from that settled place, not from fear. Keep me steady and unmoved in the ordinary tasks in front of me, and remind me that my labour in you is not wasted. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What work have you quietly decided is in vain?

days.title: Endurance When Nobody Notices

body.p: Two things are happening to Paul at once, and only one of them shows. Our outward man perish, he says. Everyone can see that part. The tiredness, the scars, the grey hair, the body slowing down.

The other part is hidden: the inward man is renewed day by day. Nobody photographs that. Nobody comments on it. Often you cannot feel it yourself. But Paul says it is happening on the same days the outward decline is happening.
Day by day is a quiet phrase. It is not a single dramatic recovery. It is a small renewal, given in the morning and used up by night, then given again.

Verse fifteen adds something surprising. Paul's endurance is not only for him. It is so that grace, through the thanksgiving of many, might overflow to the glory of God. People you will never meet may thank God because you kept going when nobody noticed.

If you are caring for an ageing parent, washing clothes no one will mention, sitting up at night with a feverish child, the outward cost is easy to count. The inward renewal is harder to see, but it is real, and it comes again tomorrow.

after: God is renewing you on the same days you feel yourself wearing out.
Unseen faithfulness is still seen by him.
days.prayer: Lord, I can see what this season is costing me, but I struggle to see anything you are building. Renew my inner life today, even if no one notices, including me. Let my quiet faithfulness turn into thanksgiving somewhere, for your glory and not mine. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who is enduring quietly near you whose faithfulness you have not noticed?

days.title: Endurance With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: It is worth remembering who wrote the words our light affliction. Paul had been beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and left hungry. He was not a comfortable man calling other people's suffering light.

He calls it light only when it is weighed against something else: a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. Light and weight. Moment and eternal. He is holding the two on a scale. The affliction is real. It simply does not outweigh what is on the other side.
That is what keeps this from being escapism. Paul has both feet on the ground. He does not deny the pain. He measures it.

Then he tells us how he does it. While we look not at the things which are seen. The word while matters. The affliction feels light only while his eyes are lifted. When he stares only at the trouble, it is as heavy as anyone's. Looking up is something you do again and again, not once.

So in the queue at the pharmacy, or on the long walk home after hard news, the invitation is not to pretend. Look at what is seen and admit it honestly. Then lift your eyes to what is not seen, which lasts longer than this and is heavier with good.

line.a: Paul does not call pain nothing.
line.b: He calls it lighter than glory.

after: Honest grief and eternal hope can stand on the same ground.
Where your eyes rest will change how heavy the day feels.
days.prayer: Father, I will not pretend my trouble is small. It is heavy to me. But lift my eyes beyond what I can see today, to the glory you have promised, until the weight of it steadies me. Keep my feet on the ground and my sight on you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you looking at most often when your trouble feels heaviest?

days.title: Endurance When You Must Begin Again

body.p: Paul talks like a farmer here. Sowing, reaping, seasons. Anyone who has planted anything knows that the work and the harvest are separated by a long stretch of nothing visible.

In due season we shall reap, if we faint not. Due season is not the season you would choose. It is the right season, the one the seed needs. Pulling up maize to check on it does not make it grow faster.

Farmers know something else too. Some years the rain fails. Some harvests are thin. And the next year they plant again. Beginning again is not a sign of failure in farming. It is simply how farming works.

That is why verse ten opens with As we have therefore opportunity. Each opportunity is a new planting. You may have tried to do good for someone and seen nothing come of it. Today is another field. You do not have to make up for the last season before you sow in this one.

Perhaps you are starting a new job after losing the last one, or rebuilding a friendship you thought was finished, or picking up a habit of prayer you let go. Plant the seed in front of you. The season is God's to name.

line.a: The field looks empty after sowing.
line.b: That is what sowing looks like.

after: A failed harvest last year is not a reason to leave the field this year.
Good done today is a seed, even if you never see what grows.
days.prayer: Lord of the harvest, I am tired of sowing and seeing nothing. Give me strength to begin again with the opportunity in front of me today. Keep me from fainting, and teach me to trust your timing instead of mine. Let me do good to the people you put in my path. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What good thing have you stopped planting because last season was thin?

days.title: Endurance In the Middle of the Work

body.p: Count how often one word appears in these three verses. Withstand, then to stand, then Stand therefore. Paul keeps coming back to it, like a coach shouting the same instruction from the touchline.
It is a surprising goal for a passage about armour. You might expect charge, advance, conquer. Instead the aim is to be still on your feet at the end. Having done all, to stand.

That is good news for anyone in the middle of something long. You may not be winning anything visible. The work is half done and the end is not in sight. Paul does not ask you to finish today. He asks you to remain standing in the evil day, the hard day, whatever yours is.

He also reminds us who the real struggle is with. We wrestle not against flesh and blood. The colleague who frustrates you and the relative who will not listen are not the enemy. That changes how you stand. You stand girded with truth, not with resentment.

Maybe you are on the third night shift of the week at the ward, or in the second year of a degree you are paying for yourself. You do not have to feel strong. You only have to stand, and then stand again.

after: Still being on your feet at the end of a hard day is a victory.
The people in front of you are not your enemy, even when they are hard.
days.prayer: Lord, I am in the middle of this and I cannot see the end. Clothe me with truth and righteousness, and help me to stand today, not to conquer everything, just to stand. Keep me from treating people as my enemy. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it look like for you simply to keep standing this week?

days.title: Endurance When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Paul begins with a confession that might surprise us from an apostle. I count not myself to have apprehended. In plain words, I have not arrived. I am not finished.

Fear usually speaks first with exactly that accusation. You are behind. You are not where you should be. Paul does not argue with it. He agrees, and then he keeps going. His not having arrived is the reason he presses on, not the reason he gives up.

Much of our fear speaks from the past, from what went wrong last time or from who we were before. Paul's answer is forgetting those things which are behind. He does not mean erasing memory. He means refusing to let yesterday steer.

Then there is the gentleness of verse fifteen. If anyone thinks differently, God shall reveal even this unto you. Paul trusts God to keep teaching people who are not there yet. That includes you, and the parts of you still afraid.

Before an exam, a job interview, a hard conversation with your landlord, fear will speak first. Let it speak. Then answer the way Paul did. I have not arrived, but this one thing I do, and lean forward toward what is ahead.

line.a: Fear says you have not arrived.
line.b: Paul says, so I press on.

after: Being unfinished is the normal state of every follower of Christ.
Yesterday can be remembered without being allowed to drive.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, fear is loud in me today, and it keeps reminding me of everything behind me. Help me to forget what I should leave behind and to reach for what is ahead. I have not arrived, but I want to keep pressing toward you. Reveal to me what I still do not see. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is fear saying to you first this morning, and what would Paul say back?

days.title: Endurance With an Open Hand

body.p: This is a prayer. Paul is telling the Colossians what he asks God for them, and in the middle of it is a sentence with enormous words: Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power.

You expect the sentence to end with miracles. All that power, for what? Paul finishes it: unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness. The glorious power of God is spent, in this prayer, on helping ordinary believers be patient.

That changes what strength looks like. It is not always the clenched fist that breaks through. Sometimes it is the open hand that waits, that bears with a difficult person for the hundredth time and does not turn bitter.

The next verse explains how the hand stays open. Giving thanks unto the Father, which hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance. An inheritance is received, not earned. Thanksgiving keeps the hand open because it remembers that everything good came as a gift.

In the slow line at the bank, with the neighbour whose generator roars all night, beside the relative who repeats the same complaint, patience with joy is not weakness. It is the power of God doing exactly what Paul prayed it would do.

after: A gentle answer may be the strongest thing you do today.
Thanksgiving keeps a tired hand from closing into a fist.
days.prayer: Father, strengthen me with your power today, not to impress anyone but to be patient. Give me longsuffering with joy toward the people who test me. Keep my hand open and my heart thankful for the inheritance you have given me in Christ. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who in your life requires the kind of patience only God's power can give?

days.title: Endurance When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Paul pairs three things in verse three, and each has two parts. Work of faith. Labour of love. Patience of hope. The first word in each pair grows out of the second.

The last pair is the one for this month. Patience grows out of hope. You do not endure because you can see the end of the road. You endure because you hope in a person, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is already there.

Notice the phrase that closes the verse: in the sight of God and our Father. You may not be able to see far ahead. But you are not out of sight. The Thessalonians were new believers under pressure, and Paul reminds them that their quiet endurance was happening in front of God.
There is a second comfort. Paul says he remembers them without ceasing. Someone else was carrying their names in prayer while they carried on. Endurance is rarely as lonely as it feels.

In harmattan season, when the haze is thick and you can barely make out the next junction, you drive slowly and trust that the road is still there. Hope works the same way. You see a few metres. God sees the whole way, and he sees you on it.

line.b: You are not out of his sight.

after: Patience is not seeing the end. It is trusting the one who does.
Someone may be praying for you today who has never told you.
days.prayer: God my Father, I cannot see far down this road, and that frightens me. Thank you that I am never out of your sight. Let my patience grow from hope in Jesus, not from knowing every answer. And thank you for those who pray for me without my knowing. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who is enduring something near you that you could carry in prayer this week?

days.title: Endurance In the Honest Answer

body.p: Lifted out on its own, this line looks like a gentle encouragement. Read where it sits, it becomes more honest. Some in the church at Thessalonica had stopped working altogether, and Paul tells them plainly to work, and eat their own bread.

Then he turns to everyone else. But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing. These are the people who had been carrying the idle ones, sharing food, covering gaps. They were tired in the particular way that comes from doing good for people who take advantage of it.

Paul does not treat that tiredness as sin. He names it, which is itself a kind of mercy. Doing good for people who do not change is wearying. The honest answer to how you are is sometimes, I am tired of helping.

Verse fourteen is firm. Some people need to feel the weight of their choices. Love is not the same as endlessly funding someone's refusal to change. But for those still doing good, the instruction is not to quit. Keep doing what is right, even while drawing wiser lines.

Maybe there is a cousin who keeps borrowing and never repays, or a colleague who always leaves you the extra work. Tell God honestly how tired you are. Then ask him what well doing looks like here. It may include a firmer no.

line.a: Paul admits well doing is tiring.
line.b: He still says, do not stop.

after: You are allowed to be honest with God about how tired you are of helping.
Doing good and drawing boundaries are not enemies.
days.prayer: Lord, I am weary of doing good for people who do not seem to change. Thank you that I can say that to you. Give me fresh strength to keep doing what is right, and wisdom to know when love means saying no. Guard my heart from bitterness. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are you tired of doing good, and what would an honest conversation with God about it sound like?

days.title: Endurance When the Cost Is Real

body.p: Tucked into the middle of verse twenty three is a phrase in brackets: for he is faithful that promised. It looks like an aside. It is actually the foundation of the whole sentence.

The command is to hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering. That sounds as if everything depends on our grip. But the bracket tells you why you can hold on. Not because your hands are strong, but because the one who promised does not let go of his word.

This letter was written to believers who knew the cost was real. Some had been mocked in public, some had lost their property, some had friends in prison. Holding fast was not easy for them. The writer never says it will be easy. He says God is faithful.

Notice too that the commands all begin with Let us. Draw near. Hold fast. Then, let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works. Endurance under cost is not a solo effort. We hold on partly by watching out for each other.
If following Christ is costing you something, laughter in the staff room, a cold silence at the family gathering, do not carry it alone. Tell someone in your church. Let them help you hold on.

after: Holding fast rests on God's faithfulness more than on your strength.
Someone near you may need you to notice what their faith is costing them.
days.prayer: Faithful God, following you is costing me more than I expected. Help me hold on without wavering, not because I am strong but because you keep your promises. Give me people who will stand with me, and make me that kind of friend to others. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who in your church knows what your faith is currently costing you?

days.title: Endurance For the Long Road

body.p: There is a gap in the middle of verse thirty six, and most of life is lived inside it. After ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise. First the doing, then the receiving. Between them, a space.

That space is why the writer says ye have need of patience. Not that you might like some patience. You need it, the way a traveller needs water on a long road. Obedience is often followed by a wait, not by an immediate reward.

He warns against one specific danger: Cast not away therefore your confidence. Confidence is something you can throw away, like a bag that feels too heavy at the fortieth kilometre. Do not drop it. It carries a reward.

Then he borrows the words of a prophet: For yet a little while, and he that shall come will come, and will not tarry. It is fair to admit this little while has been long. But God's little while is measured by his faithfulness, not our calendars, and the promise still stands that he will come.

On a long bus ride from Lagos to Abuja, the hours after the halfway point can feel worse than the start. You are tired and not yet close. That is where many believers are. Keep your confidence on your lap. The arrival is promised.

line.b: The promise comes after a road.

after: Doing God's will and receiving his promise are often separated by a long stretch.
Do not throw away your confidence because the road is longer than you thought.
days.prayer: Lord, I have tried to do your will, and the promise still feels far away. Give me the patience I need for this long stretch. Keep me from throwing away my confidence in you. Remind me that you will come, and you will not be late. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is there something you obeyed God in that you have started to regret because the reward has not come yet?

days.title: Endurance At the End of the Day

body.p: Two phrases echo each other in these verses. The race that is set before us. And the joy that was set before him. What was placed in front of Jesus helped him run his course. What is placed in front of us is the course itself.

He ran with joy ahead of him, and that joy carried him through the cross, despising the shame. He did not enjoy the cross. He endured it, looking past it. Now he is set down at the right hand of God. His race is finished.
That is why we run Looking unto Jesus. We look at someone who has already crossed the line, who knows the course because he ran a harder one.

The end of the day is a good time for the other instruction: lay aside every weight. Evening is when you take off your shoes, empty your pockets, put down your bag. It is also when you can set down the worries and grudges and sins you picked up since morning. A runner cannot carry all of them and still run tomorrow.
Tonight, before you sleep, name the weights you are carrying. Set them before God one by one. Then look at Jesus, who finished, and rest.

line.b: Tomorrow, run again looking at him.

after: Jesus ran a harder race than yours, and he finished it.
What you lay down tonight you do not have to carry into tomorrow.
days.prayer: Jesus, at the end of this day I am tired, and I am carrying more than I should. I lay these weights before you now, the worries, the hurts, the sin I keep returning to. Let me look at you, who endured and finished. Give me rest tonight and strength for the race tomorrow. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which weight are you most reluctant to put down tonight?

days.title: Endurance For What Comes Next

body.p: James uses an accountant's word: count it all joy. Not feel it. Count it. It is a decision about how to reckon something, made with the mind, often while the heart is still protesting.

He gives the reason in the next verse. The trying of your faith worketh patience. Testing produces something. Then comes the line that closes this month on endurance: let patience have her perfect work.

James speaks of patience as if she were a worker who has come to do a job in you. The instruction is simply to let her. Do not hurry her out. Do not interrupt her halfway because the work is uncomfortable.

Most of us want to leave a trial as quickly as we can, and that is natural. Sometimes we should pray for it to end. But James says there is a finished work waiting on the other side: that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing. Whole. Not missing pieces.

Anyone who has cooked a pot of beans knows that lifting the lid every five minutes does not make them soften faster. Whatever comes next for you, a new month, a new trial, a slow answer, let patience finish what she started.

line.a: Patience has work to do in you.

after: Counting a trial as joy is a decision, not a feeling.
What God is finishing in you is worth not rushing.
days.prayer: Father, I want to rush out of every hard thing. Teach me to count my trials with faith, and to let patience finish her work in me. Make me whole and steady, lacking nothing I truly need, as I step into whatever comes next. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which trial have you been trying to hurry patience out of?

days.title: Gratitude Before You Feel Ready

body.p: David wrote this song for the day the ark came home to Jerusalem. It was a day of drums and dancing, and you would expect the song to be all celebration.

Then, right after O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good, comes a line that sounds like it belongs to a harder day. Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen.
The people are told to give thanks and to cry for help in the same breath. Their thanks is not waiting for everything to be fixed. It stands beside the request, not after it.
Notice the reason given for the rescue: that we may give thanks to thy holy name. They want to be saved so they can thank him more. Gratitude is where they start and also where they hope to end.

You may not feel thankful this morning. You may be waiting on a result, a payment, a phone call that has not come. Say both lines anyway, on the walk to the bus stop if that is where you are. He is good. Save me. The song has room for both.

line.a: Thanks does not wait for the rescue.
line.b: It walks in beside the request.

after: You can be grateful and still be asking for help, because the same psalm does both.
Say thank you for one thing before you say what you still need.
days.prayer: Lord, I do not feel ready to be grateful today, and you know why. I thank you anyway, because you are good and your mercy has not run out on me. And I ask you plainly, save me from what is pressing on me, and bring me through so that I can thank you again on the other side. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it sound like to say thank you and help me in the same sentence today?

days.title: Gratitude In the Next Step

body.p: Psalm 7 is written by a man who has been lied about. The heading names a Benjamite called Cush, and the whole psalm is David asking God to judge between them.
Verse 16 is almost grim. His mischief shall return upon his own head, David says, and the old word pate just means the top of the skull. Trouble thrown upward comes back down on the one who threw it.
What David does not do is throw anything himself. He leaves the falling to God, and his very next step is a song. I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness.

That phrase sets the measure. He is not praising according to how the week went, or according to whether his name has been cleared yet. He is praising according to who God is, and God's fairness is not on trial even when David's reputation is.

If someone has spoken against you at work or in the family, you may lie awake rehearsing replies. The next step here is smaller than a reply. Hand the judging over, then thank God for being righteous, even before you see it, even standing in the queue at the bank.

line.b: Take the next step with a song.

after: You do not have to settle every account before you are allowed to praise.
God's fairness is the measure of your thanks, not the outcome of the argument.
days.prayer: Lord, you know what has been said about me and you know what is true. I give the judging to you, because I would do it badly. Help me take the next step with praise instead of a plan for getting even, and let me thank you for your righteousness before I see it worked out. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose words against you are you still carrying, and could you hand the verdict to God today?

days.title: Gratitude When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: Count the times David says I will in these two verses. Praise, shew forth, be glad, sing. Four decisions, one after another, before he has said a single thing about what God is doing right now.
These are not reports of a feeling. They are choices, set down like stepping stones across a stream.
And the first one has a size attached. With my whole heart. Not the part of the heart that happens to be free this week, not the part left over after worry has taken its share. All of it.

When life goes quiet, when prayers seem to settle into the ceiling and nothing much is happening, it is easy to think there is nothing to be thankful about. But David says he will tell of all thy marvellous works, and most of those are behind him. The past ones still count. A quiet season is a good time to remember them out loud.
Try it tonight while the rice is cooking. Name three things God did for you years ago that you have stopped mentioning. Then say the fourth I will, and sing, even if it is only humming.

after: Gratitude in a quiet season is mostly memory spoken aloud.
Say I will before you can honestly say I feel.
days.prayer: Father, the way is quiet and I have been reading the silence as absence. Give me back my memory of what you have done. I will praise you with my whole heart, not the leftover part, and I will tell someone today about a kindness of yours I had stopped mentioning. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which of God's past works have you quietly stopped telling anyone about?

days.title: Gratitude Without an Audience

body.p: The first half of Psalm 28 is a man afraid that heaven has gone quiet. Be not silent to me, he begs in verse 1, as if he were speaking into a dead line.
Then, in verse 6, the tone turns. Blessed be the LORD, because he hath heard the voice of my supplications. Not because the trouble has gone. Because he was heard.
That was the whole audience David needed. No crowd, no one at the gate admiring his faith. One listener, and the knowledge that the listener had leaned in.

Look at the order that follows. My heart trusted in him, and I am helped, and only then does his heart greatly rejoice. Trust, then help, then joy. The rejoicing happens inside him before it reaches the song, which means it was real before anyone could hear it.

Much of your thanks will happen where no one sees. In a toilet cubicle at the office, in a whispered word beside a sick bed, on the night bus home. It is not smaller for being private. It has been heard by the only one it was meant for.

after: Being heard by God is reason enough to give thanks, even before the answer comes.
Private gratitude is not wasted gratitude.
days.prayer: Lord, thank you for hearing me, even when I could not tell that you were listening. I do not need anyone to see my thanks today. You are my strength and my shield, my heart is learning to trust you, and I will give you a quiet song where nobody else is watching. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: When did you last thank God simply for hearing you, before anything changed?

days.title: Gratitude For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: The picture in verse 11 is a change of clothes. Thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness. Sackcloth was what you wore when someone died or when everything had gone wrong. God takes it off you, and ties gladness round your waist instead.
A belt is not a costume for a party. It is what you put on every morning without thinking about it.

David remembers the dramatic day, mourning turned into dancing. But the purpose he names is longer than one day: that my glory may sing praise to thee, and not be silent. Then the phrase that stretches it out: I will give thanks unto thee for ever.

For ever is mostly made of days nobody will write about. The day after the rescue. The week after the wedding. The Tuesday when the light bill is paid and nobody is sick and nothing in particular happens. Those are the days when silence is most likely, because there is no crisis to pull a prayer out of you.

This evening, as you change out of your work clothes, notice that you were dressed in gladness today too, even if you did not feel it. Say thank you for the ordinary hours. They are part of the for ever.

after: The most dangerous day for gratitude is the one where nothing goes wrong.
Thank God for a quiet Tuesday before you ask him for a better Wednesday.
days.prayer: Lord, you have taken off my sackcloth more than once, and I have often forgotten to thank you afterwards. Today nothing much is happening, and I want to thank you for that too. Keep me from silence on the easy days. Let gratitude be part of my ordinary clothing. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What ordinary thing went right today that you have not yet thanked God for?

days.title: Gratitude When Plans Change

body.p: Psalm 34 has a heading most people skip. It ties the song to the day David pretended to be mad in the city of Gath, scratching at the gate and letting spit run down his beard, so that a foreign king would send him away instead of killing him.
It was not the plan. David had run there for safety and ended up acting the fool to stay alive.
Out of that day comes I will bless the LORD at all times. Not at the good times. At all of them, including the one where your plan collapsed and you left town with your dignity on the floor.

Verse 2 adds who is listening. The humble shall hear thereof, and be glad. People who have also been brought low will hear a man who has just been humiliated still boasting in God, and it will cheer them. His ruined plan becomes someone else's courage.

Maybe the visa did not come, or the job moved cities, or the wedding date shifted again. You do not have to pretend it was what you wanted. You can still say at all times, and someone lower on the ladder than you may be glad you did.

line.b: The praise did not have to.

after: At all times includes the times you would rather forget.
Someone humble is listening to how you talk about your disappointments.
days.prayer: Lord, this is not how I planned it, and some of it has been embarrassing. I will bless you anyway, at all times, including this one. Let my boast be in you and not in how well things worked out. And let someone who is struggling hear me and be glad. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: How are you talking about your changed plans when other people are listening?

days.title: Gratitude In the Work at Hand

body.p: God asks a question in verse 13 that is almost funny. Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Israel had been bringing sacrifices as if heaven were hungry and needed feeding.
He does not need their cattle. A few verses earlier he points out that every beast of the forest is already his. So what does he want?
Three things, and none of them involves a barn. Offer unto God thanksgiving. Pay thy vows unto the most High. And call upon me in the day of trouble.

Thanksgiving here is called an offering, the thing you bring. Paying vows is simply doing what you said you would do. Calling in trouble is admitting you need him. It is a very ordinary list. It fits inside a working day.

So the work in front of you, the report, the shop counter, the children's homework, is not a distraction from worship. Do what you promised, say thank you while you do it, and ask for help when it goes wrong. That is the sacrifice he asked for.

line.a: God is not hungry for bulls.
line.b: He asked for thanks and kept promises.

after: Doing what you said you would do is part of your thanksgiving.
He would rather hear your call for help than receive an impressive gift.
days.prayer: Father, you do not need anything from me, and still you ask for my thanks. Here it is, in the middle of my work. Help me keep the promises I have made, even the small ones, and when trouble comes today, remind me to call on you before I try to fix it myself. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is there a promise you made that your thanksgiving should include keeping today?

days.title: Gratitude When You Need Clarity

body.p: Verse 29 is about as honest as prayer gets. But I am poor and sorrowful. No dressing it up. Psalm 69 began with a man saying I sink in deep mire, and he has not climbed out yet.
Then, with nothing changed in his circumstances, he says I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving.

To magnify something is to make it look bigger so you can see it properly. A magnifying glass does not change the size of the thing, it changes how clearly you see it. Thanksgiving does that with God. When trouble fills the whole view, giving thanks brings him back into focus.

Verse 31 adds a small surprise. A song pleases God better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs. The details are there on purpose, the horns and hoofs of a grown animal, the most expensive offering a farmer could bring. A poor man's song outweighs it.
