If you are stuck on a decision and cannot see the way, try this before you write another list of pros and cons at the kitchen table. Thank God for three true things about him. It will not answer every question, but it will put him back at the right size.

line.a: Trouble had filled the whole view.
line.b: Thanks put God back in focus.

after: Magnifying God does not make him bigger, it lets you see how big he already is.
A poor and sorrowful song is still the offering he prefers.
days.prayer: God, I am poor and sorrowful in some way today, and I cannot see clearly. I will magnify you with thanksgiving anyway. Bring yourself back into focus for me, so that my trouble is seen at its real size next to you. I bring you a song instead of a solution. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What has grown so large in your view that you can no longer see God clearly?

days.title: Gratitude One Choice at a Time

body.p: Verse 1 says the same thing twice. Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks. It is not a copying error. It is a people deciding, and then deciding again.
Gratitude is rarely one big decision that settles everything. It is a choice you make, and then make again an hour later when the first one has worn thin.
The reason they give is lovely. That thy name is near. God is not far off. His works are the evidence, and they are close enough to point at.

Then, unusually, God answers within the psalm. When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly. Many readers take it to mean, when I choose the time. So the people choose to give thanks, and God keeps for himself the choice of when to put things right. That is a fair division of labour.

You do not have to fix the timing of your life today. You only have to make the next choice. On the drive home, in the market line, after the hard email, say it once, and then if you need to, say it twice.

line.b: Then say it again when it wears thin.

after: You choose the thanks, and God chooses the time.
A repeated thank you is not weakness, it is how gratitude gets built.
days.prayer: God, I give you thanks, and I will need to give it again before the day is over. Help me make that choice each time it comes. Thank you that your name is near. I leave the timing of my life with you, because you judge uprightly and I do not need to rush you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it look like to choose gratitude again at the moment it wears off today?

days.title: Gratitude Under Pressure

body.p: This psalm was written for the sabbath, the day the pressure was meant to stop. It begins with a plain claim: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD.
Good, and not only for God. Good for the one giving thanks. Like water or sleep, it is the kind of good thing you notice most when you have gone without it.
Then verse 2 divides the day in two. To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night. Morning gets lovingkindness. Night gets faithfulness.

The order makes sense to anyone under strain. In the morning you need to know you are loved before you face what is coming. At night you need to look back and see that he held, that the day which looked impossible at seven o'clock was somehow carried by ten. Lovingkindness is the promise. Faithfulness is the proof.

If this week is heavy, try the psalm's rhythm. Before you open your messages tomorrow, thank God for his love. Before you sleep, name one way he was faithful in the day, even if the day was hard. The pressure may not lift, but you will have two fixed points to stand on.

line.b: Faithfulness to look back on at night.

after: Under pressure, gratitude is not a luxury but one of the good things that keeps you standing.
Tonight, look for the place where he held.
days.prayer: Lord, it is a good thing to thank you, and I need good things right now. This morning, remind me that I am loved before I face what is waiting. Tonight, show me where you were faithful in the hours I thought I would not manage. Be my morning and my night. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where was God faithful in your hardest hour yesterday?

days.title: Gratitude After the Excitement Fades

body.p: Psalm 95 opens like the start of a festival. O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. Everyone is invited, and the noise is meant to be loud.

Keep reading past verse 3 and the mood changes sharply. By verse 8 the psalm is warning, Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, remembering the wilderness where Israel quarrelled with Moses about water.

Those were the same people who had sung on the far side of the Red Sea. The excitement of that day faded within weeks, and thirst replaced thanks. The psalm puts the joy and the warning side by side because it knows how quickly one turns into the other.

Notice the name chosen for God here: the rock. In the wilderness, water came out of a rock. The very thing they complained about was where God provided. Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving is an invitation to remember that before the grumbling starts.

The new job, the new church, the new marriage, the new baby. The excitement does fade, and that is not a failure. What matters is what fills the space. Next time you catch a complaint forming on the way to work, turn it into one sentence of thanks to the rock.

after: When the thrill wears off, thanksgiving keeps the heart from hardening.
The place you are tempted to complain about may be the place he is providing.
days.prayer: Lord, the excitement has worn off something you gave me, and I have started to grumble about it. Soften my heart before it hardens. I come before you with thanksgiving, because you are still the rock of my salvation, even when the first joy has gone quiet. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What gift of God has become ordinary enough that you now complain about it?

days.title: Gratitude In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: Psalm 100 is about how to walk into a room. Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise. Worshippers coming up to the temple did not stroll in. They came through the gate already thanking.

Before that, verse 3 tells them who they are. It is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture. Not self made. Not owners of the pasture. Sheep, which is humbling and also restful.

Those two ideas belong together when you have a hard conversation ahead. You are walking into a room as well, perhaps with a husband, a landlord, a pastor, a grown child. And the person across the table is also someone God made, not someone who made themselves.

Going in with thanksgiving changes the temperature. It reminds you that you are not the shepherd of this situation. It softens the urge to win. And verse 5 puts something firm under your feet: his truth endureth to all generations. You do not have to force the whole truth into the room. It will outlast the argument.
Before you knock on that door or press call, thank God for one real thing about the other person. Then go in.

line.b: You are not the shepherd here.

after: The person you dread talking to was made by God, not by themselves.
Thanksgiving at the door lowers the heat inside the room.
days.prayer: Lord, I have a conversation ahead that I would rather avoid. Let me enter it with thanksgiving, not with my arguments sharpened. Remind me that you made me and you made them, and that we both belong to your pasture. Let your truth stand in that room even if I speak it badly. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is one thing you can honestly thank God for about the person you need to talk to?

days.title: Gratitude When Progress Is Slow

body.p: David is not talking to God at the start of Psalm 103. He is talking to himself. Bless the LORD, O my soul, he says, twice, like a man shaking his own shoulder.
Sometimes the soul needs instructions. It does not always rise on its own. It drifts, it forgets, it gets discouraged by how slowly things are moving.

Forgetting is exactly the danger he names. Forget not all his benefits. He does not say, look out for new ones. He says, do not lose hold of the ones you already have. Slow seasons are not usually short of benefits. They are short of memory.

Then the list begins, and the first item is not health or provision. It is Who forgiveth all thine iniquities. Forgiveness comes before healing in the order. If nothing else moves forward this month, that one has already been done in full.

If you are tired of how slowly your recovery, your savings or your child's progress at school is going, speak to your soul the way David did. Out loud if you can, perhaps in the car before you go in. Tell yourself what has already been given. Then keep walking at the pace you have.

line.b: The benefits are not missing, only forgotten.

after: Your soul sometimes needs to be told what to do, and that is allowed.
Forgiveness is a finished benefit, even when everything else is unfinished.
days.prayer: Lord, I am discouraged by how slowly things are changing. I tell my own soul now to bless you and to stop forgetting what you have done. Thank you first that my sins are forgiven, all of them. Give me patience for the rest, at the pace you have chosen. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which of God's benefits has your discouragement made you forget?

days.title: Gratitude At the Point of Decision

body.p: The shortest instruction in this psalm is two words long, and it closes verse 2. Let the redeemed of the LORD say so. If he has rescued you, do not keep it as a private opinion. Say it.

Psalm 107 goes on to tell four stories of rescue: travellers lost in the desert, prisoners in chains, people sick through their own foolishness, sailors in a storm. Each time, they cry out, God delivers, and they are called to give thanks.
To be redeemed is to be bought back. Someone paid to bring you out of the hand of the enemy. That changes who you belong to, and when you belong to someone it shapes the choices you make.

So when you stand at a decision, the job offer, the relationship, the move, saying so is not a small thing. Saying out loud that you are redeemed reminds you that you are not deciding as a free agent with no history. You are deciding as someone who was brought out, and who owes the one who did it.
Before you sign, reply or choose, say it, even if only to the four walls of your room. I am the Lord's redeemed. Then ask what a redeemed person would do here.

after: Speaking your gratitude out loud reminds you whose you are.
A choice made by the redeemed carries a different weight.
days.prayer: Lord, you are good and your mercy endures for ever. I say so now: you redeemed me from the hand of the enemy. As I face this decision, let me choose as someone who belongs to you, not as someone who owns themselves. Give me wisdom that fits the one who bought me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: How would remembering that you were redeemed change the decision in front of you?

days.title: Gratitude In the Waiting Room

body.p: The people in this part of Psalm 107 are lost in the desert. A few verses earlier they found no city to dwell in, and they were so hungry and thirsty that their soul fainted.

Then God led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation. Notice that the right way still went through the desert. He did not lift them out of it. He walked them along a road they could not see.
Waiting rooms feel like that. You are between the place you left and the place you hope to reach, and nothing tells you how long the corridor is.

Verse 9 is gentle with people in that spot. He satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness. It does not scold longing. It assumes you will feel it. Hunger is not a lack of faith. It is the space he means to fill.

If you are sitting in an actual waiting room today, on a plastic chair outside a consulting room or an embassy window, thank him for the right way, even before you can see the city. He has walked others through this desert. He knows where it ends.

line.a: The right way went through the desert.
line.b: It still led to a city.

after: Longing is not unbelief, it is the hunger God means to fill.
You can give thanks for the road before you can see where it arrives.
days.prayer: Lord, I am waiting and I do not know how long. Thank you that you lead by the right way even when it runs through dry ground. You see the longing in me, and you are not ashamed of it. Fill it in your time with your goodness, and keep me thankful while I wait. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What longing are you afraid to admit to God while you wait?

days.title: Gratitude When You Feel Small

body.p: Verse 11 is a confession most of us could sign. I said in my haste, All men are liars. The psalmist had been let down so badly that he decided nobody could be trusted. He admits it was said in a hurry, in a dark mood.
Then he lifts his eyes and asks a different question. What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me? What can I possibly give back?

It is the question of someone who feels very small next to what he has received. The answer he arrives at is surprising. Not a great gift. Not a promise to work harder. I will take the cup of salvation.
The way to repay God, it turns out, is to receive more from him. To take the cup he holds out, and call on his name again. You do not settle the account. You keep drinking.

If you feel small this week, too poor, too ordinary, too far behind to offer God anything worth having, this psalm was written for you. Do what it says. Take, and call. On the walk to the borehole or the train, hold out your empty hands and let that be your thanks.

line.b: So take the cup and say thank you.

after: The smallest person in the room can still hold out a cup.
Receiving from God is not rudeness, it is the answer he asked for.
days.prayer: Lord, I have spoken in haste and grown bitter about people, and I feel small before you. I have nothing to give back for all your benefits. So I will do what you ask. I take the cup of salvation and I call on your name again, with empty hands and a grateful heart. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What have you said in haste about people that God would like to replace with thanks?

days.title: Gratitude Through an Open Door

body.p: Most people know verse 24 from wall plaques and morning songs. It helps to know which day it was talking about. Verse 22 has just said The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.

So the day the Lord has made is a particular kind of day. The day the rejected thing was put in the place of honour. The door that was shut in your face, opened by someone else. This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.

The people do not take credit. They see the door open and they name the one who opened it. Then, in the very next breath, Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD. In Hebrew that cry is hosanna, the word the crowds shouted when Jesus rode into Jerusalem.
Gratitude for an open door does not mean you have stopped needing God. It means you have seen what he can do, and so you ask him again for the next step.
If something has opened for you lately, a place at school, a contract, a friendship mended after years, say clearly whose doing it was. Then walk through it still praying hosanna.

line.a: The rejected stone was set at the corner.
line.b: Name who did it, then ask again.

after: When a door opens, the first word should be about whose doing it was.
Thanks and hosanna belong in the same breath.
days.prayer: Lord, this is your doing and it is marvellous in my eyes. Thank you for the door you opened that I could not open myself. Keep me from taking the credit. And as I walk through, I still need you, so save now, Lord, and guide me in what comes next. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What has God opened for you recently that you have quietly credited to yourself?

days.title: Gratitude When the Answer Is No

body.p: Psalm 136 has the same line twenty six times. For his mercy endureth for ever. A leader would sing out one line of history, and the people would answer with the refrain, over and over.

Read the whole psalm and you notice something uncomfortable. The refrain is not only attached to the pleasant lines. It follows the plagues, the wilderness, the kings who fell. Whatever the line before, the answer is the same.

That is what makes it useful on the day God says no. The no is a line in your story, and it may be a painful one. A prayer you prayed for years, a door that stayed shut, a person who did not recover. The refrain does not deny the pain of the line. It simply refuses to change its answer.
Verse 2 adds that he is the God of gods. Above every other power you might have hoped would rescue you. If he has said no, it is not because something stronger got in his way.

You do not have to like the no. You can cry about it in the corridor outside the ward, or into your pillow tonight. But when you have said the hard line, try answering it the old way. His mercy endures. Still. For ever.

line.a: The line before it may be painful.
line.b: The answer after it does not change.

after: You can say the hard sentence and still sing the refrain after it.
A no from God is not a sign that his mercy has run out.
days.prayer: Lord, you said no to something I wanted badly, and it still hurts. I will not pretend otherwise. But I will answer my hard line with the old refrain: you are good, and your mercy endures for ever. Hold me while I learn to say it and mean it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is the hard line in your story right now, and can you answer it with the refrain?

days.title: Gratitude In What You Already Have

body.p: Daniel's life was on the line. The king had ordered every wise man in Babylon killed, and Daniel was counted among them. Then, in a night vision, God showed him the king's dream.
The first thing he did with the answer was not run to the palace. He stopped and prayed. I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers, who hast given me wisdom and might.

Listen to the pronouns. God hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee, he says, and then thou hast now made known unto us. Me, then we, then us. He had asked his three friends to pray with him, and the thanks includes them. Gratitude remembered who had stood with him.

Then verse 24. His first words to the officer are Destroy not the wise men of Babylon. Not only himself and his friends. The astrologers and magicians too, men who had been no help to him at all. What God had given him, he used straight away for people who had nothing.

You already hold something God has given you, a skill, some knowledge, a little money, a working pair of hands. Stop and thank him for it by name. Then ask who in your office or on your street it could protect today.

line.a: He thanked God for what was in his hands.
line.b: Then he used it to save others.

after: Gratitude remembers the people who prayed with you.
What God has already given you is meant to reach someone else soon.
days.prayer: God of my fathers, thank you for what you have already put in my hands, the wisdom and strength I often treat as my own. Thank you for the people who have prayed with me. Show me today who I can use it for, especially someone who cannot repay me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who could be protected by something God has already given you?

days.title: Gratitude When Nobody Notices

body.p: There is no congregation inside a fish. No one to see Jonah lift his hands, no one to say amen. And yet this is where he says But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving.
He is still inside when he says it. Verse 10 has not happened yet. He is giving thanks in the dark, in a place that smells of seaweed and death, with no sign that he will ever see daylight again.

Verse 8 explains what he has learned. They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy. Chasing empty things means walking away from the mercy that was yours. Jonah had run from God and nearly lost everything. Now he turns back, with nobody watching.
Then he says the line that may be the heart of the whole book. Salvation is of the LORD. Not of Jonah's good behaviour, not of the sailors, not of luck. And straight after, God speaks to the fish.
Much of your faithfulness will go unseen. The prayer whispered on a night shift, the thanks said over a plate of cold food when you are eating alone. Nobody notices. The one who speaks to fish does.

line.a: No one saw him in the dark.
line.b: God heard, and spoke to the fish.

after: Thanksgiving offered where no one can see is still a sacrifice.
Turn from the empty things and you turn back toward your own mercy.
days.prayer: Lord, there are places in my life where nobody sees me, and I sometimes feel forgotten there. I offer you thanks from inside those places anyway. Keep me from chasing empty things and forsaking your mercy. Salvation is yours, not mine, and I trust you to speak at the right time. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What empty thing have you been chasing that has pulled you away from God's mercy?

days.title: Gratitude With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: Ten lepers were told to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went, they were cleansed. They were healed on the road, mid stride, somewhere between Jesus and the temple.
Nine kept walking. That is not a terrible thing in itself. They were doing what they had been told. But one stopped, and Luke gives four quick details about what he did with his body.

He turned back. He used a loud voice. He fell down on his face at his feet. And he was giving thanks the whole time. This is gratitude with feet and lungs and knees, not a pleasant thought kept quietly in the head.

Then Luke adds the sting at the end: and he was a Samaritan. The outsider, the one the others would not have eaten with, was the only one who came back. Sometimes those who expect God's kindness least are the quickest to say thank you.

Gratitude can stay too spiritual, too much in the mind. Try making it physical today. Turn round and go back to someone who helped you. Say thank you loud enough to be heard. Kneel by the bed tonight, even if your knees complain.

line.a: Nine were healed on the road.
line.b: One turned back and fell on his face.

after: Gratitude that never moves your body may not have reached your heart yet.
The outsider who comes back is the one Jesus praises.
days.prayer: Jesus, I have often been healed on the road and kept walking without coming back. Turn me round today. Let my thanks be loud enough to hear and low enough to kneel. And let me not be outdone in gratitude by those I think of as outsiders. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who do you need to turn back to and thank in person?

days.title: Gratitude When You Must Begin Again

body.p: John notices the grass. Now there was much grass in the place. It is the kind of detail only someone who was there would remember, five thousand men settling down on a green hillside.

Then Jesus takes five barley loaves a boy had brought, and before anything happens to them, when he had given thanks. He thanks his Father for an amount that is plainly not enough. The multiplying comes after the thanks, not before.
When everyone has eaten, he says something easy to skip. Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost. The broken pieces mattered to him. They filled twelve baskets.

If you have to start over, after a business failed, after a divorce, after a long illness, you are probably standing among fragments. Pieces of a plan, a little savings, some friendships that survived. It can look like too little to begin with.

Do what Jesus did with too little. Give thanks for it as it is, before it grows. Then pick up the pieces carefully. He does not waste fragments. Tonight, write down what remains, and thank him for each line.

line.a: He gave thanks for too little bread.

after: Beginning again starts with thanks for what is left, not grief for what is lost.
Nothing that remains in his hands is wasted.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I am starting over with less than I had, and some of it is broken. I give you thanks for what remains, even though it looks too small. Take it, bless it, and gather up the pieces of my life so that nothing is lost. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What fragments do you have left that you have not yet thanked God for?

days.title: Gratitude In the Middle of the Work

body.p: Paul had never been to Rome when he wrote this letter. He did not plant the church there and knew only some of its people. Yet the first thing he says after the greeting is First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for you all.
First. Before the long argument of the letter, before the corrections, before he asks them to help him reach Spain. Thanks goes ahead of everything else.

He thanks God that your faith is spoken of throughout the whole world. Other people's good news was enough to make him grateful. He was in the middle of his own hard work, travelling, arguing, collecting money for poor believers, and still he noticed what God was doing in a place he had not been.
Then he calls God as witness that without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers. Gratitude and prayer for others had become part of his working routine, not a break from it.

In the middle of your work, it is easy to see only your own unfinished pile. Try Paul's order. Before you open the files, before the first meeting, thank God for one colleague or one church across town where good things are happening. Put that first.

line.a: Before the argument, before the asking.

after: Someone else's faith is a good reason for your gratitude today.
Put thanks at the top of the work, not at the end of it.
days.prayer: Father, I am in the middle of my work and my own tasks fill my view. Before I start, I thank you for the people whose faith I have heard about, near and far. Teach me to put thanks first and to keep others in my prayers without ceasing, even on busy days. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose faith could you thank God for before you start your own work today?

days.title: Gratitude When Fear Speaks First

body.p: Second Corinthians 9 is about money. Paul is asking a church to give generously for poor believers in Jerusalem, and he knows what fear will say first. If I give, I will not have enough.

So he spends the chapter answering that fear. He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly. And God is able to make all grace abound toward you. He is not promising riches. He is promising that God will not leave a generous heart without what it needs to keep doing good.
Then, at the end, he simply runs out of words. Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift. Unspeakable here means too great to be described. He means Christ himself.
Fear always speaks about what you might lose. Gratitude answers with what you have already been given, and the greatest gift cannot even be measured, so it cannot be taken away.
Next time fear gets the first word, before the bill, at the hospital desk, when the school fees are due, let it speak, and then answer it with Paul's sentence. Out loud if you can.

line.a: Fear counts what you might lose.
line.b: Thanks names a gift too big to count.

after: Let fear have its sentence, then answer it with thanks.
The greatest gift you have cannot be put into words or taken from you.
days.prayer: God, fear has spoken first again this morning, about money and about tomorrow. I hear it, and now I answer it. Thanks be to you for your unspeakable gift, for Christ, who is more than I can describe. Make me generous from that place, not anxious. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is fear saying first to you today, and what would gratitude answer?

days.title: Gratitude With an Open Hand

body.p: In Greek, verses 19 to 21 hang from one command in verse 18, be filled with the Spirit. What follows is a list of what that looks like: speaking, singing, giving thanks, submitting.
Thanks sits in the middle of that list. On one side, songs. On the other, Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God. That is an interesting neighbour for gratitude.

Thankful people find it easier to open their hands. When you know that what you hold was given, you hold it more loosely. You can let someone else go first, have their way, take the credit. The grip relaxes because you are not clinging to things you think you earned.

Paul makes the scope wide. Giving thanks always for all things. Not because every event is good, but because every one of them can be brought to God and trusted to him, the way an open hand trusts the one who fills it.

Notice where your fists are closed today. The parking space, the last word in the family chat, the seat at the front. Thank God for what you have, and then try opening one hand, just one, before evening.

line.a: What was given can be held loosely.

after: Gratitude and humility live next door to each other.
Open one hand today and see what it actually costs you.
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, fill me today. Let thanks come out of me in all things, and let it loosen my grip on what I think I have earned. Teach me to submit to others gladly, to let them go first, because everything I hold came from your hand. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where are your hands clenched today, and what would it take to open one?

days.title: Gratitude When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Just before the famous words about anxiety, Paul drops five short ones. The Lord is at hand. Near. Close by. He might mean near in time or near in place, and probably both.
That matters when you cannot see far ahead. You may not know what next year holds. But you do not need to see far to know who is near.

Then comes Be careful for nothing. In old English, careful meant full of care, anxious. Paul is not telling them to be careless. He is telling them not to be crushed by worry, and he is writing from prison, where he had every reason for it.

Look at where thanksgiving sits. By prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. Thanks is not a separate prayer for later. It goes inside the asking. And the promise is not that you will see further, but that peace will keep your hearts and minds, like a guard at a gate.
Tonight when the worry starts, ask for what you need, plainly. Then add one thank you to each request. You still will not see far. But the guard will be at the door.

after: Put a thank you inside every request today.
Peace does not show you the future, it guards you while you wait for it.
days.prayer: Lord, I cannot see far ahead and I am full of care about it. You are at hand, so I bring you my requests plainly, and I thank you with each one. Let your peace stand guard over my heart and mind tonight, even though I still do not know what is coming. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What request are you bringing to God today, and what thanks can you put inside it?

days.title: Gratitude In the Honest Answer

body.p: Paul mixes his pictures in verse 7, and the mix is the point. Rooted and built up in him. A tree and a building in the same breath. One grows quietly underground. The other is put together stone by stone.
The last phrase is about overflow. Abounding therein with thanksgiving. A rooted, built up life does not just hold thanks. It spills it.

Then verse 8 warns about being plundered. Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit. To spoil, in this old English, is to carry off as loot. Clever ideas can strip a believer of what they were given.

Gratitude is one of the best defences against that. A thankful person keeps remembering where everything came from. Verse 6 has already said it: As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him. Received. When someone offers a smooth explanation that leaves Christ out, the thankful heart gives an honest answer. I did not build this alone, and I did not grow it myself.
If a friend at work or a classmate asks why you still believe, you do not need a lecture. Tell the truth about what you received. Thanks is an honest answer.

line.a: Rooted like a tree, built like a house.
line.b: Overflowing because it was all received.

after: Gratitude keeps you honest about where your life came from.
Clever ideas lose their grip on a heart that remembers its gifts.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I received you as a gift and I want to walk in you the same way. Root me and build me up, and let thanks overflow from me. Guard me from clever words that would carry off what you gave. When people ask, give me an honest and grateful answer. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: If someone asked today where your faith came from, what honest answer would you give?

days.title: Gratitude When the Cost Is Real

body.p: Verse 15 ends with three small words that are easy to miss. And be ye thankful. They come right after a sentence about peace and about being called in one body.

One body means other people. Paul has just been listing what it takes to live with them: bearing with one another, forgiving quarrels, and putting on charity above all these things, like a coat over everything else.

That is the real cost. Not some grand sacrifice, but the daily price of living close to people who irritate you, wound you, or simply see things differently. Forgiving the same brother again. Staying in the church after the hurtful meeting.

The word rule in verse 15 meant to act as umpire. Let the peace of God rule in your hearts. When you are deciding whether to stay or walk out, whether to reply sharply or hold your tongue, let his peace make the call. And then be thankful, even for the people who cost you something.

Think of one person whose place in your life is expensive. A neighbour, an in-law, a co-worker. Before you see them next, thank God for one thing in them. It will not remove the cost. It will change how you pay it.

line.b: Pay it with peace and thanks.

after: Thankfulness is easiest to forget around the people who cost you most.
Let peace be the umpire before you decide how to answer.
days.prayer: Lord, some of the people you have placed me with cost me more than I want to pay. Let your peace be the umpire in my heart today. Clothe me with charity over everything else, and teach me to be thankful even for those I find hard, because you called us into one body. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who is costly to love right now, and what can you thank God for in them?

days.title: Gratitude For the Long Road

body.p: At the end of this letter Paul starts firing off short commands, one after another, like a parent at the door calling out final reminders. Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks. Quench not the Spirit.

Notice the small word. In every thing, not for every thing. Paul is not asking you to be glad that your father has cancer or that the business failed. He is asking you to keep giving thanks while you are in it, because God is still in it with you.

Then he says something people search for their whole lives. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. We often want to know God's will about a job or a marriage. Here is a piece of it, stated plainly, and it fits every road.
The next command is about fire. To quench is to put out. Long roads tend to dampen things, and gratitude is one of the ways the flame is kept going over years, not just weeks.

If you are a long way into something hard, a long marriage, a long illness, a long ministry in a small place, do not try to feel thankful for the whole road. Find one thing in today's stretch of it. That is enough of the will of God for this morning.

line.a: Thanks is not a feeling first.
line.b: It is a choice made in the middle of things.

after: Part of God's will for you is already known, and it can be done today.
Gratitude keeps the fire from going out on a long road.
days.prayer: Lord, this road is long and some of it hurts. I will not pretend I am thankful for all of it. But in it, I give you thanks, because you are here too. Keep the fire of your Spirit burning in me through the years, and help me do the part of your will I already know. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What part of your long road do you need to give thanks in, rather than for?

days.title: Gratitude At the End of the Day

body.p: Hebrews was written to people who had lost things. Some had their property taken, some had been pushed out of their communities. So verse 14 is not a pious phrase for them. For here have we no continuing city. They knew it from experience.
Then the writer tells them what sacrifice looks like now, offered through Jesus rather than at an altar. The fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. Words, offered continually.

But the passage does not stop at lips. To do good and to communicate forget not. In old English, to communicate means to share what you have. Thanks spoken, and goods shared. Both are called sacrifices, and with both God is well pleased.

At the end of a day, or the end of a month of practising gratitude, it is worth asking whether the thanks has reached your hands as well as your mouth. Did it cost anything? Did anyone eat because of it?

Tonight, before you sleep, say thank you for three things from the day. Then think of one thing you can share tomorrow, a meal, a visit, an hour of your time. The city here does not last. What you give from it does.

after: Gratitude that is real eventually becomes generosity.
The city does not last, but what you share from it does.
days.prayer: Lord, at the end of this day I bring you the fruit of my lips. Thank you for what you have given me, here in a city that will not last. Let my thanks reach my hands as well, so that tomorrow I do good and share with someone who needs it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Has your gratitude this month reached your hands as well as your words?

days.title: Joy Before You Feel Ready

body.p: The order of events matters here. The people heard the law read aloud, and all the people wept. They were not wrong to weep. They had just understood how far they had drifted.

Then the leaders told them to stop. Not because tears were bad, but because the day was holy, and holy days in Israel were feasts. Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet. Joy was handed to them as an instruction while their faces were still wet.
That is the surprise. Nobody waited for them to feel ready. The joy came first as something to do, a meal to eat and a plate to send, and the feeling was left to catch up.
Notice whose joy it is, too. the joy of the LORD is your strength. Not your joy in the Lord, which comes and goes, but his own gladness over his people, which holds you up when yours has run out.

So if this morning finds you heavy, do one joyful thing anyway. Cook for someone. Send a portion to the neighbour in the next flat who has nothing prepared. Let the feeling arrive later, the way it did in Jerusalem.

line.a: They were told to feast with wet faces.
line.b: Joy came first, and the feeling followed.

after: You do not need to feel glad in order to obey gladness.
Somebody near you has nothing prepared today, and that is your portion to send.
days.prayer: Lord, I am not ready to rejoice, and you know why. Give me something joyful to do before I feel it. Show me whose table is empty today, and let your own gladness over me be the strength I lean on when mine is gone. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What one joyful thing could you do today before you feel like it?

days.title: Joy In the Next Step

body.p: Peter stood up at Pentecost and quoted this psalm. He said David was not writing about himself here, since David died and was buried, but about the Holy One whose body would not see corruption. The psalm reaches all the way to an empty tomb.
Then comes verse eleven, and it is surprisingly modest. Thou wilt shew me the path of life. Not the whole map. A path, which you only ever see a few steps of at a time.
David is confident about the far end: life, presence, pleasures for evermore. He is humble about the near end. He expects to be shown, which means he does not yet know.
That is the shape of a believer's December. We wait for Christmas knowing how the story goes, a cradle and then a cross and then a garden with an open grave, and still we need showing for Monday.

If you are at a bus stop this morning wondering which way to turn on something, you do not need to see the whole road. Ask to be shown the next stretch. The fulness of joy is not only waiting at the finish. It is in thy presence, and his presence walks with you.

line.b: He still asks to be shown the next step.

after: The resurrection settles the destination. It does not excuse you from asking about Tuesday.
Fulness of joy is found in his presence, and his presence is on the path, not only at the end of it.
days.prayer: Lord, I know where this road ends, because you did not leave your Holy One in the grave. I do not know the next step. shew me the path of life for today, one stretch at a time, and let me find joy in walking it with you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which decision are you trying to see all the way through when you only need the next step?

days.title: Joy When the Way Is Quiet

body.p: The famous line is in verse five, but verse six is the honest one. in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved. David admits he got comfortable, and then something moved him.

So when he writes weeping may endure for a night, he is not offering a slogan. He has spent that night. The Hebrew word behind endure means to lodge, like a guest who arrives late and sleeps in the spare room.

Weeping is allowed to stay the night. It is not allowed to move in. And the joy that follows is not something David goes out to find. It cometh in the morning, the way morning itself comes, without being asked.
Nobody hurries a sunrise. You can lie awake at three o'clock and the dawn will not come one minute sooner. But it does come. The quiet stretch before it is not proof that morning has been cancelled.
If the house is silent tonight and the ache is loud, leave the curtains open. You do not have to produce the morning. You only have to wait for it.

line.b: It does not get to stay for good.

after: The quiet before dawn is still part of the night, and the night still ends.
Comfortable seasons can make us careless, and hard ones can make us honest.
days.prayer: Father, you know the nights I have had and the one I may be in now. I will not pretend the weeping is not real. Teach me to wait for the morning without trying to force it, and when the joy comes, let me remember who sent it. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where have you been trying to hurry a morning that only God can bring?

days.title: Joy Without an Audience

body.p: Psalm thirty two begins with a man who stayed silent about his sin until his bones ached. It ends with a shout. Everything between is the story of a confession made where no one else could hear it.
That is why the joy at the end belongs to the upright in heart. Not upright in reputation. Upright in the place only God sees, where the hiding stopped.

There is a kind of gladness we perform. We post it, we wear it to church, we put it on when the visitors come. David's joy here is not that kind. It comes from a secret that has finally been told to the right person.

Look at what surrounds the forgiven man in verse ten: mercy shall compass him about. Compass means to go all the way round. He is not standing on a stage. He is standing inside a circle of mercy, and the only one looking is the one who drew it.
On your walk to work, or alone at the sink tonight, tell God the thing you have not told him. Then let yourself be glad, even if no one else ever knows why.

line.a: Some joy is performed for others.
line.b: This joy starts with a confession nobody heard.

after: You can shout for joy in an empty room.
Mercy goes all the way round you, even on the side you hide.
days.prayer: Lord, I have kept quiet about things I should have brought to you. I bring them now, with no one watching. Surround me with your mercy, make me upright in heart and not only in appearance, and give me a gladness I do not need to show anyone. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What would it take for you to be glad today with nobody watching?

days.title: Joy For an Ordinary Tuesday

body.p: O clap your hands, all ye people. Hands are a strange place for worship to start. Not the mind, not even the heart, but palms meeting palms, loud enough to hear.

And it is addressed to all people, not only Israel. Nations who had their own gods are told to applaud this one, because he is a great King over all the earth. The word terrible in verse two means awe, the kind that stops you in the middle of a sentence.
Ordinary days do not usually feel like coronations. A Tuesday is laundry, a school run, a queue at the bank. Nothing about it seems to call for clapping.

But the psalm does not ask whether the day is special. It asks whether the King is. If he is great over all the earth, he is great over the bank queue too, and that is reason enough for the body to join in.

Try it, even quietly. In the car before you get out, or at the market stall while the trader counts your change, give thanks with your hands as well as your lips. The body sometimes teaches the heart what it has forgotten.

after: Joy does not wait for an occasion when the King is always on the throne.
Let your hands lead your heart today.
days.prayer: Lord most high, this is an ordinary day and I am an ordinary person. Remind me that you are King over all the earth, including the small corner I will walk through today. Let my hands and my voice give you thanks, even in the plain places. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What ordinary part of today could become a place of praise?

days.title: Joy When Plans Change

body.p: David does not ask for his salvation back. He asks for the joy of thy salvation. He knew the difference. You can belong to God and still lose the gladness of it.
The psalm was written after Bathsheba and Uriah, after a plan that went terribly wrong because David made it go wrong. His life had changed shape, and not in the way he would have chosen.

Look at his first fear in verse eleven: Cast me not away from thy presence. Not cast me out of the palace. His deepest fear was distance from God, and his deepest want was the joy that comes from nearness.
Then something unexpected. Then will I teach transgressors thy ways. The man who failed becomes the man who teaches failures. The broken plan is not wasted. It becomes the very thing he has to offer.

When plans change, whether a job ends or a relationship closes or you are the one who broke something, the first prayer is not for the old plan back. It is for the joy. Pray it on the bus home. Then watch who God sends you to help.

line.a: He did not ask for the old plan back.
line.b: He asked for the joy back.

after: Losing the gladness is not the same as losing God.
Your worst chapter may be what equips you to help someone else.
days.prayer: Lord, my plans changed and some of it was my own doing. Do not cast me away from your presence. Restore the joy I used to know, hold me up with your free spirit, and one day let me help someone else find their way back to you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Have you been asking God for the old plan back when what you need is the joy back?

days.title: Joy In the Work at Hand

body.p: David wrote this in the wilderness of Judah, probably on the run. He is lying awake. When I remember thee upon my bed, he says, and the night watches stretch out ahead of him.

Verse eight holds two grips at once. My soul followeth hard after thee. That is David reaching. thy right hand upholdeth me. That is God holding. The man is clinging and being held in the same breath.

Work is like that. Some days you do the reaching. You show up, you push, you keep going after God in the middle of a long shift. And all the while there is a hand under you that you did not put there.
His joy comes from remembering. Because thou hast been my help, in the past tense, he can sing in the shadow of the wings now. Yesterday's help becomes today's song.
At your desk or your workbench or your stall today, think back to one time God helped you. Name it. Then pick up the next task knowing the same right hand is still there.

after: The work in front of you is not carried by your grip alone.
Remember one past help today, and let it make you glad.
days.prayer: Lord, you have been my help before, and I want to remember it today. While I work, let my soul follow hard after you, and let me feel your right hand holding me up when I am tired. Give me joy in the shadow of your wings, even in an ordinary job. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What past help from God could you remember while you work today?

days.title: Joy When You Need Clarity

body.p: The pictures in verse two move fast. Smoke blown off by wind. Wax going soft by the fire. Things that looked solid a moment ago simply are not there anymore.

Then the turn: But let the righteous be glad. The same presence that melts wax makes the righteous glad. It is not a different God for different people. It is one God, and what you are made of decides how his nearness feels.

Confusion is often a kind of smoke. Fears, rumours, a dozen voices in the family group chat, all hanging in the air so you cannot see the way. The psalm suggests that clarity does not come from staring harder into the smoke. It comes when God arrives and the smoke is driven off.
Verse four gives him a short name, JAH. It is the name we still carry inside the word hallelujah. When everything is foggy, sometimes the shortest prayer is the best one: his name, said plainly.
Before you make the decision you have been circling, stop. Sing something, even under your breath in the corridor. rejoice before him, and let him do the clearing.

line.b: You can wait for the wind.

after: Clarity often comes after worship, not before it.
One name said plainly can clear a crowded mind.
days.prayer: God, my mind is full of smoke today and I cannot see clearly. Drive away what is confusing me the way wind drives away smoke. Let me be glad before you, sing to you, and wait for you to show me the way instead of guessing. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What smoke are you staring into, hoping to see through it on your own?

days.title: Joy One Choice at a Time

body.p: This is an old man's psalm. Earlier he asks God not to forsake him when he is old and grayheaded, and by the end he has decided what he will do with the years he has left.
Count the instruments he names. The psaltery, the harp, his lips, his soul, his tongue. Everything he has is being enlisted, one piece at a time.
And every line starts with a choice. I will also praise thee. My lips shall greatly rejoice. These are not reports of how he feels. They are decisions about what he will do next.

Joy for this man is not a mood that falls on him. It is a hundred small choices, the harp picked up again, the tongue turned toward thy righteousness all the day long. Some of those choices were made while enemies were still seeking his hurt.

You may not own a harp. You have a mouth and the next ten minutes. On the walk to the shop, choose one thing to thank God for out loud. Then choose again an hour later. That is how a whole day of praise is built.

line.a: He did not wait to feel it.
line.b: He said I will, and then said it again.

after: Joy is often made of small decisions repeated.
Whatever you have in your hands can be turned into praise.
days.prayer: O God, I do not always feel like praising you, but I can choose to. Take my lips, my tongue and whatever skill I have, and turn them toward you one choice at a time. Let me talk of your righteousness today, even while some troubles are not yet gone. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is one choice toward joy you could make in the next hour?

days.title: Joy Under Pressure

body.p: Psalm eighty nine starts with singing and ends with a complaint. Further down, Ethan the singer tells God he has made void the covenant and thrown the crown to the ground. The man who wrote these joyful verses was under real pressure, and he did not hide it.

That makes verse fifteen more striking. Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound. The joyful sound was probably the trumpet of the festivals, the call to gather. Blessed are those who recognise it.
Under pressure, we usually stop listening for it. We hear the bills, the diagnosis, the edge in the boss's voice. The joyful sound is still being blown, but it is drowned out.
Ethan anchors his joy in something underneath the circumstances. Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne. The foundation does not crack when your week does.

If you are sitting in a hospital corridor or a tense meeting today, listen for one sound of grace. A kind nurse. A message from a friend. In thy name shall they rejoice all the day, and the name is still the same name in the corridor.

line.b: The joyful sound is still being blown.

after: You can know the joyful sound and still have honest complaints.
God's throne stands on justice, not on how your week is going.
days.prayer: Lord, I am under pressure and some days I feel like you have forgotten your promises. Help me hear the joyful sound anyway. Let me walk in the light of your face, and rest on the justice and mercy that hold your throne up, even when my life feels shaken. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What sound of grace might you be missing because the pressure is so loud?

days.title: Joy After the Excitement Fades

body.p: Isaac Watts took this psalm and turned it into a carol the whole world now sings at Christmas, Joy to the World. He saw in it the coming of the King, and he was not wrong.

But notice where the noise begins. He hath remembered his mercy and his truth. The singing does not start with excitement. It starts with God remembering. Something he promised long ago, he has now done.

That matters after the excitement fades. The decorations come down, the guests go home, and January arrives with its bills. A joy built on a feeling will fade with the tinsel. A joy built on God remembering does not.
The psalmist even repeats himself: with the harp; with the harp. Some things are worth saying twice, like a choir going round the chorus again because once was not enough.

When the noise of a celebration has died down, in a kitchen full of dirty plates or a quiet car after a long day of visiting, sing the old song again. Not because you feel the thrill, but because God has remembered, and that has not changed.

after: The reason for the joy is older than the feeling of it.
Sing the chorus again, because it is still true.
days.prayer: Lord, you have remembered your mercy and your truth, and you sent your Son just as you promised. When the excitement of this season wears off, keep me singing. Let my joy rest on what you have done, not on how I feel when the house goes quiet. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is your joy this month built more on the feeling of the season or on what God has remembered?

days.title: Joy In a Difficult Conversation

body.p: Psalm one hundred is short enough to learn in a morning, and its second verse puts two words side by side that we rarely keep together. Serve the LORD with gladness.

Serving usually sounds like duty. Gladness sounds like rest. The psalm will not let them be separated. Whatever service you owe, it is meant to be carried with a glad heart, and that includes the hard service of honest words.
Then the order: come before his presence with singing. Before you come before anyone else, you come before him. The conversation you are dreading is not the first meeting of the day. This one is.
That changes the temperature. A person who has just been with God is less likely to come out swinging. They have already been seen and loved, so they do not need to win in order to feel safe.

If you have to speak to your landlord, your teenager, or a colleague who hurt you, sit in the car or the stairwell first. Sing one line, or hum it. Then go in, and serve them with your words as gladly as you can.

line.a: Meet God before you meet them.

after: Gladness is not the opposite of honesty.
You do not need to win a conversation you have already brought to God.
days.prayer: Lord, there is a conversation ahead of me that I am dreading. Before I face anyone, I come before you. Fill me with gladness so I do not speak out of fear or anger, and help me serve the other person with words that are true and kind. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who do you need to speak to, and have you come before God about it first?

days.title: Joy When Progress Is Slow

body.p: Right before this passage comes The stone which the builders refused. Something rejected was set in the most important place. it is marvellous in our eyes, the psalmist says, because no one would have planned it that way.

Then the line found on so many fridge magnets: This is the day which the LORD hath made. And straight after it, without a pause, a cry for help. Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD. In Hebrew that cry is hosanna, the very word the crowds shouted when Jesus rode into Jerusalem.
So the psalm rejoices and pleads in the same breath. It does not wait for the work to be finished before it is glad, and it does not pretend the work is finished because it is glad.
Slow progress feels like a stone the builders refused. The business that is not growing. The child still struggling to read. The recovery that comes, when it comes, an inch at a time.
On the slow job in front of you, say both prayers. Thank you for this day. Save now. You are allowed to be glad and still ask for more.

after: Rejoicing does not require the work to be done.
Hosanna is a cry for help that became a song of praise.
days.prayer: Lord, this is the day you have made, and I will be glad in it, even though the progress is slow. I also cry out to you, save now. Help me hold both, thanks and asking, and trust that you can set the rejected stone in its place. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What slow thing in your life needs both your thanks and your hosanna today?

days.title: Joy At the Point of Decision

body.p: The first people to say it were outsiders. then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them. The neighbours noticed before Israel did.

Then Israel takes the words and makes them their own. The LORD hath done great things for us. Only one word changes. Them becomes us. It is a decision to stop watching your own story from the outside.
And straight after it, a request: Turn again our captivity, O LORD. The great things were real, but the return was not finished. Joy and unfinished business sat in the same song.
Decisions can feel that way. You stand between what God has already done and what you still need him to do, and the choice in front of you seems to depend on which of those you look at.
Before you decide, say the sentence with the right pronoun. Write it on a scrap of paper at your kitchen table. The Lord has done great things for me. Then make your choice from there, not from fear.

after: What others can see in your life, you are allowed to believe too.
Gratitude for what is done can steady you for what is not.
days.prayer: Lord, you have done great things for me, not just for other people. Help me believe it as I stand at this decision. Turn again what is still captive in my life, and let me choose from gladness and trust rather than from fear. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Can you say, with your own name in it, what great things God has already done for you?

days.title: Joy In the Waiting Room

body.p: The streams in the south were the dry riverbeds of the Negev. For most of the year they are dust and stones. Then rain falls in the hills, and in a few hours the empty channels are running with water.
That is the picture of hope here. Not a slow trickle but a sudden filling of something that looked dead. And while they wait for it, they keep sowing. They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

Look at the farmer in verse six. He goeth forth and weepeth. Both verbs at once. He walks and he cries, and what he scatters is precious seed, grain his family could have eaten. He plants it anyway, because waiting is not the same as doing nothing.
The harvest is not promised for next week. The verse says he shall come again with rejoicing, and the word doubtless is in there, but the season is God's to choose.

If you are in a waiting room today, at a clinic or an embassy or outside an exam hall, sow something while you wait. A prayer for the stranger beside you. A kind word to the receptionist. Tears and seeds can be carried in the same hand.

after: Waiting does not have to mean doing nothing.
You can weep and sow on the same morning.
days.prayer: Lord, I am waiting and some days I cry while I wait. Teach me to keep sowing, to give what is precious even when I am sad. Fill the dry places in my life the way you fill the streams in the south, in your time, and bring me back with rejoicing. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What seed could you sow while you are still waiting?

days.title: Joy When You Feel Small

body.p: This chapter is read in almost every carol service. A few verses later comes For unto us a child is born. But before the child, Isaiah reaches back to an old story: as in the day of Midian.
Midian was Gideon's battle. God sent home most of the army until only three hundred were left, holding trumpets and jars and torches. The yoke was broken not by the strong but by the few.

That is how God tends to work in this chapter. A great light, yes, but shining on people in the land of the shadow of death. A kingdom without end, yes, but arriving as a baby. The rescue is enormous. The doorway into it is small.
Feeling small is not a disqualification. It may be the exact size God likes to use. Three hundred men. One young mother and a manger. One ordinary person reading this with a heavy shoulder.

Whatever yoke is on you today, the debt, the grief, the job that drains you, remember that the God who broke Midian with a tiny band is not waiting for you to grow bigger. On the walk to work, hand him the burden as you are.

line.a: God sent most of the army home.
line.b: Then the child came small, too.

after: Small is not too small for God.
The light shined on people who were still in the shadow.
days.prayer: Lord, I feel small today and my burden feels heavy. Remind me of Midian, and of the child born in Bethlehem. Break the yoke I cannot break, shine your light into my shadow, and use me as I am, not as I wish I were. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where have you assumed you are too small for God to use?

days.title: Joy Through an Open Door

body.p: Isaiah twelve is a song for in that day, the day of rescue. And in the middle of it is a working image: with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation.

Drawing water is labour. Anyone who has fetched water from a borehole or a village well knows the rope, the weight, the walk home. Yet this is done with joy, because the well is full and it belongs to you.
And the wells are plural. Not one narrow opening but many. Salvation is not a door that barely opens. It is a whole field of wells, and you are invited to every one.

Notice what happens once the bucket is up. declare his doings among the people. The joy does not stay at the well. It walks out into the street. Someone who has drunk deeply wants to tell the neighbours where the water is.
If a door has opened for you this year, a job, a recovery, a reconciliation, do not just walk through it quietly. Tell someone at the table tonight what God did. Let your gladness point to the well.

line.b: It is glad work when the well is full.

after: The door God opens is meant to be talked about.
Go back to the well today, because it has not run dry.
days.prayer: Lord, you are my salvation and my song. Thank you for every door you have opened. Teach me to draw from your wells with joy, and then to tell others what you have done, so they can find the same water. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Who could you tell this week about a door God has opened for you?

days.title: Joy When the Answer Is No

body.p: The first word of this passage is a refusal. No lion shall be there. On the road home to Zion, some things are simply not allowed.

We do not usually think of a no as a gift. We want doors opened, prayers answered our way, plans approved. But this road is safe precisely because of what God has said no to. No lion. No ravenous beast.

That does not make every no in your life easy to understand. Some refusals hurt for years and are never explained. Isaiah does not pretend otherwise. He only says that on the road the redeemed walk, there are things God keeps off it.

And look how the passage ends. sorrow and sighing shall flee away. Sorrow is the one running now. It chased us for a long time. One day it turns and runs, and everlasting joy upon their heads is worn like a crown.

If you are holding a no today, a rejection letter, a refused visa, a doctor's careful words, you do not have to pretend it is good. Carry it onto the road anyway. Walk, as the redeemed walk, one step at a time toward Zion.

line.a: Some things are not allowed on the road.
line.b: Sorrow will be the one that runs.

after: Not every no is explained, but the road is still safe.
Joy will one day be worn, not chased.
days.prayer: Lord, I received a no and it hurts. I do not understand all of it. Help me trust that you keep some things off my road for my good, and give me strength to keep walking. Let me look forward to the day when sorrow and sighing flee away. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Which no in your life are you still waiting for God to explain?

days.title: Joy In What You Already Have

body.p: Two small words carry verse thirteen. Instead of the thorn. instead of the brier. God does not move his people to a new garden. He grows something new in the same ground.
The fir tree comes up where the thorn was. The myrtle, a sweet smelling shrub Israel cut for its feasts, comes up where the brier tore at people's ankles. Same soil, same field, different harvest.

That is a quiet word for anyone who keeps waiting for a different life before they can be glad. The joy of verse twelve, mountains singing and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands, happens on the road out of where you already are.
And it is all tied to God's word in verse eleven. it shall not return unto me void. What he has spoken over you is already working in the ground you have, even if all you can see for now is thorns.
Look around your room, your street, your office today. Name one thing you already have that you have only ever seen as a thorn. Ask God what he might grow there instead.

line.a: He does not change the field.
line.b: He changes what grows in it.

after: God's word is already at work in the ground you stand on.
The thorn's place can become the myrtle's place.
days.prayer: Lord, I keep thinking I need a different life before I can be glad. Open my eyes to what you are growing where I am. Where there are thorns, plant fir trees, and where there are briers, plant myrtle. Let your word do its work in me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What thorn in your present life might God be planning to replace rather than remove you from?

days.title: Joy When Nobody Notices

body.p: Count the losses in verse seventeen. No blossom on the fig tree. No fruit on the vine. The olive fails. The fields yield nothing. The flock is gone. The stalls are empty. Six things, one after another, like a farmer walking his land and finding every corner bare.
Nobody throws a party for a failed harvest. There is no audience for this kind of loss, just a man standing in an empty field at evening.
Then one word. Yet I will rejoice in the LORD. Not because the fields came back. They did not. He rejoices in the God of my salvation, who was still there when everything else had gone.

And something odd happens at the end. A note for the chief singer on my stringed instruments. The private prayer of a man alone in a ruined field was handed to the choir. What nobody noticed became a song sung for centuries.
Maybe your loss is the quiet kind. A business that slowly closed. A friendship that faded. If no one has noticed, God has. Say your own yet tonight, at the bedside or on the walk home.

line.a: No one saw the empty field.

after: Joy in God can stand where the harvest did not.
Your quiet faithfulness may become someone else's song.
days.prayer: Lord, some of my fields are empty and few people know. Even so, I choose to be glad in you, because you are still the God who saves me. Be my strength, make my feet steady on high and difficult places, and let my quiet faith mean something in your sight. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is your yet, the place where you can choose God even though the harvest failed?

days.title: Joy With Both Feet on the Ground

body.p: Mary has just travelled into the hill country to see Elizabeth. She is young, pregnant, and not yet married, with a story most people in Nazareth would not believe. And this is what comes out of her mouth: My soul doth magnify the Lord.

Her joy is not floating. It has its feet in the dust of her real situation. he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden. She does not pretend to be important. She knows exactly how small she is, and that is what amazes her.
Regarded means looked at, noticed. God saw a girl from a village nobody respected and chose her. Her rejoicing is the joy of someone who has been seen.

There is a kind of spiritual joy that tries to rise above life. Mary's does the opposite. It stays on the ground and finds God there, in the low estate, with the gossip and the long road to Bethlehem still ahead of her.

This week, in the queue at the supermarket or on a crowded bus, remember you are seen. You do not have to feel big for God to look at you. Let your soul magnify him from exactly where you are standing.

line.a: She knew how small she was.
line.b: She knew she had been seen.

after: Grounded joy does not deny the low estate. It finds God in it.
You are regarded, even in the queue.
days.prayer: Lord, like Mary I am not important in the eyes of the world. Thank you that you have regarded me anyway. Let my soul magnify you today from where I really am, with my real troubles, and let my joy be honest and rooted, not pretended. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Where in your ordinary life do you most need to know that God has noticed you?

days.title: Joy When You Must Begin Again

body.p: The shepherds were working the night shift. Nothing about their evening was meant to change history. Then the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.
The angel's first words are Fear not. Then the news: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour. Two small phrases in there change everything. Unto you. This day.
Unto you means the shepherds, men whose work kept them on the edges of town and away from the temple courts. This day means not someday. A beginning had happened while they were minding sheep.
Every Christmas is a reminder that God begins again with something tiny. Not an army or a palace, but a newborn in a manger. The greatest fresh start in history weighed a few kilograms.

If you need to start over, after a failure, a divorce, a lost year, you do not have to wait for January. The angel said this day. Begin with something small: a phone call, an apology, a prayer at the cooker before the family wakes.

after: Fresh starts in God's story usually begin small.
The good tidings were for night shift workers first.
days.prayer: Lord, I need to begin again and I am afraid. Speak your fear not to me. Thank you that the Saviour was born for people like the shepherds, and like me. Help me take one small step today toward the new start you are offering. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What small beginning could you make this day rather than waiting for someday?

days.title: Joy In the Middle of the Work

body.p: The seventy came back from their mission thrilled. Even the devils had obeyed them. They had seen results, and the results were spectacular.

Jesus does not deny the results. He gave them the power. But he redirects their joy. in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you. but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.

Results change. Some weeks the work goes brilliantly, and some weeks nothing moves. If your joy is tied to outcomes, it will rise and fall with every report. A name written in heaven does not rise and fall.

Then Luke tells us something rare. In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit. Jesus is glad, and what makes him glad is that the Father has shown these things to babes, not to the clever. He rejoices in grace, not in performance.

In the middle of a project, a semester, a busy season at the shop, check where your joy is anchored. Write your name at the top of today's list and remember it is written somewhere far more permanent.

after: Do the work, but do not let the work be the reason for your joy.
Jesus rejoiced over grace given to ordinary people.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I am in the middle of the work and I keep measuring my joy by how it is going. Teach me to rejoice that my name is written in heaven. Let me share your gladness over the Father's grace to ordinary people, including me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Is your joy this week resting on results or on your name written in heaven?

days.title: Joy When Fear Speaks First

body.p: It is the night before the cross. Judas has gone out. Jesus knows what the next day holds. And this is when he says These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you.
My joy. Of all the things Jesus could have offered that night, he offered his own gladness. Not a lesser copy for disciples, but the joy he had in loving the Father and being loved by him.
Fear was speaking loudly in that room. Peter would deny him within hours. The others would scatter. Jesus spoke first anyway, and his words were meant to be a shelter for when fear got its turn.
And the joy is tied to something practical. That ye love one another, as I have loved you. Full joy is not a private feeling. It grows where people keep loving each other on frightening nights.

When fear speaks first in your morning, before the alarm has finished ringing, answer it with his words. Then do one loving thing for someone in your house. Make the tea. Hold the door. Joy remains where love is obeyed.

after: The joy Jesus offers is his own, not a smaller version.
Love one person well today and watch what happens to fear.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, fear often speaks before I am even awake. Let your words reach me first. Thank you for giving me your own joy, on the very night you faced the cross. Help me abide in your love and love the people around me as you have loved me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What is fear saying to you this morning, and what has Jesus already said?

days.title: Joy With an Open Hand

body.p: On Christmas Day it is worth remembering that the first Christmas included labour pains. Jesus himself uses the picture. A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come.

He does not soften it. The anguish is real. But as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world. The pain is not denied. It is swallowed up.
Mary knew that on the night in Bethlehem. And the disciples were about to know it another way, through the sorrow of the cross and the joy of seeing him again.

Then comes the phrase for an open hand. your joy no man taketh from you. Most of what we enjoy today could be taken. The food will be eaten, the gifts will wear out, the visitors will go home. We grip them tightly because we know that.

This joy is different. No one can take it, so you do not have to clutch it. Hold your Christmas loosely. Share the rice, give away the extra, sit with the relative who is grieving. The joy that came with the child is not going anywhere.

line.a: Most things we hold can be taken.
line.b: This joy cannot, so open your hand.

after: The first Christmas had labour pains, and joy came anyway.
You do not have to grip what no one can take.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you for being born into the world. Thank you that your joy is one no one can take from me. Help me hold everything else loosely today, to share freely, and to stay close to anyone around me who is sorrowing this Christmas. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: What are you gripping today that you could hold with an open hand?

days.title: Joy When You Cannot See Far

body.p: Verse fifteen sounds simple. Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep. Most people find the second half easier.

Weeping with someone feels noble. We bring food to a funeral, we sit by a hospital bed. But rejoicing with someone whose good news is the very thing you wanted, the engagement, the promotion, the baby, can be much harder.

Paul knew it. The next verse moves straight to the heart. Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Envy is a way of minding high things, of measuring yourself against others.

You may not be able to see far into your own future right now. Whether your turn will come, you do not know. But you can see the person in front of you, and you can be glad for them today without knowing how your own story ends.
When a friend's good news lights up your phone, before the twinge settles in, reply with joy. Mean it as best you can. Then tell God honestly about your own longing, later, in private.

line.a: You cannot see your own road very far.
line.b: You can see the person beside you.

after: Rejoicing with others is a quiet act of trust.
Your longing can be honest without making their joy smaller.
days.prayer: Lord, it is hard for me to rejoice with some people right now, because they have what I long for. Help me be glad for them sincerely. Keep me from minding high things, and hold my own longing gently while I wait for what I cannot yet see. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.question: Whose good news are you finding it hard to rejoice in, and why?

days.title: Joy In the Honest Answer

body.p: Paul reaches back to Isaiah: There shall be a root of Jesse. Jesse was David's father, and a root is what is left after a tree has been cut down. It is an Advent picture, life coming up from a stump.

Then the prayer. Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing. The title is unusual. God of hope. And the joy comes in believing, not in seeing. It is poured into people who still have questions.

The next verse is honest in a way that surprises. Paul tells the Romans they are able also to admonish one another. Joy and correction in neighbouring sentences. A joyful church is not one where nobody says anything hard.
Sometimes the most joyful thing a friend can do is give you the honest answer. Not the flattering one, not the safe one, but the true one, spoken by someone who believes God is still at work in you.
